scenarios.title: Why allowlisting, not another detector?
scenarios.situation: The interviewer leans in: “We already have an EDR. Convince me in ninety seconds that default-deny allowlisting is worth the operational pain.” Two engineers on the panel run detection tooling today, so the answer has to respect their work while making the prevention case.
scenarios.prompt: What is the strongest ninety-second answer?
evidence: Signature and behavior engines classify AFTER execution begins — fileless, living-off-the-land, and zero-day techniques execute before a verdict exists.
Default-deny asks one question before anything runs: is this explicitly trusted? Unknown code — ransomware, novel malware, rogue scripts — is denied without needing a signature.
EDR is still valuable: telemetry, hunting, and forensics. Allowlisting does not replace detection; it shrinks what detection must chase by preventing most execution in the first place.
choices: EDR is obsolete — allowlisting detects everything faster and cheaper

Allowlisting inverts the burden: instead of recognizing every bad thing, you approve the known-good and deny the rest by default, which stops fileless and zero-day execution that detectors must observe first; EDR then focuses on a much smaller, higher-signal workload
Allowlisting is mainly a compliance checkbox that looks good in audits
Both approaches are identical; the choice is just vendor preference
scenarios.why: This answer states the philosophical core — deny-by-default shifts the problem from enumerating badness, which can never be complete, to approving known-good, which is finite — while respecting the panel’s EDR expertise instead of dismissing it. Interviewers at a Zero Trust company listen for exactly that framing: prevention first, detection as the backstop.
scenarios.hint: Which list is smaller: everything malicious that could ever exist, or everything this business needs to run?

scenarios.title: “What do you know about us?”
scenarios.situation: “Walk me through what you know about ThreatLocker.” The hiring manager wants specifics, not slogans. You have sixty seconds before they move on, and they can tell instantly who did the homework.
scenarios.prompt: Which answer shows genuine preparation?
evidence: Founded 2017 in Orlando, Florida by Danny Jenkins (CEO), Sami Jenkins (COO), and John Carolan.
Zero Trust endpoint platform built on deny-by-default; sold heavily through the MSP channel to 70,000+ organizations.
Allowlisting, Ringfencing, Storage Control, Elevation Control, Network Control, Web Control, and the Cyber Hero MDR team.
$190M Series F in July 2026; a free six-week Zero Trust Cybersecurity Bootcamp; the annual Zero Trust World conference in Orlando.
choices: They are an antivirus company from California that sells to consumers

Founded 2017 in Orlando: a Zero Trust endpoint platform on deny-by-default — Allowlisting, Ringfencing, Storage, Elevation, and Network Control plus the Cyber Hero MDR team — sold through MSPs to 70,000+ organizations, fresh off a $190M Series F
They make firewalls and VPNs for large enterprises
A startup with no public funding history or community programs
scenarios.why: Concrete facts — founding year and city, the deny-by-default model, the product names, the MSP channel, a recent milestone — signal homework. Vague praise or wrong facts (consumer AV, California, firewalls) signal the opposite, and interviewers keep score.
scenarios.hint: Name the year, the city, the philosophy, and at least three products.

scenarios.title: Explain Ringfencing to a CFO
scenarios.situation: The panel asks you to explain Ringfencing to a non-technical executive in under a minute. The CFO cares about risk and cost, not process trees or API hooks. Everyone in the room will remember whether you translated or lectured.
scenarios.prompt: Which explanation lands?
evidence: Ringfencing constrains what an ALLOWED application may do: which other apps it can launch, which files and registry keys it can touch, and where on the network it can go.
Most ransomware does not arrive as malware — it hijacks trusted tools like Word or PowerShell. Ringfencing keeps those tools on a leash.
“Word is allowed to run, but it may not launch PowerShell, read the credential store, or phone home — so a hijacked Word cannot become ransomware.”
choices: Ringfencing is a kernel-level API-hooking framework that intercepts NT syscalls via a minifilter driver and evaluates IRP_MJ_CREATE operations against a policy DAG…

Word is allowed to run, but Ringfencing keeps it on a leash: it cannot launch PowerShell, read the credential store, or reach the internet — so even a compromised Word cannot turn into ransomware, which is how most modern attacks actually start
Ringfencing blocks all Microsoft Office applications for security
Ringfencing is the same thing as antivirus signatures, just renamed
scenarios.why: Executives buy outcomes, not mechanisms. The winning answer translates the four restriction dimensions into one vivid business image — a trusted tool on a leash — and ties it to how attacks really work. Jargon-first answers lose the room; wrong answers (blocking Office entirely) lose the interview.
scenarios.hint: If the CFO remembers one sentence after you leave, what should it be?

scenarios.title: The local-admin request
scenarios.situation: A department head asks IT to make her whole team local admins “to stop the UAC prompts.” The ticket lands with you ten minutes before the panel’s scenario round, and you know they will ask how you handled it.
scenarios.prompt: What is the Zero Trust answer?
evidence: Permanent local-admin rights turn every compromised account into a domain-wide incident; most privilege escalation starts from standing admin.
Just-in-time elevation grants a SPECIFIC approved application admin rights for a specific user, time-boxed — no admin credentials exposed, no standing rights restored.
An elevated app can spawn other tools. Ringfence the elevated process so it cannot hop to PowerShell or cmd.
choices: Grant local admin to the team — productivity first, audit later
Refuse outright and close the ticket with no alternative

Offer just-in-time Elevation Control: elevate only the approved application they actually need, time-boxed, with the elevated process ringfenced against hopping to PowerShell or cmd — and every elevated session logged
Tell them to disable UAC on their machines
scenarios.why: The Zero Trust move is least privilege with usability preserved: scope the elevation to the app, bound it in time, ringfence it, and audit it. Blanket admin restores the exact risk the company exists to remove; a flat refusal without an alternative fails the service test the panel is also scoring.
scenarios.hint: What does the team actually need — admin rights, or one app that runs elevated?

scenarios.title: The angry customer wants the policy off
scenarios.situation: A customer on a support call demands you disable the blocking policy “right now” because payroll software is frozen on twelve machines. Their tone is rising. You can see the deny events in Unified Audit: the updater’s child MSI is unsigned and unmatched by any rule.
scenarios.prompt: What is the best response?
evidence: Unified Audit shows exactly what was denied and why: the updater’s child MSI is unsigned and unmatched by any rule.
The customer is not wrong to be upset — payroll is down. Empathy and a timeline rebuild trust faster than defensiveness.
Disabling the policy to clear the symptom trades a payroll delay for an open endpoint. The narrow fix is a scoped rule for the signed updater plus its child process.
choices: Disable the policy immediately to restore service, then re-enable it later

Acknowledge the urgency, give a concrete timeline, use Unified Audit to identify the blocked child process, and apply a scoped rule for the signed updater — validating the install works while unrelated unsigned code stays denied
Tell the customer the block is correct and end the call
Blame the customer’s software vendor for shipping an unsigned installer
scenarios.why: Cyber Hero culture is prevention plus service: translate the technical state into plain language, set expectations, and fix narrowly. Disabling the control solves the ticket and creates the incident; lecturing the customer solves neither. The double validation — good path works, denied path stays denied — is what separates a fix from a bypass.
scenarios.hint: The audit already told you the precise, narrow fix. What does the customer need to hear first?

scenarios.title: “Do we still need the VPN?”
scenarios.situation: In the technical round, an infrastructure engineer asks: “We run a traditional VPN concentrator for remote access. Why would Zero Trust Network Access change anything?” They want architecture reasoning, not a brochure.
scenarios.prompt: Which answer shows you understand the network-control story?
evidence: A VPN concentrator is an open inbound port and a trusted tunnel: authenticate once, roam the flat network. It is a favorite initial-access target.
ZTNA brokers per-session, per-application connections — commonly over port 443 — with no open inbound ports and no implicit trust after authentication.
Network Control is the host-based firewall foundation; ZTNA extends deny-by-default from the endpoint to network access itself.
choices: VPNs are fine; ZTNA is just marketing for the same tunnel

A VPN opens an inbound port and grants broad network trust after one login; ZTNA brokers per-app, per-session connections with no open inbound ports and no standing trust — it applies the same deny-by-default philosophy to network access that allowlisting applies to execution
ZTNA means removing all firewalls
The answer is to buy a bigger VPN concentrator
scenarios.why: The parallel is the point: allowlisting denies unknown execution, ZTNA denies unknown network access. Naming the concrete weaknesses of VPN posture — open inbound ports, flat trust after authentication — shows you think in Zero Trust terms rather than product slogans, which is exactly what the infrastructure engineer is testing.
scenarios.hint: Apply “never trust, always verify” to the network path the same way allowlisting applies it to the file path.

scenarios.title: The unknown updater
scenarios.situation: Approval Center shows a user request: “Acme Updater 4.2” — unsigned, first seen in the environment, requested by Finance ten minutes before month-end close. The hash matches nothing in your catalog. Neither trust nor malice is established.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct triage sequence?
evidence: Unsigned, unknown hash, first-seen, urgent business need. Neither trust nor malice is established — this is a question, not a verdict.
A one-button cloud VDI sandbox can detonate the installer and log AV-vendor flags, canary-file access, and registry/system changes before any production decision.
Certificate rules outrank hash rules; hash outranks path. An unsigned first-seen binary earns no standing rule today.
choices: Approve it by path — Finance needs it now
Deny it permanently and close the request
Detonate it in the Testing Environment first, review the risk-center findings, then decide: clean behavior earns a narrowly scoped rule, suspicious behavior earns a deny with documented evidence
Approve the hash globally so nobody is blocked again
scenarios.why: Unknown does not mean malicious, and urgent does not mean trusted. The sandbox turns a guess into observed behavior; the scoped rule gives Finance a path forward without granting a permanent, global exception for an unsigned binary. Urgency never upgrades the rule.
scenarios.hint: You need evidence, not a coin flip. What tool turns “unknown” into “observed”?

scenarios.title: “Why ThreatLocker — why not somewhere bigger?”
scenarios.situation: The hiring manager asks the motivation question with an edge: 'You could work at a much larger security company. Why us?' The panel watches for sincerity versus flattery. You have ninety seconds.
evidence: Whether your interest is specific (this company's mission, model, stage) or generic (any security job). Specificity is sincerity's evidence.

The deny-by-default philosophy as a technical conviction, the MSP-channel mission (protecting the 70,000+ organizations that can't staff a SOC), the growth stage ($190M Series F — building, not maintaining).
Flattery ('you're the best!'), money-talk, or trashing larger companies. None of them answer 'why THIS company.'
scenarios.prompt: What is the strongest ninety-second answer?
choices: ThreatLocker is the best cybersecurity company in the world and I've always wanted to work here

Deny-by-default is the security model I believe in technically — I've run the triage loop in my homelab and seen the difference judgment-first prevention makes; the MSP mission means protecting organizations that can't staff a SOC themselves, which is impact at scale; and at this growth stage I'd be building, not maintaining — that's the work I want
The pay and benefits are very competitive
Large companies are too bureaucratic and slow
scenarios.hint: What is SPECIFIC to this company in your answer — and what is it specific ABOUT YOU?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it gives three specific, verifiable reasons (philosophy as technical conviction with homelab evidence, the MSP mission as impact, the growth stage as the work desired) — each tied to the candidate, none flattering or generic. A is wrong: superlative flattery with no specifics is the insincerity signal. C is wrong: leading with compensation answers a different question than the one asked. D is wrong: trashing larger companies is unprofessional and says nothing about why THIS company.

scenarios.title: The ThreatLocker Interview Prep Mystery
scenarios.situation: Users report that ThreatLocker Interview Prep is not working correctly. The obvious checks pass — the components are online, basic connectivity works. You need to think in systems, not symptoms.
scenarios.prompt: Using the systems anatomy method (whole → cut open → step through → pull apart), how would you systematically trace a failure in ThreatLocker Interview Prep?
choices: Walk the full journey: start from the trigger, verify each handoff in sequence, check dependencies at every step, and isolate where the flow breaks — then examine that specific layer
Restart all components — ThreatLocker Interview Prep issues are always fixed by restarting
Check the most common cause from memory and apply that fix immediately
Escalate to senior support — ThreatLocker Interview Prep is too complex to troubleshoot systematically
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Systems thinking means tracing the living flow: (1) Whole: what is ThreatLocker Interview Prep supposed to do end-to-end? (2) Cut open: what are the layers/stages? (3) Step through: verify each handoff — where does the expected output diverge from actual? (4) Pull apart: isolate the broken layer and examine it in detail. This method works for any ThreatLocker Interview Prep failure in Tl Interview.
scenarios.hint: Don't jump to the fix. First map the journey, then find where it breaks.
objectives: Apply systems anatomy to ThreatLocker Interview Prep
evidence: All ThreatLocker Interview Prep components report 'online'. Basic health checks pass.
Functionality is broken despite green status indicators. The failure is in the flow, not the components.

scenarios.title: The follow-up: “What don't you know about us?”
scenarios.situation: You nail the company brief. The interviewer smiles: 'Good homework. Now — what DON'T you know about us? What's the gap in your research?' The panel watches how you handle the edge of your knowledge.
evidence: Intellectual honesty and self-awareness: can you map the boundary of your knowledge without bluffing or collapsing?
Name a real gap ('I know the product stack publicly, but I don't know how the teams are organized internally — that's a question for you'), show how you'd close it, and turn it into curiosity.
Bluffing ('I pretty much know everything'), false modesty ('I know nothing'), or naming a gap that's actually a basic ('I don't know what year you were founded' — after nailing it).
scenarios.prompt: How do you answer?
choices: I think my research was pretty comprehensive — I can't think of gaps

Name a genuine boundary: 'I know the public stack and philosophy well, but I don't know how the Cyber Hero team structures its shifts, or how product feedback flows from MDR to engineering — those are insider workings I'd love to hear about.' Then ask them
I don't really know much beyond the website
Make up an insightful-sounding gap
scenarios.hint: They just watched you nail the brief. What does an HONEST boundary sound like — specific, real, and curious?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it names a genuine, specific boundary (internal workings, not public facts), shows the shape of the gap precisely, and converts it into curiosity — honesty plus engagement. A is wrong: 'no gaps' after a 60-second brief is either arrogance or bluffing. C is wrong: false modesty contradicts the brief you just delivered. D is wrong: inventing a gap is bluffing with extra steps — at a security company, fatal.

scenarios.title: The MSP channel question
scenarios.situation: 'We sell primarily through MSPs. Why does that matter — for the product, and for this role?' The interviewer wants to know if you understand the business, not just the tech.
evidence: The customers are IT providers serving many small/mid businesses: the product must be multi-tenant manageable, the support must scale across providers, and the 'customer' is often two layers deep.
Design for manageability at scale: policies that deploy across tenants, audit that serves the MSP's reporting needs, and a learning curve an MSP technician can climb.
Every support interaction may involve an MSP technician advocating for THEIR client: empathy for two audiences, and communication that the MSP can relay. The Cyber Hero standard, doubled.
scenarios.prompt: Why does the MSP channel matter?
choices: It's just a sales strategy; it doesn't affect the work

The MSP channel means the product must be multi-tenant manageable and support must serve two layers (the MSP and their client) — for this role, that means every interaction may involve a technician advocating for their client, so communication has to be relayable and empathy runs two deep
MSPs are middlemen; direct sales would be better
It means the product is simpler than enterprise tools
scenarios.hint: Two layers of customer. What does that demand from the product — and from YOU?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it understands the channel's operational consequences (multi-tenancy, two-layer support, relayable communication) and connects it to the role directly. A is wrong: 'just sales' misses that the channel shapes the product and the job. C is wrong: second-guessing the go-to-market in the interview is presumptuous and irrelevant. D is wrong: 'simpler' misreads the channel — MSP products are manageability-complex, not simple.

scenarios.title: The growth-stage question
scenarios.situation: 'We just raised a $190M Series F. What does that tell you about working here versus a public company?' They're testing whether you understand growth-stage reality.
evidence: Late-stage private: significant scale (70,000+ orgs via MSPs) with startup velocity still — building systems, not maintaining them; ambiguity is normal; ownership is wide.
More building, less process; more ownership, less structure; faster change, more ambiguity. The candidate who wants this names the tradeoffs as attractions, not surprises.
Money-talk ('great runway!') or naivety ('so everything's figured out?'). The mature read is operational: what the stage means for the WORK.
scenarios.prompt: What does the Series F tell you?
choices: It means the company is basically a public company now — stable and process-driven

Late-stage growth means building over maintaining: I'd expect wide ownership, real ambiguity, systems still being built — which is exactly the work I want; the tradeoff is less structure, and I'm choosing that deliberately
It means great job security and big bonuses
It doesn't really affect day-to-day work
scenarios.hint: Series F, 70,000+ orgs, still private. What does that combination mean for the WORK — and is that what you want?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it reads the stage operationally (building, ownership, ambiguity), names the tradeoffs honestly, and connects them to motivation — the mature growth-stage answer. A is wrong: Series F private is not 'basically public' — the velocity and ambiguity differ materially. C is wrong: leading with compensation answers a question not asked. D is wrong: the stage profoundly affects day-to-day work; claiming otherwise signals naivety.

scenarios.title: The Orlando question
scenarios.situation: 'We're in-office five days in Orlando. How do you feel about that?' The interviewer is direct. Your situation: you're relocating and aligned — but the panel wants to hear it, not assume it.
evidence: Alignment without hedging: the policy is stated, and they want a clear answer — not a negotiation, not a sigh.

Direct affirmation with the reason: 'I'm relocating to the area and I want the collaboration density — mentorship, hallway debugging, culture transmission. That's part of why I'm here.' Aligned AND understanding the why.
Hedging ('I guess that's fine'), negotiating ('could I do hybrid?'), or complaining about the commute you haven't started.
scenarios.prompt: How do you answer?
choices: I guess that's fine — I can make it work

Directly: 'I'm aligned — I'm relocating to the area, and I want the in-person collaboration: mentorship, faster debugging together, actually absorbing the culture. The policy is part of the attraction, not a concession.'
Could we discuss hybrid after the probation period?
I prefer remote but I'll do what's required
scenarios.hint: They stated the policy plainly. What does a plain answer sound like — and what does hedging signal?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it's direct, gives the substantive reason (collaboration density, mentorship, culture), and frames the policy as attraction — no hedging, no negotiation. A is wrong: 'I guess' hedging signals reluctant compliance. C is wrong: negotiating the stated policy in the interview signals you didn't hear it. D is wrong: 'prefer remote but' is the hedge with a bow on it.

scenarios.title: The competitor question
scenarios.situation: 'How are we different from [large endpoint vendor]?' The interviewer names a competitor. You must differentiate without trashing — and without naming them back incorrectly.
evidence: Philosophy-first differentiation: deny-by-default prevention versus detection-led models — then the MSP-channel mission and the Cyber Hero service standard as the business differentiation.
Differentiate on YOUR strengths, never on their weaknesses: 'we lead with prevention; they lead with detection' — not 'their product misses things.' Trash-talk is disqualifying.
Don't invent their roadmap or metrics. Differentiate on public, verifiable positioning — philosophy, channel, service model.
scenarios.prompt: How do you differentiate?
choices: Their product is weaker — everyone knows their detection misses zero-days

The core difference is philosophical: deny-by-default prevention first — we approve the known-good and deny the rest, which stops what detection must observe first. On top of that, the MSP-channel mission and the Cyber Hero service standard: prevention plus white-glove response for the organizations that can't staff a SOC
We're basically the same; it's just marketing
I don't follow competitors
scenarios.hint: Name the differentiation WITHOUT naming their flaws. What's left — and is it enough?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it differentiates on philosophy (verifiable positioning), adds the business differentiation (channel + service), and never trashes — professional and substantive. A is wrong: trashing the competitor is disqualifying regardless of technical merit. C is wrong: 'basically the same' surrenders the entire positioning question. D is wrong: 'don't follow competitors' signals unawareness in a competitive market.

scenarios.title: The bootcamp question
scenarios.situation: 'We run a free six-week Zero Trust bootcamp. Why would a company give away training for free?' The interviewer tests whether you see the strategy — and the culture.
evidence: Community as go-to-market: educated practitioners recommend, deploy, and champion the philosophy — the bootcamp builds the market's literacy in YOUR model. Talent pipeline too.
Teaching freely signals confidence and generosity: a company that educates the market — including non-customers — believes in its philosophy beyond the sale.
Connect it personally: 'it's also why I'm prepared — the philosophy-first teaching is what drew me to study it deeply.' The program becomes part of YOUR story.
scenarios.prompt: Why the free bootcamp?
choices: It's a marketing gimmick to get emails

The bootcamp builds the market's literacy in the deny-by-default model — educated practitioners become champions — and it signals a teaching culture; honestly, that philosophy-first generosity is part of what drew me to prepare this deeply
They have nothing better to do with the team
Free training is always low quality
scenarios.hint: A company teaching its philosophy for free. What does that strategy build — and what does it signal?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it reads both the strategy (market literacy, champions, pipeline) and the culture (teaching generosity), then connects it personally without sycophancy. A is wrong: 'gimmick' is cynical and misses the strategy entirely. C is wrong: dismissive and unserious. D is wrong: a blanket dismissal that insults the interviewer's own program.

domains.name: Product Deep-Dive
domains.description: The stack in depth: Allowlisting, Ringfencing, Storage, Elevation, Network, Web Control, and Cyber Hero MDR — how they compose into Zero Trust.

scenarios.title: “Walk me through what happens when I double-click a Word doc”
scenarios.situation: The technical interviewer: 'Word document, double-click. Walk me through every control that engages, in order.' They want the composition narrated — not a feature list.
evidence: Web Control (if it arrived via download: category/file-type policy) → Allowlisting (winword.exe: approved, signed → runs) → the document's macro content executes INSIDE Word.
Ringfencing governs what Word may do: macro spawns PowerShell → app-to-app leash denies. Credential-store read attempt → file leash denies. Callback attempt → network leash denies.
Each deny is a detection: the audit records the walk, the analyst (or Cyber Hero) investigates the delivery. The story ends with the hunt, not the block.
scenarios.prompt: Walk them through it.
choices: Word opens because it's allowlisted; the macro runs; antivirus scans it

Narrate the layers in order: fetch policy (if downloaded), execution approval (Word runs — it's signed and approved), then Ringfencing's four leashes on Word's behavior (macro-to-PowerShell denied, credential-store denied, callback denied) — and each deny as a detection that triggers the delivery investigation
Word is blocked from opening unknown documents
The firewall stops the macro
scenarios.hint: Double-click to investigation. How many controls engage — and in what ORDER?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it narrates the composition in order (fetch → execution → behavior leashes → detection → hunt), names the specific leashes, and ends with the investigation. A is wrong: it skips Ringfencing entirely and misattributes the macro to antivirus. C is wrong: Word isn't blocked from opening documents — its BEHAVIOR is constrained. D is wrong: the firewall doesn't see macro execution; the leashes do.

scenarios.title: “Which control would have stopped [incident]?”
scenarios.situation: 'Last year a peer company got hit by ransomware via a phishing email with a macro document. Which of your controls would have stopped it — and be specific about which layer.' The test: precision, not slogans.
evidence: Phishing email with macro doc: Web Control's category/file-type policy is the first possible catch (macro-enabled docs from untrusted senders).

The macro executes inside approved Word: Allowlisting allows Word (correctly). The malicious BEHAVIOR — macro spawning PowerShell, encrypting files, reaching C2 — hits Ringfencing's leashes: app-to-app, file, network.
Ringfencing is the specific stop: the ransomware's impact (mass encryption, lateral spawn, callback) is behavior, and behavior is Ringfencing's jurisdiction — with each deny feeding detection.
scenarios.prompt: Which control, specifically?
choices: Allowlisting — it blocks all malware

Ringfencing, specifically: the macro document is the delivery (Web Control may catch it), Word itself is legitimately approved — but the ransomware's behaviors (spawning processes, mass file writes, C2 callback) each hit a Ringfencing leash (app-to-app, file, network), and every deny becomes a detection
The firewall
Cyber Hero would have called them
scenarios.hint: Word is approved. The macro runs. WHAT, exactly, does the ransomware need to DO — and which control governs DOING?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it maps the incident to layers precisely (delivery vs execution vs behavior), names the specific leashes, and notes the detection feed. A is wrong: 'blocks all malware' is a slogan — Allowlisting approves Word, which is the whole point of the question. C is wrong: the firewall doesn't govern Word's process behavior. D is wrong: Cyber Hero responds; the question asked which CONTROL stops it.

scenarios.title: “What can't your product do?”
scenarios.situation: The interviewer asks the limits question directly: 'What can't the platform do? Where does it not help?' They're testing honesty — and whether you've thought about it.
evidence: Malicious use of fully-approved apps within their leashes (the authorized user doing the wrong thing deliberately); social engineering that never touches the endpoint (credential phishing to the webmail); physical access; and the human layer generally.
Every security product has limits; the candidate who names them is trusted on everything else. The candidate who claims total protection is disbelieved on everything.
'Here's what the platform covers brilliantly, and here are the honest boundaries — which is why the Cyber Hero team and the customer's own practices matter.' Limits plus the compensating layer.
scenarios.prompt: What can't it do?
choices: Nothing significant — it's comprehensive Zero Trust protection

Honest boundaries: malicious use of fully-approved apps within their leashes, social engineering that never touches the endpoint (like credential phishing), physical access — no endpoint control covers those; that's why the human layer (Cyber Hero) and customer practices are part of the story
Everything has limits, but I can't think of specific ones
It can't protect against nation-states
scenarios.hint: They asked for limits. What does the CANDID answer signal — and what does evasion signal?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it names specific, real boundaries (not vague hand-waving), keeps the framing constructive (limits + compensating layers), and demonstrates the candor. A is wrong: 'comprehensive' is the evasion the question was designed to catch. C is wrong: 'can't think of specifics' after claiming product depth is the contradiction. D is wrong: 'nation-states' is a dodge — the real limits are the mundane ones (insider misuse, off-endpoint phishing).

scenarios.title: “Elevation Control vs just removing admin rights”
scenarios.situation: 'Why not just remove everyone's admin rights and be done? What does Elevation Control add?' The interviewer probes whether you understand the usability half of least privilege.
evidence: 'Just remove admin' breaks legitimate work: installers, drivers, updates — the business needs elevated actions; removing the capability removes the work.

Just-in-time, per-app, time-boxed elevation: the SPECIFIC app gets admin for the SPECIFIC task, no credentials exposed, ringfenced against hopping, every session logged. Least privilege WITH usability.
A flat 'no admin' without a path breeds shadow IT and bypasses. The bounded yes — 'the installer runs elevated for 60 minutes, logged' — is what makes least privilege deployable.
scenarios.prompt: What does it add?
choices: Nothing — removing admin rights is sufficient

Elevation Control makes least privilege deployable: instead of standing admin (or broken users), specific apps elevate just-in-time, time-boxed, ringfenced against hopping, and logged — the business keeps working while the attack surface shrinks; a flat 'no' without a path just breeds bypasses
It's mainly a compliance checkbox
It gives IT an audit trail, which is nice
scenarios.hint: Remove all admin: what breaks? Now — what's the alternative that DOESN'T break it?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it names what breaks under the naive approach, explains the JIT mechanism completely (specific, time-boxed, ringfenced, logged), and adds the service insight (flat no breeds bypasses). A is wrong: it ignores the legitimate elevated work the business needs. C is wrong: 'compliance checkbox' trivializes the core privilege-control function. D is wrong: the audit trail is a property, not the purpose — the purpose is usable least privilege.

scenarios.title: “Storage Control: why not just ban USB?”
scenarios.situation: 'Why the granularity — serial numbers, time windows, read-only? Why not just ban USB drives?' The interviewer tests whether you understand usable security.
evidence: Blanket bans get bypassed: the contractor emails the files instead (worse), the executive demands an exception (unscoped), the business need doesn't vanish because policy said so.
Serial-scoped, user-bound, time-boxed, read-only-for-third-parties: the contractor CAN work — on their drive, this week, reading not writing. Usable yes beats unenforceable no.
Every approved transfer is logged: what moved, when, by whom. The ban alternative has no log — because the transfers happen anyway, invisibly.
scenarios.prompt: Why not just ban USB?
choices: Because bans are simpler to manage

Blanket bans get bypassed (email instead — worse; executive exceptions — unscoped) while the business need persists: serial-scoped, time-boxed, read-only granularity gives a usable yes, and every approved transfer is audited — the ban's transfers happen anyway, invisibly, which is the worse outcome
USB drives are obsolete anyway
Most companies just ban them, so it's fine either way
scenarios.hint: The ban is simple. What happens the Monday after the ban — and where does the data go?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it predicts the bypass paths accurately (email-worse, exception-unscoped), explains the granular alternative, and adds the audit dividend — the complete usable-security argument. A is wrong: 'simpler to manage' ignores that unmanaged bypasses are the actual outcome. C is wrong: USB is not obsolete in the real world of contractors and air-gaps. D is wrong: 'everyone does it' is not a security argument.

scenarios.title: “Cyber Hero: what does the human layer add?”
scenarios.situation: 'You have all these automated controls. What does the 24/7 human MDR team actually add?' They're testing whether you understand people-plus-technology.
evidence: Context, judgment, and conversation: the 3 AM call where the customer is panicking, the ambiguous alert that needs a human read, the containment decision with business tradeoffs.
Speed with judgment: a human analyst triaging in about a minute — the combination is the product. Fast automation plus human sense.
The MSP channel's customers often lack their own SOC: Cyber Hero IS their security team. The human layer is how the mission ('protect the organizations that can't staff a SOC') becomes operational.
scenarios.prompt: What does the human layer add?
choices: It's mostly marketing; the tech does the work

Judgment, context, and conversation at 3 AM: the ~60-second human response on top of automated prevention — and for MSP-served customers without their own SOC, the team IS the security function; that's the mission made operational
Humans to watch the dashboards
It's a premium upsell
scenarios.hint: Automated controls, 3 AM, panicking customer, ambiguous alert. What handles THAT?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it names what humans uniquely provide (judgment under ambiguity, conversation under pressure), cites the response stat, and connects it to the mission — the complete answer. A is wrong: dismissing the human layer misses the product's stated design and insults the team. C is wrong: 'watch dashboards' trivializes triage judgment. D is wrong: 'upsell' cynically misreads the mission architecture.

scenarios.title: Outlook Cannot Open Attachments
scenarios.situation: Users report that double-clicking attachments in Outlook does nothing, or the attachment opens but cannot save changes. This started after the security team enabled stricter application containment.
scenarios.prompt: What is happening, and how should it be addressed?
choices: Ringfencing is constraining what Outlook is allowed to do: the file leash or application leash is preventing Outlook from launching child processes or writing to certain locations. Review the Ringfence policy for Outlook and adjust the leashes to permit the legitimate attachment workflow while keeping risky behaviors fenced
The email server is down
Users need local admin rights to open attachments
Outlook is corrupted on all machines and needs repair
scenarios.why: Ringfencing places per-application boundaries (leashes) on what an app may do: which files it can touch, which processes it can launch, which network destinations it can reach. Overly strict leashes on Outlook break legitimate attachment handling. The fix is surgical: examine which specific leash is denying (file, application, network, or registry) and relax only that behavior for the legitimate workflow, preserving containment of genuinely risky actions like macro-launched PowerShell.
scenarios.hint: What control limits what an already-approved application is allowed to DO?
evidence: outlook.exe attempted to launch winword.exe (child process) | Action: Denied by Application leash
120 users | Attachment open/save workflow broken since policy v14 applied

scenarios.title: Browser Cannot Download Files
scenarios.situation: After a Ringfencing policy update, users can browse normally but all file downloads fail silently in Chrome. The help desk is flooded.
scenarios.prompt: Where should the engineer look first?
choices: Reinstall Chrome on every machine

Inspect the Ringfence policy for the browser: a file or network leash is likely blocking writes to the Downloads folder or the download stream itself. Identify the denying leash in the audit log and scope an exception for the legitimate download path
The internet connection is too slow for downloads
Chrome needs to be added to the allowlist
scenarios.why: Browsing works but downloads fail, which points squarely at a Ringfence leash on the browser rather than an execution problem (Chrome itself is clearly approved and running). The audit log will show exactly which leash denied the write. The fix is to permit the legitimate download path while keeping the browser fenced from dangerous behaviors like writing executables to startup locations. Reinstalling the browser changes nothing about policy.
scenarios.hint: The application runs fine. Only one specific behavior is blocked. Which control governs behavior?
objectives: Isolate behavior blocks from execution blocks
evidence: chrome.exe → Write to C:\Users\*\Downloads\report.pdf | Denied by File leash (policy: Browser-Hardened v3)
All 400 workstations | Started 2026-10-10 08:02 after policy push

scenarios.title: Application Cannot Reach Network Share
scenarios.situation: A document management client can open local files but fails to connect to the file server share. Other applications on the same machine reach the share without issues. Network connectivity is fine.
scenarios.prompt: What is the most likely cause?
choices: DNS is misconfigured on the workstation
The file server is offline

Ringfencing on the document management application is denying its network access to the share. Other apps work because their own Ringfence policies permit it; this app's network leash needs the file server destination allowed
The user's password expired
scenarios.why: The key clue is that other applications on the same machine reach the share fine, which rules out network, server, credential, and DNS issues — those would affect everything. Ringfencing is per-application, so a network leash on this specific app can block its share access while leaving other apps untouched. The engineer should check the app's Ringfence network leash and add the file server as an allowed destination.
scenarios.hint: Same machine, same network, same server — but only one app fails. What is scoped per-application?
objectives: Use differential diagnosis with per-app controls
evidence: docmgmt.exe → SMB to \\fileserver\share (TCP 445) | Denied by Network leash

scenarios.title: Excel Macro Blocked from Running Scripts
scenarios.situation: A finance user has an Excel workbook with macros that automate monthly reporting. The macros are blocked. The user says the workbook is from a trusted colleague and has worked for two years.
scenarios.prompt: How should the engineer respond?
choices: Tell the user macros are banned and they must do the reporting manually
Disable the agent on the finance user's machine
Unblock macros for Excel across the whole company so finance is never interrupted

Recognize this as Ringfencing working as designed: Office macros launching scripts is a classic attack vector. Verify the workbook's legitimacy, then create a targeted exception (e.g., allow the specific signed macro or the specific workbook) rather than opening macros globally
scenarios.why: Macro-to-script execution is one of the most abused attack chains in existence, so Ringfencing constrains it by default — the control is doing its job. The right move is not to remove the fence but to build a gate: verify the specific workbook is legitimate and create a narrow exception for it (signed macro, known file hash, or approved publisher). A global macro exemption would re-open the exact attack path the control exists to close.
scenarios.hint: Is the control broken, or is it doing exactly what it was designed to do?
objectives: Build narrow exceptions for legitimate macro use
evidence: excel.exe → spawned powershell.exe via macro | Denied by Application leash (Office-Hardened)
Monthly_Report_v8.xlsm | Macros signed by Finance-Dept cert (valid) | In use since 2024

scenarios.title: PDF Reader Cannot Print
scenarios.situation: Users can open PDFs but printing fails with a generic error. The printers work from every other application. The issue appeared after the PDF reader's Ringfence policy was tightened.
scenarios.prompt: What should the engineer check?
choices: Check the Ringfence policy for the PDF reader: printing requires the application to communicate with the print spooler (a device/peripheral interaction), and a device or application leash may be denying it. Allow the spooler interaction for the reader while keeping other restrictions
Reinstall the PDF reader on all machines
The PDF files are corrupted
Replace all the printers
scenarios.why: Printing from an application means talking to the print spooler service, which is a cross-process/device interaction that Ringfencing can restrict. Since printing works from other apps, the printers and spooler are healthy — only this reader's leash is denying the interaction. The fix is to permit the spooler communication for the reader specifically. Reinstalling or replacing printers addresses components that are demonstrably working.
scenarios.hint: Printing is an app talking to another service. What governs what an app may talk to?
evidence: reader.exe → interact with spoolsv.exe | Denied by Application leash
winword.exe → print | Allowed (same printer, same machine)

scenarios.title: Legitimate App Cannot Reach the Internet
scenarios.situation: A newly deployed CRM client cannot connect to its cloud service. Browsers on the same machine reach the internet fine. The CRM vendor's documentation lists the required domains and ports.
scenarios.prompt: What is the likely cause and fix?
choices: The internet is down

Network Control (the application firewall) has no rule permitting the CRM client. Browsers work because they have their own rules. Create a firewall rule allowing the CRM executable to reach the vendor's documented domains/ports
The CRM license expired
Reinstall the CRM client
scenarios.why: Network Control filters per-application, so one app's blocked traffic does not imply a network outage — the browsers working proves connectivity is fine. The CRM client simply lacks a firewall rule. The fix is to add a rule permitting that executable to the vendor's documented destinations. This is the deny-by-default firewall doing its job: unknown app traffic is denied until explicitly permitted.
scenarios.hint: Browsers work, one app does not. What filters traffic per-application?
evidence: crmclient.exe → api.vendor.com:443 | Denied: no matching Network Control rule

scenarios.title: New SaaS App Blocked
scenarios.situation: The company adopted a new SaaS HR platform. The web portal works, but the desktop sync client cannot connect. The SaaS vendor provided a list of required URLs and ports.
scenarios.prompt: What should the engineer do?
choices: The SaaS vendor's software is incompatible and must be replaced
Tell HR to only use the web portal
Build Network Control rules for the sync client covering the vendor's documented URLs and ports, test connectivity, and document the rules for the next SaaS onboarding
Disable the firewall for the HR department
scenarios.why: The web portal works because browsers already have HTTPS rules; the sync client is a separate executable with no rule. Using the vendor's published URL/port list, the engineer creates precise firewall rules for the client. This also establishes a repeatable SaaS onboarding pattern: collect vendor network requirements, create scoped rules, test, document. Disabling the firewall for a department trades a small configuration task for a large security gap.
scenarios.hint: The browser and the sync client are different executables. What does each need?
objectives: Onboard SaaS clients through firewall policy
Build a repeatable SaaS network-requirements workflow

scenarios.title: VPN Client Blocked from Connecting
scenarios.situation: Remote users cannot establish VPN connections. The VPN client launches but fails during the connection phase. This began after Network Control policies were tightened.
scenarios.prompt: What should the engineer check?
choices: Remote users should come to the office instead
Uninstall the VPN client from all machines
The VPN server is down; call the ISP

Verify Network Control permits the VPN client's required protocols and ports (e.g., UDP 500/4500 for IPsec, or the vendor's ports). A tightened firewall can block the tunnel establishment itself. Add precise rules for the VPN executable
scenarios.why: VPN tunnel establishment needs specific protocols and ports allowed for the VPN client executable. When firewall policies are tightened without accounting for the VPN client, the tunnel cannot form and users see connection failures. The engineer should check the VPN vendor's port/protocol requirements against the current Network Control rules and add what is missing. The timing (right after tightening) strongly implicates the policy change.
scenarios.hint: What changed just before the failures started? What does a VPN client need at the network layer?
objectives: Correlate policy changes with new failures
Permit VPN protocols through application firewall
evidence: 2026-10-09 18:00: Network Control policy 'Strict-Egress' applied to Remote-Users group

scenarios.title: Internal App Cannot Cross VLANs
scenarios.situation: A monitoring dashboard on the IT VLAN cannot collect data from agents on the workstation VLAN. The agents are online and the dashboard worked before the network segmentation project.
scenarios.prompt: How should the engineer approach this?
choices: Treat it as a Network Control rule problem: identify the dashboard executable, the agent ports/protocols, and the direction of traffic, then create rules permitting the dashboard's cross-VLAN collection while keeping the segmentation intact
The agents are all broken and need reinstalling
Monitoring is not important; disable the dashboard
Flatten the network back to a single VLAN
scenarios.why: Segmentation is working as intended by denying cross-VLAN traffic by default; the dashboard simply needs explicit permission as a known-good exception. The engineer maps the exact flow (which executable, which ports, which direction) and writes a narrow rule. Flattening the network would undo the security benefits of segmentation to solve a configuration task, and the agents are demonstrably online.
scenarios.hint: Segmentation denies by default. What is the legitimate exception here, and how narrowly can it be drawn?
evidence: 1,204 agents online, last check-in < 5 min (they just cannot be reached FROM the dashboard)

domains.name: Zero Trust Philosophy
domains.description: Never trust, always verify: the philosophy beneath the product — deny-by-default, assume breach, least privilege — and defending it in interviews.

scenarios.title: “Isn't Zero Trust just a marketing term?”
scenarios.situation: The skeptical engineer on the panel: 'Zero Trust — isn't that just marketing? Every vendor says it.' The room is watching how you handle skepticism about the company's core word.
evidence: 'You're right that the term is overused — vendors slap it on anything. The question is whether the architecture behind the word is real.'

Then the operational tests: deny-by-default execution (is unknown denied?), assume-breach behavior controls (are approved apps leashed?), least-privilege admin (is standing admin gone?). 'If those three are true, the word is earned.'
'I judge the term by the architecture — and the architecture here is specific enough to argue with, which is what I like about it.'
scenarios.prompt: How do you handle the skeptic?
choices: Agree that it's all marketing; the term is meaningless

Steelman first ('the term IS overused'), then the substance test: deny-by-default execution, assume-breach behavior leashes, no standing admin — 'if those three are architecturally true, the word is earned; here they're specific enough to argue with, which is what I like'
Defend the term vigorously; it's the company's core message
Change the subject to the products
scenarios.hint: Skepticism about the core word. Do you defend the WORD — or test the ARCHITECTURE?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it validates the skepticism (steelman), then replaces word-debate with architecture-tests — three specific, falsifiable claims — and closes with genuine conviction. A is wrong: agreeing it's meaningless insults the company's core while trying to bond. C is wrong: vigorous word-defense is marketing, not engineering — the skeptic asked for substance. D is wrong: changing the subject dodges the question everyone heard.

scenarios.title: “What would you change about the philosophy?”
scenarios.situation: 'You clearly believe in this model. What would you CHANGE about it — where is it weakest?' The interviewer tests whether your conviction has edges.
evidence: The operational weight (approvals, baselining — the machinery is the tax); the approved-app blind spot (malicious use within leashes); the human layer (no philosophy survives users working around it).

'I'd invest in making the machinery lighter — faster approvals, smarter baselining — because the philosophy is only as strong as its deployability. The principle is right; the friction is the frontier.'
Saying 'nothing' (uncritical) or attacking the core (unconvinced). The sweet spot: conviction in the principle, restlessness about the implementation.
scenarios.prompt: What would you change?
choices: Nothing — the philosophy is perfect as is

The principle is right; I'd attack the friction — lighter-weight approvals, smarter baselining, better usability engineering — because deny-by-default is only as strong as its deployability; conviction in the principle, restlessness about the implementation
The whole model needs rethinking; detection is the future
I'd make it stricter — more controls, fewer exceptions
scenarios.hint: Conviction with edges — or conviction without thought? What does the STRONG believer change?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it holds the principle while naming real weaknesses (operational weight, approved-app blind spot), and aims the restlessness at implementation — the mature believer's answer. A is wrong: 'nothing' signals uncritical fandom, not conviction. C is wrong: abandoning the model contradicts everything else you've said. D is wrong: 'more strict' confuses strictness with strength — the frontier is deployability, not severity.

scenarios.title: “Our competitor says they do Zero Trust too”
scenarios.situation: '[Competitor] also claims Zero Trust. What's actually different?' No trashing allowed — differentiate on architecture.
evidence: Ask of any 'Zero Trust' claim: is execution deny-by-default (or detection-led)? Are approved apps behavior-leashed (or trusted once running)? Is admin just-in-time (or standing)? The answers separate architecture from adjective.

'Many vendors use the term; the testable differences are the defaults: what's denied without explicit approval, what's leashed after approval, and what privilege stands. I'd compare those three defaults specifically.'
No claims about the competitor's internals you can't verify. The test is offered as a lens, not a verdict — confident without trashing.
scenarios.prompt: What's actually different?
choices: They're lying; only we do real Zero Trust

Offer the architectural test: deny-by-default execution vs detection-led, behavior leashes on approved apps vs trust-after-approval, just-in-time vs standing admin — 'those three defaults are where I'd compare any two claims; they're specific enough to verify'
We have better marketing
I don't know their product
scenarios.hint: Two vendors, one phrase. What TEST separates architecture from adjective — without trashing?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it provides the three-default test (verifiable, architectural, non-trashing) and frames it as a lens rather than a verdict — confident and professional. A is wrong: 'they're lying' is the trashing the question forbids. C is wrong: crediting marketing concedes the architecture question. D is wrong: 'don't know' after claiming depth is the contradiction.

scenarios.title: “Where does Zero Trust NOT apply?”
scenarios.situation: 'Interesting philosophy. Where does it NOT apply — where would you not use it?' The interviewer probes for judgment boundaries.
evidence: Safety-critical real-time systems where verification latency is unacceptable (the philosophy bends to physics); tiny trust domains where the machinery outweighs the risk (a two-person shop's single laptop); and the human relationship layer (trust-but-verify with people is a management philosophy, not an endpoint policy).
Knowing where a principle DOESN'T apply proves you understand it — principles without boundaries are slogans. 'Everywhere, always' is the fanatic's answer.
'The principle scales down to the risk: the machinery should always be lighter than the threat it addresses. Where it isn't, that's the boundary.'
scenarios.prompt: Where doesn't it apply?
choices: Everywhere, always — it's a universal principle

Honest boundaries: real-time safety systems where verification latency is unacceptable, tiny trust domains where the machinery outweighs the risk — the principle scales to the threat; knowing the boundary proves the understanding
Nowhere — if it's not applied, it's not Zero Trust
It doesn't apply to small businesses
scenarios.hint: 'Everywhere, always' — is that understanding, or fandom? What proves you know a principle?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it names real boundaries (latency-critical safety, machinery-vs-risk economics), states the scaling principle, and frames boundary-knowledge as understanding — the mature answer. A is wrong: universal claims are fandom, and the interviewer asked for judgment. C is wrong: definitional gatekeeping dodges the question. D is wrong: small businesses are exactly the MSP channel's mission — the worst possible boundary to name here.

scenarios.title: “Convince the skeptic in 60 seconds”
scenarios.situation: Final round. The CEO (hypothetically) gives you sixty seconds: 'Convince me Zero Trust endpoint is worth the operational cost.' One minute, no slides, the economic buyer.
evidence: Cost of the alternative (one ransomware event: downtime, recovery, reputation) → the inversion (finite known-good vs infinite known-bad) → the operational honesty (the cost is real; here's the machinery) → the close (prevention is cheaper than incident response, every time).
Outcomes and economics, zero mechanisms: 'the question isn't whether you pay — it's whether you pay in prevention or in incidents.'
End with the choice framed: 'You pay for security either way. Deny-by-default means you pay on your schedule, not the attacker's.'
scenarios.prompt: Sixty seconds. Go.
choices: List the product features quickly; there's a lot to cover

'A single ransomware event costs more than years of prevention: downtime, recovery, reputation. Default-deny inverts the problem — instead of recognizing infinite badness, you approve the finite known-good. The operational cost is real, and it's managed with baselining and fast approvals. You pay for security either way — deny-by-default means you pay on your schedule, not the attacker's.'
Zero Trust is the industry standard now; everyone is doing it
Our competitors can't stop ransomware, but we can
scenarios.hint: Sixty seconds, economic buyer, no slides. What survives — features, or economics?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it's structured (alternative cost → inversion → honest cost → close), speaks economics not mechanisms, and lands the memorable close — the complete executive minute. A is wrong: feature-listing to a CEO in 60 seconds is the classic misread of audience. C is wrong: 'everyone's doing it' is bandwagon, not argument. D is wrong: competitor-trashing to the CEO is disqualifying.

scenarios.title: “Teach it back to me”
scenarios.situation: 'Pretend I'm a new MSP technician, first week. Teach me deny-by-default in two minutes.' The interviewer tests teaching — the culture's core skill.
evidence: Hook (the ransomware that signatures missed) → the inversion (two questions: 'known-bad?' vs 'explicitly trusted?') → the finite list (the business's real apps) → the job (your approvals keep the list true) → the payoff (you're the reason the next zero-day doesn't run).
Teaching generously and plainly IS the Cyber Hero culture in miniature: the interviewer is watching whether you lift the beginner up or talk down.
End with their role in it: 'and that's why your approval decisions matter — you're the human in the loop that keeps the list honest.' Empowerment, not lecture.
scenarios.prompt: Teach it in two minutes.
choices: Deny-by-default is a security model where only approved applications execute, using allowlisting with certificate, hash, and path rules governed by policy...

Hook with the story (the ransomware no signature caught), then the inversion: 'old thinking asks IS THIS KNOWN-BAD — and unknown stuff runs free. We flip it: IS THIS EXPLICITLY TRUSTED? The business needs a finite list of apps — you know them — and everything else waits for approval. Your approval decisions are what keep that list honest — you're the human in the loop.'
Read them the product documentation
Tell them to take the free bootcamp
scenarios.hint: First-week technician. Do they need the rule taxonomy — or the story, the inversion, and their place in it?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it teaches in the right shape (story → inversion → finite list → their role), speaks plainly, and empowers — the teaching performance the culture question tests. A is wrong: rule taxonomy at a first-week tech is the lecture, not the lesson. C is wrong: 'read the docs' is the abdication of teaching. D is wrong: outsourcing the teaching to the bootcamp dodges the question you were asked.

domains.name: Cyber Hero Culture
domains.description: The service standard: 24/7/365 US-based MDR with ~60-second response — empathy plus competence, and demonstrating it in every answer.

scenarios.title: The third call this week
scenarios.situation: The queue shows a small-business owner, third call this week: 'my computers keep blocking my payroll software.' Frustration is high; the previous two calls 'fixed it temporarily.' You're the Cyber Hero on this call.
evidence: Third call, same issue, temporary fixes: the previous calls treated symptoms. The customer isn't angry about the block — they're angry about the REPEAT.

Acknowledge the repeat explicitly ('third time is unacceptable — let's fix it permanently today'), diagnose the root (the pattern: updates change hashes — the temporary hash approvals keep breaking), and fix structurally (certificate rule for the vendor).

Explain the pattern in plain language ('every update changes the app's fingerprint; we've now approved the publisher, so updates won't break it'), confirm payroll runs, and give them a direct path if it ever recurs. The third call becomes the last call.
scenarios.prompt: How do you handle the third call?
choices: Fix it the same way as before; it worked twice

Acknowledge the repeat as the real issue ('third time is unacceptable'), diagnose the root pattern (update-churn breaking temporary hash approvals), fix structurally with a certificate rule, explain the why in plain language, confirm the fix, and leave a direct path — the third call becomes the last call
Escalate to tier 2; it's their problem now
Offer a discount for the inconvenience
scenarios.hint: Third call, same issue. What's the customer ACTUALLY angry about — the block, or something else?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it identifies the repeat as the real grievance, fixes the root pattern (not the symptom), explains plainly, and closes the loop permanently. A is wrong: the same temporary fix guarantees a fourth call. C is wrong: escalating a repeat customer without owning it is the abdication. D is wrong: a discount doesn't fix the pattern — the fourth call still comes.

scenarios.title: The customer who is wrong
scenarios.situation: A customer insists the block is YOUR fault: 'your update broke my system!' The audit shows: their own IT pushed a conflicting policy change at 2 AM, then blamed the vendor. The customer is angry and wrong. How do you handle it?
evidence: Their 2 AM change caused it; the audit proves it. You're right and they're wrong — which is the most dangerous position in support.
'You're wrong' never de-escalates, even when true. The goal is the fix and the relationship — not the verdict on blame.

'Let's look at the timeline together — I see a policy change at 2 AM from your console; let's walk through what it did.' Collaborative diagnosis lets the evidence speak while you stay on their side. The customer discovers the cause WITH you — no blame assigned, problem solved.
scenarios.prompt: They're angry and wrong. Now what?
choices: Prove them wrong with the audit log; facts are facts

Collaborative diagnosis: 'let's walk the timeline together' — surface the 2 AM change as a joint discovery, fix it together, no blame assigned; being right is less valuable than the relationship and the resolution
Agree it was your fault to calm them down
Escalate; angry customers are management's problem
scenarios.hint: You're right, they're wrong, they're angry. What wins — the argument, or the outcome?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it gets the fix and the relationship by making the discovery collaborative — the evidence convinces without the confrontation. A is wrong: winning the blame argument loses the customer. C is wrong: false confession destroys your credibility and teaches nothing. D is wrong: escalating a solvable ticket is abdication.

scenarios.title: The 3 AM page from a panicking MSP
scenarios.situation: 3:12 AM: an MSP technician pages — ransomware indicators on a client's host, they're panicking, it's their biggest client. You're the Cyber Hero on shift. Walk through the first five minutes.
evidence: Calm and command: 'I'm on it — here's what happens in the next ten minutes.' Panic needs a plan more than it needs sympathy.
Verify the signal in the audit, isolate the host via policy quarantine, start the evidence freeze — narrating each step to the technician ('host isolated, I'm pulling the audit trail now').
The technician needs competence they can relay to THEIR client: give them the plain-language status to pass on ('contained, investigating, update in 30 minutes'). You're serving two layers.
scenarios.prompt: First five minutes?
choices: Tell them to calm down and call back in the morning

Take command calmly with an explicit plan, verify and isolate via policy while narrating to the technician, freeze evidence, and give them relayable status for their client — competence performed at speed, empathy in the steadiness
Immediately start a full forensic investigation yourself
Wake the whole team
scenarios.hint: 3 AM, panicking technician, biggest client. What do they need in minute one — sympathy, or a plan?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it leads with command (the plan calms), executes the operator's seat (verify, isolate, freeze), and serves the dual audience with relayable status. A is wrong: 'call back in the morning' during ransomware is the abdication. C is wrong: solo forensics instead of containment inverts the priorities. D is wrong: waking everyone before verifying and containing is panic with extra steps.

scenarios.title: The feature request you can't grant
scenarios.situation: A long-time customer requests a feature the platform deliberately doesn't offer (blanket execution exemptions for a department). They say 'we'll switch vendors if you don't.' Your answer?
evidence: Real revenue risk versus the philosophy: blanket exemptions are the anti-pattern the product exists to prevent. Granting it would betray the model — and every other customer.

Understand the underlying need (what's the department actually blocked on?), solve THAT with the platform's tools (scoped rules, faster approvals, staged rollout) — the 'no' to the feature with a 'yes' to the need.
'I can't grant that — it's the one thing the model won't do, because it would undo the protection. Here's what I CAN do...' Honest boundaries keep trust; false promises keep no one.
scenarios.prompt: They threaten to leave. Your answer?
choices: Grant the exemption; retention matters most

Hold the boundary honestly ('that's the one thing the model won't do — it would undo the protection'), diagnose the underlying need, and solve THAT with scoped tools — the 'no' to the feature with a working 'yes' to the need
Promise to raise it with product and stall
Call their bluff; they won't leave
scenarios.hint: Revenue versus philosophy, stated as an ultimatum. What does the HONEST 'no' sound like — and what accompanies it?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it holds the philosophical boundary (the exemption would undo the product), finds the real need beneath the demand, and solves it within the model — honest no, working yes. A is wrong: granting the anti-pattern for retention betrays the product and every other customer. C is wrong: stalling with false product promises is dishonest. D is wrong: calling bluffs is gambling with the relationship, not serving it.

scenarios.title: The teammate's mistake
scenarios.situation: Your teammate's rule change just blocked 200 endpoints. They're panicking, the queue is flooding, and they're freezing. You're the senior on shift. What do you do — for the incident AND the teammate?
evidence: You take command of the technical response: assess, roll back or narrow-fix, validate — the queue needs action, not a postmortem, in the first ten minutes.

Calm, specific, forward: 'I've got the rollback — pull the audit for the change while I do this.' Give them a useful task (restores agency), zero blame in the moment (blame can wait; it usually shouldn't come at all).
The debrief is blameless and structural: what in the PROCESS allowed it (no canary? Friday push?) — and you model it by naming your own past mistake first. The culture is built in these ten minutes.
scenarios.prompt: Incident and teammate — your move?
choices: Fix it yourself and tell them to take a break; they're useless right now

Take command of the technical response, give the teammate a concrete useful task (restoring agency, zero blame), then run a blameless structural debrief after — modeling ownership by naming your own past mistake first
Let them fix their own mistake; it's their responsibility
Report them to the manager for the bad change
scenarios.hint: Two hundred blocked, teammate freezing. What does the TEAM need from you in minute one — and what does the teammate need?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it separates the incident (command the response) from the human (restore agency, zero blame), then builds the culture in the debrief — leadership as service. A is wrong: sidelining the teammate with contempt destroys them and teaches the team that mistakes are shameful. C is wrong: 'their responsibility' abandons both the incident and the person. D is wrong: reporting instead of responding inverts every priority.

scenarios.title: The thank-you that matters
scenarios.situation: A customer writes: 'Your analyst stayed on the call for two hours at midnight and saved our quarter-end. I want their manager to know.' You're the manager. What do you do — and what does the team learn?
evidence: Recognize specifically and publicly: name what they did (the two hours, the calm, the narrow fix), tie it to the standard ('that's Cyber Hero'), and make sure the customer hears it was received.
The peer-voted 'most helpful' culture runs on exactly this: specific recognition of helpfulness, visible to the team. Recognition is the culture's fuel.
Debrief the call as a team teaching moment (with the analyst's permission): what did the two hours contain? The team learns the standard from the example — and the analyst learns the work is seen.
scenarios.prompt: What do you do?
choices: Forward it to HR for the file
Recognize specifically and publicly — name the behaviors, tie them to the Cyber Hero standard, close the loop with the customer, and (with permission) debrief it as a team teaching moment
A private 'good job' is enough
Nothing; it's just their job
scenarios.hint: Two hours at midnight, quarter saved, customer writing in. What does the TEAM learn from what you do next?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it recognizes specifically (behaviors, not just outcome), ties to the standard, closes the customer loop, and converts it into team learning — the full culture move. A is wrong: HR-filing buries the recognition where the team never sees it. C is wrong: private praise misses the peer-signal the culture runs on. D is wrong: 'just their job' is how cultures of excellence die — unrecognized.

domains.name: Behavioral Questions
domains.description: The STAR repertoire: mistakes, conflicts, pressure, learning — answered with ownership, specificity, and the lesson.

scenarios.title: “Tell me about a time you failed”
scenarios.situation: The behavioral round opens: 'Tell me about a time you failed.' The panel leans in. You have two minutes.
evidence: The ownership arc — acknowledgment, remediation, process fix — not the failure's drama. Vulnerability with structure.
A real failure with real cost, your actions in the first ten minutes, and the habit born from it. Ninety seconds, no defensiveness.
Humblebrag ('I work too hard'), blame ('the tooling failed'), minimize ('it was minor'), or 'I've never really failed' (the panel stops listening).
scenarios.prompt: Two minutes. Go.
choices: I've never really had a major failure — I prepare carefully

A real one: my Friday-afternoon rule tweak skipped the canary and blocked payroll Monday. First ten minutes: acknowledged it was mine, rolled back, re-issued correctly. The process fix: no Friday pushes without canary, ever — that failure is why my change discipline exists
My biggest failure is that I care too much about the work
The monitoring tool failed to alert, so I couldn't have known
scenarios.hint: They asked for failure. What are they actually grading — the fall, or the recovery?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it's a real failure with real cost, the first-ten-minutes ownership, and the process fix as the origin story of a discipline — the complete ownership arc. A is wrong: 'never failed' is either dishonest or inexperienced — both fail. C is wrong: the humblebrag is the scored evasion. D is wrong: blaming the tooling is the abdication the question hunts.

scenarios.title: “Disagreement with your manager”
scenarios.situation: 'Tell me about a time you disagreed with your manager.' The power dynamic makes this the hardest behavioral question. Two minutes.
evidence: A real technical disagreement, your manager's side steelmanned ('she was right that the deadline mattered'), how it resolved (data won — the pilot proved the inventory gap), and the relationship after (stronger — she trusted my pushback next time).
Respect for hierarchy PLUS intellectual honesty: did you raise it well, argue the work, and commit fully once decided? Disagree-and-commit is the senior signal.
'We never disagree' (sycophancy), trashing the manager (character failure), or 'I won and she admitted it' (victory framing).
scenarios.prompt: Two minutes. Go.
choices: My manager and I have always seen eye to eye

We disagreed on the rollout date — she needed Friday for the business, I needed another week for the inventory. She was right that the date mattered; I showed her the uncommon-list data, we compromised on a phased Friday (ready departments first), and I committed fully to making it work. She trusted my pushback more after that — because I'd argued the work, not her
I told her she was wrong and eventually she agreed
I just do what I'm told; it's not my place to disagree
scenarios.hint: Disagreeing upward. What do they score — the disagreement, or what surrounded it?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it steelmans the manager, resolves via data and compromise, commits fully, and shows the relationship strengthened — disagree-and-commit done right. A is wrong: 'always eye to eye' reads as sycophancy or inexperience. C is wrong: 'told her she was wrong' is the victory framing that fails the character test. D is wrong: 'not my place' surrenders the intellectual honesty the role requires.

scenarios.title: “A time you went above and beyond”
scenarios.situation: 'Tell me about a time you went above and beyond.' They're testing whether your 'beyond' serves others or yourself.
evidence: A situation where the job description ended and you continued: the midnight call you stayed on, the documentation nobody asked for that the whole team now uses, the teammate you mentored through their first incident.
Other-centered initiative: did the 'beyond' help someone else — a customer, a teammate, the team? Self-serving 'beyond' (your own project, your own visibility) scores less.
Humblebrag marathons ('I worked 90 hours'), credit-taking ('I single-handedly'), or 'beyond' that was actually the job.
scenarios.prompt: Two minutes. Go.
choices: I once worked the entire weekend to finish my own project early

An MSP tech called at midnight, panicking about their client's quarter-end — outside my queue, not my account. I stayed two hours: contained it, wrote them a plain-language summary for their client, and built a runbook from it so the next midnight call resolves in twenty minutes. They still mention it
I always go above and beyond; it's just who I am
I stayed late once to help a coworker with something small
scenarios.hint: Above and beyond — for WHOM? What distinguishes service from stamina?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it's other-centered (the MSP tech, their client), specific (two hours, the summary, the runbook), and the 'beyond' compounded into a team asset — service with a multiplier. A is wrong: your own project early is stamina, not service. C is wrong: 'it's just who I am' is the claim without the story. D is wrong: 'something small' undersells the question — and the vagueness shows it.

scenarios.title: “How do you handle criticism?”
scenarios.situation: 'How do you handle criticism — especially when you think it's wrong?' The composure question. Ninety seconds.
evidence: Listen fully first ('I take notes before I respond'), separate the signal from the delivery, test it against evidence, and act on what's true — including the case where the criticism is wrong (then: 'I checked, here's what the data showed, and here's what I took from it anyway').
Non-defensiveness under direct challenge: do you get curious or do you get armored? The security field runs on blameless postmortems — this is the culture question in disguise.
'I love criticism!' (unbelievable), defensiveness disguised as explanation, or 'I ignore wrong criticism' (the curiosity failure).
scenarios.prompt: Ninety seconds. Go.
choices: I love all feedback and always agree with it

I listen first and take notes before responding — then I separate the signal from the delivery and test it against evidence. When it's right, I change; when it's wrong, I verify and say so plainly, and I still look for the grain of truth. A senior once told me my triage notes were vague — stung, but she was right, and my notes have had the five-line shape ever since
Criticism doesn't bother me; I just move on
If it's wrong, I explain why they're mistaken
scenarios.hint: Criticism you think is WRONG. What's the move — armor, or curiosity with verification?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it's non-defensive (listen, notes), evidence-driven (test it), honest about wrong criticism (verify and say so), and ends with the converted lesson — the complete maturity arc. A is wrong: 'love all feedback and always agree' is unbelievable sycophancy. C is wrong: 'just move on' is the curiosity failure — nothing learned. D is wrong: leading with 'why they're mistaken' is the armor the question hunts.

scenarios.title: “Why should we hire you?”
scenarios.situation: The closer: 'Why should we hire you over the other candidates?' Ninety seconds, no rambling, land it.
evidence: Three specific reasons, each tied to THEIR needs: the philosophy conviction (with homelab evidence), the service reflex (the Cyber Hero answers you've given all day), and the trajectory (what you'll build in the first 90 days).
Direct without arrogance: 'Because...' stated plainly, then the evidence. Hedging ('I think maybe...') in the closer undoes the whole interview.
End looking forward: 'and in the first 90 days I'd...' — the candidate who's already planning the work. That's the last impression.
scenarios.prompt: Ninety seconds. Land it.
choices: Because I'm passionate, hardworking, and a fast learner

Three reasons: I believe in deny-by-default as an operator, not a slogan — my homelab triage work is the evidence.
