I answer like a Cyber Hero — you've seen it all day: impact first, narrow fixes, plain language. And I'm already planning the first 90 days: learn the queue, earn the team's trust, ship one process improvement. That's the trajectory you're hiring
Because I really want this job
I'm the best candidate you've interviewed
scenarios.hint: Ninety seconds, the closer. What beats adjectives — and what does the last sentence do?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: three specific reasons tied to their needs, evidence for each, and the forward-looking close — confident without arrogance. A is wrong: adjectives without evidence are the generic closer. C is wrong: 'really want it' is motivation without differentiation. D is wrong: 'best candidate' is arrogance without evidence — and insults the other candidates.

scenarios.title: “What are you working on improving?”
scenarios.situation: 'What's a weakness — something you're actively working on?' The growth question. They're testing self-awareness plus trajectory.
evidence: A real weakness (not a humblebrag), what it costs, and the ACTIVE work: the system, the practice, the measurable progress. 'Working on it' needs evidence.

'My written triage notes used to be vague — cost me rework. Now I use the five-line shape on every ticket, and my handoffs stopped bouncing. Still working on speed.' Real, costly, systematized, in-progress.
Humblebrag ('perfectionism'), disguised strength ('I work too hard'), 'no weaknesses' (the panel laughs, then rejects), or a fatal flaw ('I hate talking to customers' — for a service role).
scenarios.prompt: What's the weakness?
choices: I'm a perfectionist; I care too much about quality

A real one: my triage notes used to be vague — analysts had to call me for context, which cost us time. I built the five-line note shape and use it on every ticket now; handoffs stopped bouncing. Still working on writing them faster under pressure — that's the current edge
I don't really have weaknesses; I address things as they come
I'm not great with people, but I'm working on it
scenarios.hint: Weakness with a system around it — or weakness as confession? What shows trajectory?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: real weakness, real cost, active system, measurable progress, and the honest current edge — self-awareness with trajectory. A is wrong: the perfectionism humblebrag is the scored evasion. C is wrong: 'no weaknesses' fails the self-awareness test outright. D is wrong: 'not great with people' for a service-culture role is the fatal flaw — and 'working on it' without a system is the confession without the trajectory.

domains.name: Technical Questions
domains.description: The technical rounds: triage narration, rule-strength judgment, containment reasoning, and the hands-on depth interviewers probe.

scenarios.title: The whiteboard: design the policy
scenarios.situation: 'Whiteboard: design the allowlist policy for a 25-person company. Go.' The interviewer hands you the marker. Five minutes.
evidence: Draw the layers before any rule: baseline (gold image, cert rules) → department overlays → exceptions (ticketed, time-boxed). Structure earns the first marks.

A sample rule with full metadata (type, scope who/what/where/when, owner, ticket, review date), the strength ladder stated ('cert over hash over path — never path in writable'), and the exception process box.
Talk while drawing: 'I'm starting with structure because...' — the whiteboard tests thinking, and silent drawing hides it. End with 'and I'd validate with...'
scenarios.prompt: Five minutes, marker in hand. What do you do?
choices: Start listing applications to allowlist

Structure first (three layers drawn and labeled), then a sample rule with full metadata and scope axes, the strength ladder stated aloud, the exception process boxed — narrating throughout, ending with validation; the whiteboard shows thinking, not just answers
Draw the network diagram
Ask for more time to think silently
scenarios.hint: Marker, five minutes, policy design. What goes on the board FIRST — rules, or structure?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it leads with structure (the senior move), shows a complete sample rule (metadata + scope), states the ladder, boxes the exception process, and narrates throughout — the whiteboard as thinking display. A is wrong: listing apps without structure is the junior move — rules without architecture. C is wrong: the network diagram answers a different question. D is wrong: silent thinking wastes the scored minutes — narrate.

scenarios.title: The live triage: talk me through this alert
scenarios.situation: The interviewer shares their screen: an audit entry — updater.exe denied on 14 endpoints at 08:04, signed by the known vendor, hash not in catalog, rule: default-deny. 'Talk me through it. Live.'
evidence: 'Scoping: 14 endpoints, one binary, 08:04 — widespread, simultaneous. The audit: signed by the known vendor, hash not in catalog, default-deny fired — so the inventory missed the new version.'
'Version-change false positive: signer trusted, bytes changed. The fix is a scoped certificate rule for the updater plus its child — hash would break again next update.'
'Validate: install works, unrelated unsigned binary still denied. And I'd check what else shipped in that vendor update — the child installer needs the same treatment.'
scenarios.prompt: Live. Talk.
choices: It's probably a false positive; I'd approve the hash

Narrate the read aloud (scope, audit anatomy, the version-change diagnosis), give the verdict with the rule-strength reasoning (certificate over hash), and close with the double validation plus the child-installer check
It's malware; isolate all 14 machines
I'd need more information before saying anything
scenarios.hint: Live screen, fourteen endpoints, signed updater, changed hash. What does the PANEL hear — silence, or the loop?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it narrates the full loop aloud (scope → observe → verdict → fix → validate), applies the ladder correctly, and adds the child-installer thoroughness — the complete live-triage performance. A is wrong: 'probably' plus a hash approval is the guess with the wrong rule type. C is wrong: isolating 14 machines over a signed vendor updater is the panic misread. D is wrong: 'need more info' when the audit already decided is the freeze the exercise hunts.

scenarios.title: “How would you attack this setup?”
scenarios.situation: 'You just designed that policy. Now attack it — where are the holes?' The interviewer flips the whiteboard. They're testing adversarial thinking.
evidence: 'Gladly — here's where I'd go:' then the honest holes: the path rule in the locked-but-shared tools folder (writable by IT — insider or compromised admin), the broad vendor publisher grant (their bundled utilities ride it), the exception process (social-engineer the approver).
Attacking your OWN design crisply — no defensiveness, no 'but it's fine because.' The holes named specifically, each with the abuse path.
'And here's how I'd close each: ...' — the attack followed by the remediation. Red team then blue team, in the same answer.
scenarios.prompt: Attack your own design. Go.
choices: It's pretty solid; I don't see major holes

Name the holes crisply with abuse paths: the shared-tools path rule (writable by IT — drop-and-execute), the broad publisher grant (bundled utilities ride the trust), the exception process (social-engineer the approver) — then close each with the remediation; red team then blue team, no defensiveness
I'd need proper red-team tools to answer that
Attackers couldn't get past the allowlist
scenarios.hint: Your own design, now hostile. Do you defend it — or dissect it?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it dissects without defensiveness, names specific holes with abuse paths (not vague 'weaknesses'), and closes each with remediation — the adversarial fluency being tested. A is wrong: 'pretty solid' is the defensiveness that fails the exercise. C is wrong: the question tests thinking, not tooling — the holes are architectural. D is wrong: 'couldn't get past' is the complacency the flip was designed to expose.

scenarios.title: The troubleshooting chain: “It's slow”
scenarios.situation: 'Users report the endpoint agent makes machines slow. Diagnose it.' Deliberately vague — they want your diagnostic structure, not the answer.
evidence: 'Slow' needs decomposition: WHEN (boot? all day? specific apps?), WHO (all machines? some? which?), WHAT changed (agent update? policy push? OS update?), and MEASURED how (CPU? disk? subjective?).

Scope the population, correlate with changes (agent version, policy pushes, OS updates), check the agent's own resource usage vs the policy's scan behavior, and reproduce on a test box before changing anything fleet-wide.
Jumping to the fix ('exclude the AV scan') before the diagnosis — or blaming the agent without evidence. Structure first, always.
scenarios.prompt: 'It's slow.' Diagnose it.
choices: Exclude the busiest folders from scanning; that usually fixes it

Decompose first: when (boot? all day?), who (all or some machines?), what changed (agent/policy/OS updates?), measured how? — then correlate with changes, check the agent's resource profile, reproduce on a test box before any fleet-wide change
Reinstall the agent on the slow machines
It's probably the network, not the agent
scenarios.hint: 'Slow' — the vaguest ticket in the queue. What are your FIRST four questions?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it decomposes before diagnosing (when/who/what-changed/measured), correlates with changes, and reproduces before fleet-wide action — the diagnostic structure being tested. A is wrong: excluding scan folders before diagnosis is the fix-before-cause failure. C is wrong: reinstalling without diagnosis is the hope-based method. D is wrong: 'probably the network' is the guess the structure exists to prevent.

scenarios.title: “Explain DNS to a five-year-old” — the simplicity test
scenarios.situation: 'Explain DNS to me like I'm new to IT.' The simplicity test: can you teach a fundamental plainly?
evidence: Analogy first ('the internet's phone book'), then the one job it does (names to numbers), then why it matters here (every connection starts with a question to DNS — which is why we scope and monitor it).
No jargon without immediate translation, one analogy held throughout, and the 'why it matters' tied to THEIR world (the endpoint work).
The condescending simple ('it's really easy, just...') or the jargon avalanche ('recursive resolvers iterate the hierarchy...'). Plain, not dumbed-down.
scenarios.prompt: Explain DNS simply.
choices: DNS is a hierarchical distributed naming system using recursive resolvers...

Think of it as the internet's phone book: you type a name, DNS finds the number. Every connection your endpoint makes starts by asking DNS a question — which is exactly why we give it scoped rules and watch for weird questions, like thousands to strange names at 3 AM
It's really simple — just names to numbers, anyone gets it
DNS isn't really relevant to endpoint work
scenarios.hint: New to IT. Do they need the hierarchy — or the phone book, the one job, and why it matters to THEM?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: analogy held throughout, the one job stated, and the 'why it matters' tied to their endpoint world (scoped rules, anomaly watching) — plain, respectful, relevant. A is wrong: the jargon avalanche is the failure the test hunts. C is wrong: 'really simple, anyone gets it' is condescension wearing simplicity. D is wrong: DNS is deeply relevant to endpoint work — the tunneling lesson proves it.

scenarios.title: The edge: “Have you ever...?”
scenarios.situation: The interviewer probes past your depth: 'Have you ever done kernel-level debugging?' You haven't. The room is quiet. This is the honesty test at the edge of knowledge.
evidence: 'I haven't done kernel debugging specifically. What I HAVE done is [adjacent depth: user-mode debugging, crash-dump triage...], and here's how I'd approach it: [reproduce, isolate, escalate to the right expert, learn].' Honest edge, adjacent evidence, approach.
The edge handled without bluffing or collapsing: honesty plus the adjacent depth plus a credible learning approach. The probe STOPS at honesty — it continues through bluff.
Bluffing ('a bit, yeah...') — the follow-up question will end you. Or collapsing ('I know nothing about that') — which discards your adjacent depth.
scenarios.prompt: You haven't. Now what?
choices: A bit, yeah — in my homelab I looked at some drivers once

'I haven't done kernel debugging specifically. I have done user-mode crash triage [specifics], and my approach would be: reproduce in the lab, isolate with driver-verifier-style tooling, and escalate to the platform team with a clean repro — then learn everything I can from their analysis.'
I don't know anything about that area
Can we move on to something I know?
scenarios.hint: The probe found the edge. What STOPS the probe — and what makes it continue?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: honest edge, adjacent depth with specifics, credible approach (repro, isolate, escalate, learn) — the composure that stops the probe. A is wrong: 'a bit, yeah' is the bluff the follow-up exists to kill. C is wrong: collapsing discards the adjacent depth that would have passed. D is wrong: 'move on' surrenders the question instead of answering it.

scenarios.title: PowerShell Script Blocked
scenarios.situation: A sysadmin's logon script that maps drives and sets printers is being blocked on every workstation. The script has not changed in a year. The customer recently tightened their ThreatLocker policies.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct way to allow this legitimate script while keeping script-based attacks blocked?
choices: Approve the specific script by hash in the policy, or sign it and approve the certificate, so that exact script is allowed while unknown scripts remain denied
Allow powershell.exe unrestricted so all scripts run
Disable script blocking for the entire domain
Convert the script to a batch file, which is not inspected
scenarios.why: The script itself is legitimate, so it should be explicitly approved: allowlisting the script by hash (or better, signing it and trusting the certificate) permits that exact script while every other unknown script stays denied. Allowing powershell.exe broadly or disabling the control would also permit malicious scripts, which defeats the purpose. Batch files are equally subject to policy, so converting the format changes nothing.
scenarios.hint: Deny-by-default means unknown scripts are denied. How do you make a known-good script 'known'?
objectives: Allow legitimate scripts under application control
Distinguish script approval from interpreter approval
evidence: Denied: C:\Scripts\logon.ps1 | Reason: Script not on allowlist | Parent: powershell.exe
2026-10-08: 'Script Control' tightened from Audit to Deny for Workstations group

scenarios.title: Driver Installation Blocked
scenarios.situation: A customer is installing a new printer fleet. The printer driver installer is blocked on every machine. The driver is signed by the printer manufacturer.
scenarios.prompt: What should the engineer check and do?
choices: Drivers cannot be allowlisted; the customer must use a different printer brand
Verify the driver's signature and approve it through the appropriate kernel/driver control policy, since signed drivers from the legitimate vendor can be explicitly permitted
Disable ThreatLocker on the print server permanently
Install the driver in Safe Mode to bypass the agent
scenarios.why: Signed drivers from a legitimate vendor can be approved through policy. The engineer should verify the signature chains to the expected manufacturer and then permit the driver via the kernel-mode/driver approval path. ThreatLocker does inspect driver loads because malicious drivers are a persistence technique, so there is a deliberate approval workflow rather than an automatic pass. Bypassing via Safe Mode or disabling the agent circumvents the control instead of using it correctly.
scenarios.hint: Why would a security product inspect driver loads at all? How do legitimate ones get approved?
objectives: Handle driver approvals through proper policy channels
Explain why driver loads are inspected
evidence: Denied: prndrvr.sys | Reason: Driver not approved | Signer: PrinterCorp Inc. (valid)
New printer fleet rollout, 45 devices, driver package v2.8 from vendor site

scenarios.title: User Needs Admin for One App Only
scenarios.situation: A user needs to run a legacy inventory tool that requires administrator rights, but company policy prohibits making users local admins. The help desk has been manually entering admin credentials for months.
scenarios.prompt: What is the proper solution?
choices: Make the user a local administrator; it is the only way legacy apps work
Create an Elevation Control policy that permits elevation for that specific application only. The user remains a standard user everywhere else, and the elevation is audited
Uninstall the legacy tool and tell the department to buy a modern replacement immediately
Share the local admin password with the user
scenarios.why: Elevation Control exists precisely for this: grant administrative rights to a specific application without making the user an administrator. The policy elevates just that executable, the action is logged in the audit trail, and the user's own account stays standard. Making the user a full admin or sharing the admin password grants far broader rights than needed and destroys accountability.
scenarios.hint: How do you give admin rights to an application without giving them to the person?
objectives: Apply just-in-time elevation for specific apps
evidence: 47 manual admin-credential entries for inventory.exe in the last 90 days
Company standard: no standing local admins (compliance requirement)

scenarios.title: Elevation Prompt Not Appearing
scenarios.situation: A user right-clicks an installer and chooses 'Run as administrator', but no elevation prompt appears and the installer fails. Elevation Control is deployed. Other users get prompts normally.
scenarios.prompt: What should the engineer investigate?
choices: The installer is corrupted; download it again
The user's monitor is too small to display the prompt

Check whether an Elevation Control policy is silently denying (rather than prompting) for this user or application, verify the agent is healthy on the machine, and confirm the user is in the group the elevation policy targets
Reinstall Windows on the machine
scenarios.why: When prompts appear for others but not this user, the cause is policy or agent state, not the installer. Elevation Control can be configured to auto-deny certain elevations without prompting, the agent might not be running properly on that machine, or the user might fall outside the policy's targeted group. The engineer should check the effective elevation policy for that user/machine and the agent's health before assuming media or OS problems.
scenarios.hint: It works for others. What differs for this user or machine?
objectives: Check policy targeting and agent health
evidence: Machine WKST-1142: agent service running, last check-in 4 min ago
Elevation policy 'Installers-Standard-Users' targets group 'Branch-Users'; affected user is in 'Branch-Users-Temp'

scenarios.title: Developer Needs Local Admin for Dev Tools
scenarios.situation: A software developer needs to install SDKs, run debuggers, and modify system paths. IT will not grant standing local admin. The developer is blocked several times per week waiting for help desk elevation.
scenarios.prompt: What balanced approach should the engineer propose?
choices: Tell the developer to do all work on a personal laptop outside company policy
Remove ThreatLocker from developer machines entirely
Grant the developer permanent local admin; developers always need it

Build a scoped Elevation Control policy covering the developer's toolchain (approved IDEs, SDK installers, debuggers), possibly time-bound or ticket-linked, so the developer is unblocked while every elevation is audited and limited to known tools
scenarios.why: Developers genuinely need elevated operations, but standing admin violates least privilege. A scoped elevation policy for the known toolchain gives the developer autonomy for legitimate work while keeping everything else standard and every elevation logged. Time-bounding or tying elevation to change tickets adds further control. Exempting machines or using personal devices removes visibility entirely, which is worse for security.
scenarios.hint: How do you unblock legitimate admin work without granting unlimited admin?
objectives: Design scoped elevation for power users
evidence: Developer filed 23 elevation requests in 30 days (SDK installs, debugger attaches, PATH edits)
Approved: VS Code, .NET SDK, WinDbg, Docker Desktop (all signed, vendor-verified)

scenarios.title: Elevation Approved but App Still Fails
scenarios.situation: An elevation request for a system utility was approved and the UAC-style prompt was accepted, but the utility still fails with 'Access denied' when writing to a protected directory.
scenarios.prompt: Why might an approved elevation still fail?
choices: Elevation grants the application's process administrative rights, but other controls still apply: Ringfencing leashes on the application can still deny the specific file write, or the destination may be protected by additional policy. Check the audit log for the subsequent deny after the elevation succeeded
The user clicked the wrong button on the prompt
The computer needs more RAM
Elevation Control is broken and should be uninstalled
scenarios.why: Elevation and containment are independent layers. Elevation Control answers 'may this run as admin?' while Ringfencing answers 'what may it do even as admin?'. An elevated process can still be denied a specific action by its Ringfence leashes. The audit log will show two events: the elevation allowed, then the file write denied by a leash. The fix is to adjust the relevant leash, not to re-elevate or remove the controls.
scenarios.hint: Two different controls answer two different questions. Which question did elevation answer, and which remains?
evidence: 10:02:14 Elevation approved: sysutil.exe (user: jdoe) | 10:02:15 Denied: sysutil.exe → write C:\Windows\System32\drivers\etc\hosts (File leash)
'I approved the prompt but it still says Access denied'

scenarios.title: Policy Changes Not Applying
scenarios.situation: An admin updated an Application Control policy in the portal two hours ago, but endpoints are still enforcing the old rules. The admin is certain they clicked Save.
scenarios.prompt: What should the engineer check, in order?
choices: Verify the policy was actually deployed/published (not just saved as draft), confirm the agents have checked in since the deployment, and check whether the endpoints are in the group the policy targets
Reinstall the agent on every endpoint
The portal is broken; wait 24 hours
Rebuild the entire portal database
scenarios.why: Policy changes follow a pipeline: edit → save → deploy/publish → agent check-in → enforcement. A break at any stage produces this symptom. The most common causes are a policy left in draft, agents that have not checked in yet, or endpoints sitting outside the targeted group. Walking the pipeline in order isolates the stage quickly, while reinstalling agents or waiting blindly skips the actual diagnostic steps.
scenarios.hint: Saving is not deploying, and deploying is not enforcing. What are the stages in between?
evidence: Policy 'Standard v15': status Draft (last edited 2h ago, never deployed)
Median check-in age: 6 min (agents are communicating fine)

scenarios.title: New Computer Not Getting Policies
scenarios.situation: A newly imaged workstation has the agent installed and shows in the portal, but none of the customer's policies apply to it. It behaves as if it has no policy at all.
scenarios.prompt: What is the most likely cause?
choices: The agent installer is corrupted; reinstall Windows
The machine is not assigned to the correct group (or any group) in the portal, so no group-targeted policies apply to it. Verify group assignment and onboarding workflow
New computers need 48 hours before policies apply
The portal license is expired
scenarios.why: Policies target groups, not individual machines by default. A new machine that lands in the portal but in no group (or the wrong group) receives no group policies — exactly the 'no policy at all' symptom. The fix is to check the machine's group membership and the onboarding process that should assign it. Agent reinstalls and waiting periods do not address group assignment.
scenarios.hint: Policies target groups. Where does a brand-new machine land?
evidence: WKST-2201: agent online, group = 'Ungrouped' (0 policies target this group)
Step 7: 'Assign to department group' — marked optional, frequently skipped

scenarios.title: Conflicting Policies, Unexpected Denies
scenarios.situation: An application is approved in the company's baseline policy but keeps getting denied on a subset of machines. Those machines have an additional departmental policy applied.
scenarios.prompt: How should the engineer resolve the conflict?
choices: Remove the departmental policy entirely
Delete all policies and start over

Review policy precedence and merging: determine which policy's deny is winning on the affected machines, then reconcile the two policies (adjust the departmental policy's rule or its precedence) so the intended approval takes effect without weakening the departmental restrictions that matter
Approve the application a second time in the departmental policy and hope it sticks
scenarios.why: When multiple policies apply, they merge according to precedence rules, and a deny in one can override an allow in another. The engineer must identify which policy is producing the effective deny and understand the merge order before changing anything. Blindly duplicating approvals or deleting policies risks breaking the protections the departmental policy was built for. The goal is a reconciled policy set where both the baseline approval and the departmental intent hold.
scenarios.hint: Two policies apply. One says allow, the effective result is deny. What decides the winner?
evidence: Baseline: invoicer.exe Allowed | Departmental: *.exe in C:\DeptApps\ Denied (precedence: higher)
C:\DeptApps\invoicer.exe — matches the departmental deny pattern

scenarios.title: Agent Shows Offline in Portal
scenarios.situation: Twelve machines show as offline in the portal even though users are actively working on them. The machines were online yesterday.
scenarios.prompt: What is the systematic troubleshooting order?
choices: The portal is down for everyone
Ignore it; offline agents still enforce the last policy
Reimage all twelve machines immediately

Check in order: is the agent service running on the endpoints, can the endpoints reach the portal (network/proxy/firewall), and did anything change (maintenance window, network change, certificate expiry)? Start with the endpoint service, then connectivity, then recent changes
scenarios.why: Offline-in-portal means the heartbeat is not arriving, so the diagnostic order is: endpoint (is the agent service running?), path (can it reach the portal through the network, proxy, and firewall?), and change (what changed since yesterday when it worked?). This ordered approach isolates the layer quickly. Reimaging is disproportionate before knowing the cause, and while offline agents do enforce cached policy, losing visibility and future updates is itself a problem to fix.
scenarios.hint: The agent phones home on a schedule. What could stop the call at each stage?
evidence: 2026-10-09 18:00: Firewall rule change on site edge (outbound 443 restricted)

domains.name: Customer Scenarios
domains.description: The customer-facing rounds: angry callers, confused users, MSP technicians, and executives — empathy plus competence, every time.

scenarios.title: The payroll call
scenarios.situation: Monday 8:10 AM: 'This is Maria from Harbor Dental — NOBODY can run payroll, the updater is blocked on every machine, and I have 25 people waiting for paychecks.' She's upset. You're the analyst on the call. Go.
evidence: Payroll blocked fleet-wide Monday morning: maximum business impact, maximum emotion. The technical facts (signed updater, changed hash) matter less than the first 15 seconds.

Acknowledge ('Maria, I hear you — payroll morning blocked is urgent, I'm on it right now'), diagnose aloud from the audit (the updater's new version changed its fingerprint), timeline ('fix in the next 15 minutes'), fix (scoped certificate rule), validate, close with the why.

'The update changed the app's fingerprint, so our system treated it as new — I've now approved the publisher, so future updates won't break it. Payroll should be running — can you confirm on one machine?' Confirm, explain, prevent.
scenarios.prompt: You're on the call. Go.
choices: Let me look into the technical details and call you back

'Maria, I hear you — payroll blocked on payday morning is urgent, and I'm on it right now.' [Diagnose from the audit aloud, in plain language.] 'I can see the cause: the updater's new version changed its fingerprint. I'm approving the publisher now — 15 minutes, and I'll stay on until you confirm payroll runs.' [Fix, validate, close with the why and the prevention.]
Calm down, Maria — these blocks happen after updates
The policy is working as designed; the updater needs approval
scenarios.hint: Twenty-five paychecks, one upset caller, 15 seconds. What does she need to hear FIRST?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: acknowledgment first (impact + 'I'm on it'), plain-language diagnosis as it happens, explicit timeline, narrow fix, validation, and the close with the why and prevention — the complete call shape. A is wrong: 'call you back' to a payroll-morning caller is the abandonment. C is wrong: 'calm down' is the escalation phrase — never. D is wrong: 'working as designed' to an upset user is the lecture, not the service.

scenarios.title: The 'you broke it' accusation
scenarios.situation: 'YOUR update broke our entire office! Everything was fine until YOUR agent updated last night!' The audit shows: their admin pushed a bad GPO at midnight that conflicts with the agent. The caller is furious and wrong. Handle it.
evidence: Their midnight GPO caused it; the audit proves it. You're right, they're wrong and furious — the most dangerous support position.

Collaborative diagnosis, not confrontation: 'Let's look at what changed overnight together — I see a policy push at midnight from your side; let's walk through what it did.' The evidence convinces; you stay on their side.
Fix it together, document the interaction cause for their admin, no blame assigned. The customer discovers the cause WITH you — relationship intact, problem solved.
scenarios.prompt: Furious and wrong. Handle it.
choices: You're mistaken — your admin's GPO caused this, not our update

'Let's figure out what changed overnight together.' [Walk the timeline collaboratively; surface the midnight GPO as a joint discovery.] 'Here's the fix, and here's a note for your admin on the interaction — no harm done, let's get you running.' [Fix together, document, no blame.]
You're right, our update must have caused it — sorry
Transfer them to a manager
scenarios.hint: Furious, wrong, and YOUR evidence proves it. What wins — the argument, or the customer?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: collaborative discovery lets the evidence do the convincing while you stay allied — fix together, document for their admin, zero blame. A is wrong: winning the blame argument loses the customer. C is wrong: false confession destroys credibility and teaches nothing. D is wrong: transferring a solvable ticket is abdication.

scenarios.title: The non-technical owner
scenarios.situation: The practice owner (a dentist, not IT): 'I don't understand any of this computer stuff. Just tell me — are my patients' records safe?' The audit shows a blocked intrusion attempt, fully contained. Answer her.
evidence: Safety, in her language: are the records safe? What happened? What did you do? What should she do? Four questions, plain words.

'Yes, they're safe — here's what happened in plain terms: a bad email tried to get in, our system stopped it automatically, I verified nothing got through, and I've closed the hole it tried. You don't need to do anything.'
Zero jargon, zero mechanisms, complete honesty: 'stopped automatically' is true; 'verified nothing got through' is the investigation stated simply. She hears safety, not systems.
scenarios.prompt: Are the records safe? Answer her.
choices: The Ringfencing policy denied the WINWORD.EXE process-tree escalation and the audit shows no lateral movement...

'Yes — your patients' records are safe. A harmful email tried to get in this morning; our protection stopped it on its own, and I've double-checked that nothing got through. I've also closed the gap it tried to use. You don't need to do anything — but I wanted you to hear it from me directly.'
Probably safe; these things are hard to be sure about
Your IT person can explain the technical details
scenarios.hint: Dentist, not IT, asking about patient records. What does she need — mechanisms, or safety?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: direct safety answer first, plain-language what-happened, the verification stated simply, the proactive outreach ('hear it from me') — trust built in four sentences. A is wrong: process-tree jargon to a dentist is the failure the question hunts. C is wrong: 'probably safe' destroys the confidence the situation allows. D is wrong: deflecting to 'your IT person' abandons the trust moment.

scenarios.title: The MSP tech's relay
scenarios.situation: MSP technician, terse: 'Client down, 10 machines, need status I can forward. Go.' They need three sentences for an angry client. What do you give them?
evidence: Relayable status: quotable verbatim to an angry client. Three sentences, zero jargon, timeline included.

'Contained: the affected machines are isolated and the cause is identified. Fix validating now — I expect full restoration within 30 minutes. No data left the network; I'll update you at the half hour.'
Brevity plus completeness: the tech forwards it as-is, looks competent to their client, and the timeline manages the anger. That's the peer service.
scenarios.prompt: Three sentences. Go.
choices: We're investigating the issue and will update you when we have more information

'Contained: the 10 machines are isolated and we've identified the cause — a blocked update, not an attack. Fix is validating now; I expect everyone back within 30 minutes. No data was at risk at any point — I'll update you at the half hour mark.'
The allowlist policy denied the updated binaries due to hash mismatch...
Can you give me the ticket number first?
scenarios.hint: Terse tech, angry client, three sentences. What makes status RELAYABLE?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: contained (with the 'not an attack' reassurance), timeline (30 minutes), risk stated (no data at risk), next update committed — forwardable verbatim. A is wrong: 'investigating, will update' is the empty status that helps no one. C is wrong: hash-mismatch jargon can't be forwarded to an angry client. D is wrong: process questions before status inverts every priority.

scenarios.title: The repeat caller by name
scenarios.situation: You recognize the voice: it's the third call from the same owner this month. Before they explain, what do you do — and why does it matter?
evidence: 'Hi Maria — I remember we spoke about the updater last time. Is this the same issue back again?' Recognition before explanation: you've collapsed the intake to zero.
Being remembered is the service differentiator: the customer feels known, not ticketed. And you already have the history — the pattern (repeat!) is visible to you before they describe it.
If it's the same issue: 'this shouldn't have come back — let me fix it permanently today and find out why the last fix didn't hold.' The repeat is now YOUR problem to close, permanently.
scenarios.prompt: Third call, same voice. Your opening?
choices: Can I have your ticket number please?
'Hi Maria — I remember the updater issue from last time. Is it back again? If so, this one's on me to fix permanently today — let me pull up your history while you tell me what you're seeing.'
Please describe the issue from the beginning
Let me transfer you to the technician who helped last time
scenarios.hint: Same voice, third time. What's the most powerful first sentence — process, or recognition?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: recognition by name and history, ownership of the repeat ('on me to fix permanently'), and the history already loading — the relationship move that also happens to be the diagnostic shortcut. A is wrong: ticket-number-first to a recognized repeat caller is the process over the person. C is wrong: 'from the beginning' discards the history you already have. D is wrong: transferring away the relationship you just recognized.

scenarios.title: The compliment and the complaint
scenarios.situation: End of a resolved call: 'You were great, but honestly your product is too complicated — my staff can't deal with these blocks.' Compliment plus complaint. How do you close?
evidence: Take both seriously: thank them for the compliment specifically, and receive the complaint without defensiveness — 'too complicated' is product feedback wearing a support ticket.

'Thank you — and you're right that the blocks interrupt your staff. Here's what I'd suggest: [one concrete simplification — the approval fast-lane / the exception SLA / a staff briefing]. Can I set that up for your team?' Complaint converted to improvement.

Log the feedback for product: 'customer finds blocks disruptive — suggested fast-lane.' The support call becomes product intelligence — and tell the customer you logged it. They hear their voice traveling upward.
scenarios.prompt: Compliment and complaint. Close it.
choices: Thanks! Glad I could help. Goodbye

'Thank you — that means a lot. And I hear you on the complexity: the blocks shouldn't interrupt your staff's day. Here's what I can set up — [concrete simplification]. I'll also log this feedback for our product team, because you're not the first to say it.' [Set it up, log it, close the loop.]
Our product is actually quite simple once you learn it
The blocks are necessary for security; your staff will adapt
scenarios.hint: Great service, complicated product. What do you do with the SECOND half of that sentence?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: receives both parts genuinely, converts the complaint into a concrete improvement (set up, not promised), and logs it as product intelligence with the customer's knowledge — the complete close. A is wrong: 'glad I could help, goodbye' drops the product feedback entirely. C is wrong: 'actually quite simple' argues with the customer's lived experience. D is wrong: 'staff will adapt' is the arrogance that manufactures churn.

scenarios.title: Legitimate App Blocked After Update
scenarios.situation: A customer's accounting team reports their invoicing application stopped launching this morning, right after the vendor pushed an automatic update overnight. The ThreatLocker agent shows a block event for the new executable. The previous version ran fine for months.
scenarios.prompt: What is the most likely cause, and what should the engineer do first?
choices: Tell the customer to roll back the update and disable automatic updates permanently
The update is malware; quarantine the machine immediately and wipe it

The application's file hash changed with the update, so the old allowlist entry no longer matches. Verify the new file's signature and publisher, then approve the updated version in the Application Control policy
Disable Allowlisting for the accounting group so updates never break again
scenarios.why: ThreatLocker Allowlisting is deny-by-default and identifies files by hash. When a vendor updates an application, the executable hash changes and the old approval no longer matches, which produces exactly this symptom: worked yesterday, blocked today. The correct response is to verify the new file is legitimate (check the digital signature, publisher, and source) and then approve the new version. Disabling the control or rolling back updates weakens security posture and does not address the root cause.
scenarios.hint: What identifies a file to an allowlisting engine? What changed overnight?
objectives: Diagnose hash-change blocks after legitimate updates
evidence: Denied: C:\Program Files\Invoicer\invoicer.exe | Reason: File not on allowlist | SHA256: 9f2c...a41b (previous approved hash: 7d11...e903)
Digital signature: Valid, issued to Invoicer Inc. | Signed: 2026-10-09 23:14 UTC | Source: vendor auto-update channel

scenarios.title: New Software Deployment Blocked Org-Wide
scenarios.situation: An IT admin is rolling out a new approved PDF editor to 300 endpoints via their deployment tool. Installations are failing everywhere with ThreatLocker block events. The software is legitimate and the customer wants it deployed today.
scenarios.prompt: How should the engineer enable this deployment without weakening the security posture?
choices: Tell the admin to install it manually on each machine with local admin rights
Whitelist the entire deployment tool so it can run anything
Put all 300 machines in Disabled Mode until the rollout finishes
Add the installer to the allowlist, or use Learning Mode / an installation policy scoped to the deployment window so the installer and its components are approved as they execute
scenarios.why: The clean approach is to approve the installer (and its child processes) through policy: add the installer hash or certificate to the allowlist, or run a time-scoped Learning Mode / installation policy during the deployment window so legitimate components are learned and approved. This keeps deny-by-default intact for everything else. Disabled Mode or blanket-whitelisting the deployment tool creates a gap where anything the tool touches would execute unchallenged.
scenarios.hint: How do you approve something new without turning off the control for everything?
objectives: Enable legitimate mass deployments under deny-by-default
evidence: Denied: pdfeditor-setup.exe | 214 endpoints | Reason: File not on allowlist
Approved software: PDF Editor v4.2 (vendor MSI, signed) | Target: All workstations | Window: today 09:00-17:00

scenarios.title: App Works on Some Machines, Blocked on Others
scenarios.situation: A line-of-business application launches fine on 40 machines but is blocked on 15 others. Same installer, same version. The customer insists the policy is applied everywhere.
scenarios.prompt: What is the most likely explanation?
choices: The 15 machines are infected and the blocks are correct
The 15 machines have a corrupted agent and need to be reinstalled
The machines are in different policy groups. The application is approved in one group's policy but not the other's, so group membership or policy scoping differs between the two sets
The application is randomly choosing whether to run
scenarios.why: Inconsistent behavior across identical software almost always points to policy scoping: the machines sit in different groups with different policies, and the application is approved in one but not the other. The engineer should compare group membership and the effective policy for a working vs. a blocked machine. Jumping to reinstallation or assuming infection skips the obvious configuration check, and application behavior is deterministic, not random.
scenarios.hint: Same file, same version, different result. What differs between the machines?
evidence: Group: Workstations-East | Policy: Standard v12 | invoicer.exe: Allowed
Group: Workstations-West | Policy: Standard v11 | invoicer.exe: Denied (not on allowlist)

scenarios.title: Portable App Blocked from USB
scenarios.situation: A traveling sales rep runs a portable presentation tool from a USB drive. It is blocked on her laptop. The same tool runs fine when copied to the local drive on her colleague's machine.
scenarios.prompt: Which two controls are interacting here, and how should the engineer resolve it?
choices: USB ports are physically broken on her laptop
The application is incompatible with USB drives
Only the antivirus is involved; add an exclusion

Storage Control is denying execution from removable media, and Allowlisting has no entry for the portable executable. Resolve by approving the executable's hash and, if business-justified, creating a scoped Storage Control exception for that device or file
scenarios.why: Two controls intersect: Storage Control governs what removable media can do (many policies block execution from USB outright), and Allowlisting independently requires the executable itself to be approved. The colleague's machine works because the file sits on an allowed path and may already be approved. The fix addresses both layers: approve the file hash and create a narrowly scoped storage exception if the business need justifies it, rather than opening USB execution broadly.
scenarios.hint: Two different policies can each independently deny the same action. Which two?
objectives: Create scoped exceptions instead of broad openings
evidence: Denied: E:\presenter\present.exe | Reasons: (1) Execution from removable media denied by Storage Control; (2) File not on allowlist

scenarios.title: USB Drives Blocked for Everyone
scenarios.situation: After enabling Storage Control, no USB drives work anywhere in the company — including for the IT staff who need them for legitimate work. The security team wants USB restricted but not unusable for authorized purposes.
scenarios.prompt: What is the right configuration?
choices: Disable Storage Control; USB blocking causes too many complaints

Keep the default deny, then build scoped exceptions: allow specific encrypted device models, or specific AD groups (like IT), or require encryption. Deny-by-default stays, legitimate use gets a defined path
Allow all USB drives for everyone to stop the complaints
Physically glue all USB ports shut
scenarios.why: Storage Control's value is deny-by-default on removable media; the complaints come from having no defined legitimate path, not from the control itself. The mature configuration keeps the deny and adds narrow exceptions: approved encrypted drive models, authorized groups, or per-device approvals. This preserves the security benefit (unknown USB devices still blocked) while giving IT and others a workable process.
scenarios.hint: The control is not the problem; the missing piece is the legitimate path through it.
evidence: Storage Control: Deny all removable storage (applied org-wide 2026-10-07)
63 USB-related tickets in 3 days, including 11 from IT staff

scenarios.title: Encrypted USB Works, Unencrypted Blocked
scenarios.situation: A user reports their personal unencrypted USB drive is blocked, but the company-issued encrypted drive works fine. They demand the personal drive be allowed.
scenarios.prompt: How should the engineer respond?
choices: Format the personal drive and hope it starts working
Allow the personal drive; the user needs it

Explain this is the policy working as designed: Storage Control permits encrypted, company-approved devices and denies unencrypted personal media to prevent data loss. Offer the approved encrypted drive process instead of making an exception
Disable encryption requirements for everyone
scenarios.why: This is not a malfunction — it is the intended outcome of an encryption-enforcing storage policy. Unencrypted removable media is a data-loss vector, so the policy deliberately permits only encrypted approved devices. The correct response is to explain the design and route the user to the approved device process. Allowing the personal drive would create exactly the gap the policy was built to close.
scenarios.hint: Is anything actually broken here? What is the policy trying to achieve?
evidence: Storage Control: Allow only BitLocker-encrypted removable drives (company-issued)
Personal drive: unencrypted, unknown origin | Company drive: BitLocker, issued 2026-06-15

scenarios.title: One-Time USB Need for Presentation
scenarios.situation: An executive needs to present from a USB drive at a client site in two hours. Company policy blocks unapproved USB devices. There is no time for the normal device-approval process.
scenarios.prompt: What is the best handling?
choices: Tell the executive to cancel the presentation
Disable Storage Control on the executive's laptop indefinitely
Permanently allow all USB drives so this never happens again
Grant a time-limited, audited exception for the specific device (or copy the presentation to an approved encrypted drive). Log the exception, set it to expire, and review it afterward
scenarios.why: Urgent legitimate needs should be met through temporary, scoped, audited exceptions — not permanent policy changes. Approving the specific device for a few hours (or moving the files to an approved encrypted drive) solves the immediate need, the expiration automatically restores the secure baseline, and the audit trail records who approved what and why. Permanent changes made under time pressure tend to persist long after the emergency.
scenarios.hint: How do you say yes to the emergency without saying yes forever?
evidence: Exec needs USB access 14:00-18:00 today for client presentation
Normal device approval SLA: 2 business days (cannot meet the deadline)

scenarios.title: Ransomware Detained at the Gates
scenarios.situation: At 09:14, a user opened a weaponized spreadsheet from a phishing email. Within seconds, the ThreatLocker agent blocked a cascade of malicious actions: a macro spawning PowerShell, PowerShell attempting to disable recovery, and an encryption routine targeting network shares. The SOC wants a full timeline of what engaged, in order, and confirmation that nothing executed.
scenarios.prompt: Reconstruct the attack chain and map each stage to the ThreatLocker control that stopped it. What do you report to the SOC?
choices: Walk the chain: the spreadsheet arrived (fetch policy), Excel launched (allowlisted, approved), the macro's PowerShell spawn was denied by Ringfencing's application leash, the recovery-disable attempt was denied by the registry/file leashes, and the share-encryption attempt was denied by the network/file leashes. Each deny is logged as a detection. Recommend isolating the machine for forensic imaging, hunting for lateral movement, and reviewing how the phishing email bypassed email filtering
Wipe the machine immediately without investigation
Disable macros for the entire company and close the ticket
Report that the antivirus caught everything and no further action is needed
scenarios.why: A proper incident report narrates the kill chain against the controls: each stage of the attack met a specific deny, and the audit log holds the evidence. The value is in the ordered mapping — it proves nothing executed and shows exactly where the attack died. Wiping without imaging destroys forensic evidence, and claiming antivirus handled it misattributes the controls. The follow-through (isolate, hunt laterally, fix the email vector) is what separates a block from a resolved incident.
scenarios.hint: Map each attacker action to the control that denied it, in order. Then think about what happens AFTER the block.
objectives: Map a ransomware kill chain to layered controls
evidence: excel.exe spawned powershell.exe via macro | Denied by Application leash
powershell.exe attempted vssadmin delete shadows | Denied (process never launched; parent denied)
Unapproved binary 'enc.exe' attempted execution | Denied by Allowlisting (hash unknown)
Phishing email passed SPF/DKIM; attachment scanned clean by signature (zero-day macro)

scenarios.title: False Positive on Critical Business App
scenarios.situation: At 10:30 on month-end close day, the finance team's ERP client is suddenly blocked on all 60 machines. Finance is escalating to the CIO. The block started 20 minutes ago, coinciding with an automatic ERP update. The business cannot close the books.
scenarios.prompt: How do you resolve this urgently without creating a lasting security gap?
choices: Put the whole company in Monitor Only mode until finance is done

Confirm the block is a hash-change from the legitimate ERP update (verify signature and source), push an emergency approval for the new version scoped to the ERP executable, verify finance is unblocked, then schedule a review of the update-approval workflow so future vendor updates are pre-approved
Tell finance to wait until tomorrow
Uninstall ThreatLocker from the finance machines
scenarios.why: This is the classic speed-vs-safety incident: the business is stopped, but the fix must not be a permanent hole. The correct play is verify-then-approve under pressure — confirm the new binary is the legitimate vendor update (signature, source, timing correlation), approve that specific version immediately, and confirm restoration. Monitor Only mode or uninstalling would leave the entire estate unprotected. The post-incident action (pre-approving vendor updates) prevents recurrence.
scenarios.hint: What changed 20 minutes ago? How do you fix it fast AND safely?
evidence: Denied: erpclient.exe | 60 endpoints | Started 10:10 | Reason: hash not on allowlist
ERP vendor pushed auto-update v9.4.1 at 10:05 (signed, legitimate channel)
Month-end close blocked | Escalation: CIO | 60 finance users idle

scenarios.title: Policy Conflict Causes Widespread Blocks
scenarios.situation: After a junior admin pushed a new 'hardened' policy to the entire organization, hundreds of users report blocked applications. The help desk queue has 400 tickets. The admin who made the change is on leave. You have portal access and 30 minutes before the next status call.
scenarios.prompt: What is your incident response sequence?
choices: Wait for the junior admin to return from leave
Delete the new policy immediately and hope the old one comes back

Triage: identify the new policy's scope and the deny patterns in the audit log, roll back or narrow the policy change (revert to the previous version or scope it to a pilot group), verify blocks stop, then establish a change-control process requiring peer review and staged rollouts for future policy changes
Tell all users to reboot
scenarios.why: A bad policy push is an incident like any other: triage first (what changed, what is it denying), contain (roll back or narrow the scope), verify (confirm blocks stop), then fix the process (change control, peer review, staged rollouts). Deleting policies blindly can leave machines with no policy or create new gaps. The 30-minute status call needs a clear story: cause identified, containment done, prevention planned.
scenarios.hint: Treat the bad policy like any incident: triage, contain, verify, then fix the process.
evidence: 2026-10-10 07:55: Policy 'Hardened-v2' pushed org-wide by jadmin (now on leave)
Denied: 2,140 events in 35 min | Top: chrome.exe updates, teams.exe, vpnclient.exe (all legitimate, previously allowed)
400 tickets | Common: 'my apps stopped working after this morning'

scenarios.title: Agents Offline Across a Site
scenarios.situation: The entire Springfield branch (85 machines) shows offline in the portal. Users are working normally. The branch manager reports 'the internet was flaky this morning.' No policy changes were made. The SOC is concerned about losing visibility.
scenarios.prompt: How do you diagnose and restore visibility?
choices: Ignore it; the agents will come back on their own eventually
Recreate all 85 computer objects in the portal
Drive to Springfield and reinstall every agent

Work the connectivity chain: confirm the agent services are running locally, test the path to the portal (including the morning's network flakiness, proxy, and firewall), check for anything that changed at the site edge, and restore the path. Note that endpoints continue enforcing cached policy while offline, so protection persists during the visibility gap
scenarios.why: Eighty-five machines going offline together points to a site-level path issue, not 85 individual agent failures — especially with 'flaky internet' reported that morning. The diagnostic chain is endpoint (service running?) → path (can it reach the portal?) → change (what happened at the site edge?). Importantly, offline agents keep enforcing their last policy, so the branch is still protected; the incident is about visibility and future updates, which frames the urgency correctly for the SOC.
scenarios.hint: 85 machines at one site, same morning the internet was flaky. Individual failure or common cause?
objectives: Distinguish protection continuity from visibility loss
evidence: 85 machines, site=Springfield: last check-in 08:12 (staggered over 4 min, suggesting network event)
WKST-SPR-022: agent service running, Test-NetConnection to portal: FAILED (timeout)

scenarios.title: Zero-Day Execution Attempt
scenarios.situation: An unknown executable with no signature and no reputation appeared in a user's Downloads folder and attempted to run. ThreatLocker denied it. The file does not match any known malware signature. The user claims they 'don't know where it came from.'
scenarios.prompt: The block worked. What is the complete response?
choices: Treat the deny as a detection: preserve the file for analysis, image the machine for forensics, hunt for how it arrived (browser history, email, USB), check for lateral movement indicators across the estate, and brief the SOC on the delivery vector so defenses can be tuned
Delete the file and tell the user to be more careful
Approve the file so you can see what it does
Close the ticket; the block handled it
scenarios.why: Deny-by-default shines against zero-days precisely because it does not need a signature — unknown means denied. But the block is the beginning of the response, not the end. The file is evidence: its delivery vector (how did it get into Downloads?), its behavior (what did it try to do?), and whether siblings exist elsewhere in the estate. Closing the ticket at the block leaves the intrusion vector open for the next attempt.
scenarios.hint: The block is a detection. What does a detection demand next?
objectives: Hunt delivery vectors for unknown files
evidence: Denied: invoice_2026.exe | SHA256: unknown, unsigned, first seen in estate | Downloads folder
'I don't know where it came from' (browser history shows a typo-squatted domain visit 20 min prior)
Same hash found on 0 other machines (isolated incident, so far)

scenarios.title: Insider Data Exfiltration Attempt
scenarios.situation: HR flagged a departing employee. The audit log shows the employee plugged in a personal USB drive and attempted to copy the customer database export (4 GB) to it. Storage Control denied the copy. The employee claims it was 'just personal files.'
scenarios.prompt: What actions should the engineer take, and in what order?
choices: Allow the copy; the employee says they are personal files

Secure the evidence first: preserve the audit logs and block events, confirm what was and was not copied (was any data actually exfiltrated before the deny?), notify HR/security leadership per the insider-threat playbook, and keep the machine isolated for investigation. The deny is evidence, not the end of the matter
Confront the employee directly and demand an explanation
Delete the audit logs to protect the employee's privacy
scenarios.why: A denied exfiltration attempt is a security incident requiring the insider-threat playbook: preserve evidence before anything else (logs can be the basis for legal action), determine the actual data movement (did anything leave before the deny, via other channels?), and escalate through proper channels rather than confronting the individual. The engineer's role is evidence and containment; HR and legal own the personnel response. Deleting logs would destroy evidence and potentially constitute obstruction.
scenarios.hint: The deny stopped this attempt. But what must be established before anyone declares victory?
objectives: Determine actual vs. attempted data movement
evidence: Denied: copy of C:\Exports\customers_2026Q3.csv (4.1 GB) → E:\ (personal USB, unencrypted)
Employee resignation submitted yesterday; drive plugged in 09:40 today
No previous USB usage by this user in 12 months (anomaly)

scenarios.title: Elevation Abuse Attempt
scenarios.situation: The audit log shows a standard user repeatedly attempting to elevate an unapproved system tool over three days, including renaming the executable to match an approved application's name. Elevation Control denied each attempt.
scenarios.prompt: How should this be handled?
choices: Rename the approved application so the trick stops working
Approve the elevation; the user is persistent and probably needs it

Recognize the pattern as deliberate bypass attempts (especially the renaming): deny, document the timeline, escalate to the user's manager and security team as a policy violation, and review whether the underlying business need is legitimate (if so, solve it through proper channels, not through the bypass)
Ignore it since every attempt was denied
scenarios.why: Repeated elevation attempts culminating in executable renaming is not a confused user — it is a deliberate bypass attempt and a policy violation. The denials worked, but the behavior must be escalated: document the timeline, involve management and security, and address any legitimate underlying need through proper approval workflows. Ignoring it misses both the personnel issue and the chance to solve the real need legitimately.
scenarios.hint: One attempt is confusion. Renaming the file to impersonate an approved app is something else. What?
evidence: Day 1: 3 elevation attempts (sysutil.exe) denied | Day 2: 5 attempts denied | Day 3: sysutil.exe renamed to notepad.exe, 4 attempts denied
Standard user, no approved business need on file for this tool

scenarios.title: Lateral Movement Blocked
scenarios.situation: Overnight, a compromised service account attempted to move laterally: SMB connections to 12 workstations, WMI queries against the domain, and a credential-dumping tool execution attempt. Network Control and application controls denied the movements. The SOC needs to know the blast radius.
scenarios.prompt: What is the engineer's role in scoping this incident?
choices: Shut down the entire network immediately
Reset every password in the company without investigation
Nothing was blocked, so there is no incident

Use the deny logs as the incident map: enumerate every denied lateral movement (which targets, which protocols), confirm the attacker's foothold machine, verify no movement succeeded (check for any allows in the same timeframe), and hand the SOC a scoped timeline showing the contained blast radius plus the initial compromise vector to remediate
scenarios.why: The deny logs are a gift to incident response: they enumerate exactly what the attacker tried and where, which is precisely the blast-radius map the SOC needs. The engineer's job is to turn those logs into a scoped timeline — foothold, attempted movements (all denied), and confirmation that nothing succeeded — plus the initial vector for remediation. Panic responses like shutting down the network or mass resets without scoping cause more damage than the contained attack.
scenarios.hint: Every denied attempt is a data point. What story do they tell together?
evidence: svc-backup → SMB (445) to 12 workstations | All denied by Network Control (no rule for this account)
mimikatz.exe attempted execution on WKST-007 | Denied by Allowlisting
WKST-007: svc-backup logged on interactively at 02:14 (anomalous; service accounts should not log on interactively)

scenarios.title: Mass Deployment Gone Wrong
scenarios.situation: IT pushed a new VPN client to 500 machines using a Learning Mode window. After the window closed, 120 machines cannot connect to VPN. The deployment team says 'it worked on the pilot group.' The VPN project deadline is tomorrow.
scenarios.prompt: What went wrong, and how do you fix it under deadline?
choices: Diagnose the delta: the pilot group and the failing 120 likely differ (different OS build, different existing policy, or the learning window missed components that only execute on first real connection). Identify the missing approvals from the deny logs, push targeted approvals for the VPN client's full component set, verify on a failing machine, then roll out. Document the pilot-vs-production gap for next time
Deploy a different VPN product
Tell the 120 users to work from the office
Reopen Learning Mode indefinitely until it works
scenarios.why: Learning Mode only learns what actually executes during the window — if the pilot did not exercise every component (e.g., the tunnel driver that loads on first real connection), those components remain unknown and get denied later. The fix is to find the delta via the deny logs, approve the missing pieces deliberately, and verify. Reopening Learning Mode indefinitely reintroduces the risk the window was meant to bound, and the deadline pressure is exactly when deliberate verification matters most.
scenarios.hint: Learning Mode learns what runs during the window. What if something important did not run then?
objectives: Compare pilot vs. production execution paths
evidence: Denied: vpnfilter.sys (driver) | 120 machines | Never executed during learning window
Pilot group tested 'connect' but not 'reconnect after sleep' (which loads the filter driver)

scenarios.title: Multi-Vector Attack Simulation (Capstone)
scenarios.situation: Exercise: a red team simulated a full attack — phishing delivery, macro execution, credential theft attempt, USB drop, and lateral movement — against a ThreatLocker-protected estate. You are given the complete audit log. Walk the exercise as the blue team lead: for each vector, state what the attacker tried, which control engaged, and what residual risk or follow-up remains.
scenarios.prompt: What does a complete blue-team readback cover?
choices: Everything was blocked, so the readback is one sentence: 'We are secure.'

Vector by vector: (1) phishing email → attachment macro → PowerShell spawn denied by Ringfencing application leash; residual: tune email filtering. (2) credential-store read attempt → denied by Ringfencing; residual: verify no cached creds exposed. (3) USB drop with unknown binary → denied by Storage Control + Allowlisting; residual: physical security review. (4) lateral SMB → denied by Network Control; residual: segment review. For each: the deny, the evidence, and the hardening follow-up. The readback proves defense-in-depth with an improvement backlog, not just 'blocked.'
The red team cheated; the exercise is invalid
Delete the audit logs to keep the report short
scenarios.why: A mature readback does not stop at 'blocked' — it walks each vector, names the engaging control, cites the evidence, and extracts the residual risk and hardening action. This is the capstone skill: converting control telemetry into a narrative that both proves the defense worked and produces an improvement backlog. 'We are secure' is a conclusion without evidence; the vector-by-vector walk is the evidence.
scenarios.hint: For each attack vector: what was tried, what stopped it, and what still needs hardening?
objectives: Synthesize multi-vector telemetry into a narrative
Extract residual risks from successful defenses
evidence: Macro → powershell.exe spawn | Denied (Ringfencing application leash)
Credential-store read by excel.exe | Denied (Ringfencing file leash)
SMB lateral to 6 hosts | Denied (Network Control)

domains.name: Demo Skills
domains.description: Showing, not telling: whiteboard design, live triage narration, teaching moments, and the demo discipline interviewers remember.

scenarios.title: “Show me how you'd investigate”
scenarios.situation: 'Here's a block event [shows audit entry]. Show me — don't tell me — how you'd investigate.' The interviewer wants the performance, not the description.
evidence: Read the entry aloud, extract the anatomy (who/what/rule/when/prevalence/verdict), state the hypothesis with the reasoning visible, name the next three checks, and the verdict they'd produce.

'Who: FIN-04, k.osei. What: updater.exe, signed Acme, hash not in catalog. Rule: default-deny, no match. When: 08:04, 14 endpoints. So: widespread, signed, post-push — version-change false positive. Next: confirm the signer, check the child installer, then the scoped certificate rule.'
'And I'd validate both ways before closing.' The investigation shown end to end — that was the ask.
scenarios.prompt: Show them. Don't tell them.
choices: I would start by gathering information about the event and then analyze it systematically

[Read the entry aloud.] 'Who, what, rule, when, prevalence — 14 endpoints, signed vendor, changed hash, default-deny. That's version-churn: my next three checks are the signer confirmation, the child installer, and the prevalence trend — then the scoped certificate rule, validated both ways.' [The investigation, performed, not described.]
I'd escalate this to the senior analyst
I'd approve the hash so the user can work
scenarios.hint: Show, don't tell. What does the panel SEE in the winning answer — and what's missing in the others?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it performs the investigation live (reads aloud, extracts anatomy, hypothesizes visibly, names next checks, closes with validation) — showing, not telling. A is wrong: describing investigation generically is the telling the question forbids. C is wrong: escalating a diagnosable false positive is the abdication. D is wrong: hash approval is both the wrong rule type and the unperformed answer.

scenarios.title: The whiteboard freezes
scenarios.situation: Mid-whiteboard (designing the policy), you blank: the marker hovers, the structure evaporates, the panel watches. Thirty seconds of silence. What do you do?
evidence: Name it lightly and rebuild from the smallest piece: 'Lost the thread for a second — let me restart from the one thing I'm sure of: the three layers.' The restart is the recovery; the honesty is the composure.
Panels watch recovery more than perfection: the candidate who rebuilds calmly demonstrates the on-shift skill (incidents blank you too). The freeze handled well OUTSCORES the flawless board.
Always start whiteboards from the memorized skeleton (layers, loop, tree) — the skeleton survives blanks; improvisation doesn't.
scenarios.prompt: Thirty seconds of silence. Your move?
choices: Keep staring until it comes back

'Lost the thread — restarting from what I'm sure of: the three layers.' [Redraw the skeleton, rebuild aloud.] The calm rebuild demonstrates exactly the composure incidents require — panels score recovery over perfection
Apologize profusely and ask to skip the exercise
Fill the silence with random rules
scenarios.hint: Blanked, marker hovering, panel watching. What are they scoring NOW — the board, or something else?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it recovers via the memorized skeleton, names the blank lightly (honesty, not shame), and rebuilds aloud — turning the freeze into a composure demonstration. A is wrong: staring silently lets the freeze become the story. C is wrong: profuse apology plus skipping surrenders the exercise. D is wrong: random rules to fill silence is panic made visible.

scenarios.title: The panel's skeptical question mid-demo
scenarios.situation: Mid-demo (walking the triage), an engineer interrupts: 'But wouldn't the attacker just use a signed binary?' Good question — slightly adversarial. Handle it without losing the demo.
evidence: 'Great question — yes, and that's exactly where Ringfencing comes in.' Welcome the interruption: it shows engagement, and your answer shows depth.

Signed-binary attacks are the assume-breach case: the allowlist approves the binary (correctly — it's signed), and Ringfencing governs its behavior (the malicious USE hits the leashes). 'The model expects this — that's why it's two questions, not one.'
'...which brings us back to the triage: with the behavior leashed, the deny becomes our detection.' Bridge back to the demo — the interruption answered, the thread resumed.
scenarios.prompt: Interrupted, slightly adversarial. Handle it.
choices: That's out of scope for this demo

'Great question — that's the assume-breach case the model is built for: the signed binary gets approved (correctly), and Ringfencing governs what it may DO — the malicious use hits the behavior leashes. Two questions, not one.' [Bridge back:] 'Which is why the deny becomes our detection — back to the triage...'
Um, that's a really advanced topic...
Ignore it and continue the demo
scenarios.hint: Good adversarial question, mid-demo. What does welcoming it signal — and what does dodging signal?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: welcomes the question, answers it substantively (assume-breach, two questions), and bridges back to the demo — engagement plus depth plus control. A is wrong: 'out of scope' dodges the exact question the model is designed to answer. C is wrong: 'advanced topic' is the dodge wearing humility. D is wrong: ignoring an engaged panelist is the relationship failure.

scenarios.title: The 'teach me' ambush
scenarios.situation: No warning: 'Teach me Ringfencing. Two minutes. Starting now.' The ambush tests preparation meeting composure.
evidence: Hook ('imagine Word trying to become ransomware'), core ('approved apps get leashes'), the four leashes (named fast), the one-liner close ('Word on a leash'), empowerment ('that's why your approvals matter').
No panic, no throat-clearing: straight into the hook. The ambush tests whether the teaching is memorized-structure or improvised — structure wins.
Two minutes means 100 seconds of content and a 20-second buffer. The disciplined close at 1:40 beats the ramble into overtime.
scenarios.prompt: Two minutes. Starting now.
choices: So, Ringfencing is, um, a security control that, like, restricts applications...

'Picture Word trying to turn into ransomware: Ringfencing puts it on a leash — it can run, but it can't launch PowerShell, read your saved passwords, or phone home. Four leashes: what it can launch, what files it touches, what registry keys, where on the network. That's assume-breach in one product: we design as if Word is already compromised. And that's why the approval decisions you'll make matter — you're holding the leash.'
Ringfencing constrains application behavior across four dimensions...
Can I have a minute to prepare?
scenarios.hint: Ambush, two minutes, no prep. What carries you — improvisation, or memorized structure?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: hook, core, four leashes, one-liner, empowerment — the memorized teaching structure deployed instantly, conversational not recited. A is wrong: the 'um, like' opening is the improvisation the ambush hunts. C is wrong: the dimension-listing is accurate but unhooked — no story, no empowerment. D is wrong: asking for prep time surrenders the ambush's entire test.

scenarios.title: The demo that fails live
scenarios.situation: You're demoing the triage live — and your example breaks: the 'signed updater' you picked turns out to have an expired certificate in your notes. The panel notices. Recover.
evidence: 'Good catch — my example just got more interesting: expired cert changes the triage. Now the signer verification FAILS, so this becomes hold-and-verify, not approve. The method handles it — watch.'
The broken example becomes the BETTER demo: it shows the method adapting to new evidence in real time — which is the actual skill being tested. Perfection wouldn't have shown it.
No covering, no breezing past: acknowledge, incorporate, continue. The panel's 'catch' becomes your demonstration.
scenarios.prompt: Your example just broke, live. Recover.
choices: Pretend you didn't notice and continue

'Good catch — that actually improves the demo: expired certificate means the signer check FAILS, so my verdict changes from approve to hold-and-verify. That's the method working — new evidence, new verdict, stated aloud.' [Continue with the revised triage.]
Apologize and pick a different example
Blame your notes
scenarios.hint: Live demo, broken example, panel watching. Is this a disaster — or the best thing that could happen?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: it converts the break into the better demo (method adapting to evidence, live), acknowledges honestly, and continues stronger — the recovery as performance. A is wrong: breezing past a caught error destroys credibility. C is wrong: restarting wastes the gift — the adaptation WAS the demo. D is wrong: blaming notes is the smallness the moment punishes.

scenarios.title: The closing demo: your 90 days
scenarios.situation: 'Last one: show me your first 90 days. Whiteboard it.' The closing demo — they're picturing you in the role. Make them see it.
evidence: 30/60/90 on the board: 30 — learn (queue, audit, team rhythms; earn trust; no big changes). 60 — contribute (own a domain, ship one tuning, first process improvement). 90 — lead (a wave, a review, a measurable win).

'First I learn the operation before I touch it — the queue, the audit patterns, how the team triages. Then I contribute: I'd want to own [domain] and ship one real improvement. By 90, I'd lead something measurable — with the team's trust earned, not assumed.'
End with the measurable: '...and you'd see it in [metric].' The candidate who's already planning the work — on their whiteboard, in their interview — is the candidate they hire.
scenarios.prompt: Whiteboard your 90 days. Go.
choices: I'd spend the first month learning and then see what needs doing

[Draw 30/60/90.] 'Thirty: learn the operation — the queue, the audit rhythms, how this team triages. No big changes; earn trust. Sixty: contribute — own a domain, ship one tuning win, propose one process improvement. Ninety: lead something measurable — a wave, a review — with trust earned. You'd see it in [approval turnaround / block rate].' [Circle the 90-day metric.]
I'd hit the ground running on day one
I'd need to see the environment first before planning
scenarios.hint: They're picturing you in the role. What do they need to SEE — eagerness, or a plan?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: 30/60/90 with the learn-then-contribute-then-lead arc, narrated with humility ('earn trust, not assumed'), ending on the measurable — the hireable vision. A is wrong: 'learn then see' is the plan without the plan. C is wrong: 'hit the ground running' is the eagerness that breaks things on day one. D is wrong: refusing to plan until seeing the environment dodges the vision question.

domains.name: Homelab Evidence
domains.description: Built, not just read: the homelab as interview proof — what to build, how to story it, and turning tinkering into evidence.

scenarios.title: “Tell me about your homelab”
scenarios.situation: The depth probe, plainly asked: 'Tell me about your homelab.' The panel settles in. Sixty seconds of specifics — or sixty seconds of vague.
evidence: Build-break-lesson with specifics: 'Three VMs — DC, workstation, isolated net. I simulated allowlist triage: changed a binary's hash, watched the deny, wrote the triage note, fixed it with a scoped rule. First attempt blocked the domain logon — the audit showed my baseline missed it. Lesson: inventory before enforcement, always.'
