Specifics (tool names, configs, errors), the breakage (debugging thinking), and the role link ('which is why I'd canary every change here').

'I have some VMs set up' (vague = fail), reciting tutorial steps (no thinking shown), or 'I don't really have one' (the honesty option — then pivot to the plan: 'here's what I'm building this month').
scenarios.prompt: Sixty seconds. Go.
choices: I have a homelab with a few VMs where I practice security concepts

'Three VMs: domain controller, workstation, isolated attacker network. I run allowlist triage drills — rehash a binary, watch the deny, write the triage note, fix with a scoped rule. First run blocked the domain logon because my baseline missed it; the audit showed me exactly where. Lesson I keep: inventory before enforcement — which is why I'd canary every policy change here.'
I followed some online tutorials for setting up a lab
I don't have one, but I'm a fast learner
scenarios.hint: Sixty seconds, specifics or vague. What does the panel LEAN IN for — and what makes them check out?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: build-break-lesson with real specifics (three VMs named, the rehash drill, the logon blockage, the audit read), the lesson stated, and the role link — the complete depth performance. A is wrong: 'a few VMs, security concepts' is the vagueness that fails the probe. C is wrong: tutorial-following without the breakage story shows no thinking. D is wrong: 'fast learner' without the plan is the empty pivot — the plan ('building this month, here's the design') would have saved it.

scenarios.title: “What broke?”
scenarios.situation: They liked the homelab story. Follow-up: 'What broke? Tell me about the debugging.' They're drilling for the thinking.
evidence: The break ('my policy blocked the domain logon'), the confusion ('I assumed the baseline was complete'), the investigation ('the audit showed the logon binary's hash changed with the update — version churn, my old friend'), the fix ('certificate rule for the vendor'), the lesson.
The debugging PATH: hypothesis, evidence, revision. 'I assumed X, the evidence showed Y, so I...' — the thinking made visible.
'Nothing really broke' (then you didn't push it), or a breakage story with no investigation ('I just reinstalled').
scenarios.prompt: What broke? Walk me through the debugging.
choices: Nothing major broke; it went pretty smoothly

'My first policy blocked the domain logon — machines couldn't authenticate. I assumed the baseline was complete; the audit showed the logon binary's hash had changed with the update — version churn. So the assumption was wrong, not the engine: I replaced the hash rule with a certificate rule for the vendor, validated logons worked, and the lesson stuck — inventory the churners, don't hash them.'
I just reinstalled when things broke
The hypervisor was buggy
scenarios.hint: 'What broke?' — why is this the question they're REALLY asking?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: the break, the wrong assumption named, the evidence that corrected it, the fix with the reasoning, the lesson — debugging as thinking, fully visible. A is wrong: 'nothing broke' means nothing was pushed — the anti-story. C is wrong: 'just reinstalled' skips the entire investigation the question wants. D is wrong: blaming the hypervisor is the evasion.

scenarios.title: “No budget, no lab — now what?”
scenarios.situation: 'Suppose you had zero budget and no homelab. How would you stay sharp?' The resourcefulness probe, sharpened.
evidence: The free-tier plan (one VM on a free hypervisor, community bootcamp, open-source tooling, documentation labs), the depth-over-width choice, and the documentation habit — delivered as a plan, not a wish.
Initiative under constraint: the candidate who builds with nothing is the candidate who'll learn with anything. Excuses are the failure mode.
'I'd need the company to provide training' (the dependency answer) or 'I'd read a lot' (passive).
scenarios.prompt: Zero budget. How do you stay sharp?
choices: I'd need proper training resources to really learn

'One VM on a free hypervisor, deep not wide: triage drills, a policy paper I red-team myself, log-reading reps from generated data — plus the free community bootcamp and open-source tooling. And I'd document everything: the write-ups are the portfolio. Constraints pick the focus — depth over topology.'
I'd read documentation and watch videos
I'd wait until I could afford proper equipment
scenarios.hint: Zero budget. Is that a barrier — or a filter for resourcefulness?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: the concrete free-tier plan, the depth-over-width principle, the documentation habit — resourcefulness as a plan, not a posture. A is wrong: 'need proper resources' is the dependency the probe hunts. C is wrong: passive consumption isn't sharpness. D is wrong: waiting is the opposite of initiative.

scenarios.title: The write-up review
scenarios.situation: 'You mentioned a write-up. Walk me through it — what's in it?' They want to see the documentation instinct.
evidence: 'One page per exercise: the objective, the setup (with versions), the steps I ran, what broke, the triage notes verbatim, the fix, and the lesson. The triage notes are the heart — five lines each, evidence first.'
The documentation instinct: does this person write things down so others (or future-them) can use them? The write-up's existence is the signal; its structure is the proof.
'It's mostly in my head' (then it doesn't exist) or a 50-page dump (undisciplined). One page per exercise, structured, is the sweet spot.
scenarios.prompt: Walk me through the write-up.
choices: It's mostly in my head; I know my lab well

'One page per exercise: objective, setup with versions, steps run, what broke, the triage notes verbatim — five lines, evidence first — then the fix and the lesson. The notes are the heart of it; anyone should be able to replay the exercise from the page.'
I have a long document with everything in it
I haven't written it up yet but I plan to
scenarios.hint: 'Walk me through the write-up.' What are they really checking — the lab, or the habit?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: the structure (one page per exercise, the components), the replayability standard ('anyone should be able to replay it'), and the triage notes as the heart — the documentation instinct demonstrated. A is wrong: 'in my head' means it doesn't exist as evidence. C is wrong: the undifferentiated dump shows no discipline. D is wrong: 'plan to' is the future tense of not having it.

scenarios.title: The tutorial trap
scenarios.situation: 'A lot of candidates follow tutorials. What did you do that WASN'T in the tutorial?' The originality probe.
evidence: The deviation: 'the tutorial stopped at the allow rule — I kept going: I attacked my own rule with a renamed binary in a writable path, watched it get trusted, and then fixed the hole. The tutorial taught the feature; the deviation taught the judgment.'
Curiosity past the instructions: did you ask 'what if?' and follow it? The deviation is where the thinking lives.
'I followed it exactly' (no curiosity) or inventing a deviation (the bluff — the follow-up will ask for the specifics).
scenarios.prompt: What did you do that wasn't in the tutorial?
choices: I followed the tutorial exactly; it was comprehensive

'The tutorial ended at writing the allow rule — I kept going and attacked it: dropped a renamed binary into the writable path the rule allowed, watched it get trusted, then closed the hole with a signer rule and a locked directory. The tutorial taught the feature; breaking my own rule taught the judgment.'
I improved the tutorial's steps slightly
I don't remember the details
scenarios.hint: Past the tutorial's last step. What lives there — and why is THAT the interview answer?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: the genuine deviation (attacking the own rule, the writable-path hole, the fix), framed as feature-vs-judgment — curiosity with evidence. A is wrong: 'followed exactly' is the curiosity failure the probe hunts. C is wrong: 'slightly improved' is vague and unconvincing. D is wrong: 'don't remember' surrenders the question.

scenarios.title: The portfolio question
scenarios.situation: 'Where can I see your work?' The portfolio moment. What do you show — and how?
evidence: 'My write-ups are [location]: the triage exercises with the notes verbatim, the policy paper with the red-team findings, and a two-minute teaching recording. The [specific exercise] is the one I'd start with — it shows the full loop.'
Curation: do you know which piece is strongest, and can you guide them to it? 'Here's everything' is undifferentiated; 'start here' is confident.
Nothing to show ('it's all local'), or everything uncurated ('here's my 200-page doc'). The portfolio is curated evidence, not a data dump.
scenarios.prompt: Where can I see your work?
choices: It's all on my local machines; I can describe it

'My exercise write-ups are [location] — one page each: the triage drills with notes verbatim, the policy paper including the red-team findings against my own rules, and a two-minute teaching recording. Start with the [triage exercise]: it's the full loop — block, triage, narrow fix, double validation.'
Here's a link to my 200-page lab journal
I haven't published anything
scenarios.hint: 'Where can I see your work?' What distinguishes the portfolio from the pile?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: curated (the location, the components), guided ('start with...'), and the strongest piece named with its content previewed — confidence through curation. A is wrong: 'all local, I can describe' is the claim without the evidence. C is wrong: the undifferentiated dump is the pile, not the portfolio. D is wrong: 'haven't published' ends the evidence conversation — the pivot would be the plan, not the absence.

domains.name: Interview Logistics
domains.description: The unglamorous half of winning: scheduling, research, follow-up, references, and the thousand small things done right.

scenarios.title: The timezone trap
scenarios.situation: Confirmation says '10:00 AM' — no timezone. The company is in Orlando (ET), you're in Apopka (ET), but the recruiter who sent it is in Phoenix (MT). What do you do?
evidence: No-timezone confirmations are the classic miss: every party assumes their own zone. The recruiter in Phoenix writing '10:00 AM' might mean THEIR 10 AM.
Ask, explicitly, in the confirmation reply: 'Confirming 10:00 AM Eastern — is that correct? I'll join at [time] ET.' One sentence kills the ambiguity; the written confirmation is the record.
Every time, every zone, stated explicitly — in the confirmation, the calendar invite, and the day-before recheck. Timezone discipline is free; timezone misses are expensive.
scenarios.prompt: 10:00 AM, no zone, three timezones in play. Your move?
choices: Assume Eastern — everyone's in Florida anyway
'Confirming 10:00 AM Eastern — want to make sure I have the timezone right. I'll be ready at 10:00 AM ET on [date] via [format].' [Written, explicit, on the record.]
Show up at 10:00 AM Phoenix time to be safe
Email asking 'what timezone?' with no proposal
scenarios.hint: No timezone on the confirmation. What costs more — one clarifying sentence, or the miss?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: proposes the explicit time with the zone, asks for confirmation, creates the written record — the ambiguity killed in one sentence. A is wrong: assuming is how the trap closes (the recruiter's zone may differ). C is wrong: guessing Phoenix-time is the same assumption with extra steps. D is wrong: the bare question without a proposal is weaker than proposing-and-confirming.

scenarios.title: The panel surprise
scenarios.situation: You arrive (video) expecting one interviewer. Four faces appear: the manager, two engineers, and — surprise — a C-level executive. Thirty seconds to adjust. How?
evidence: Welcome it: 'Great to meet everyone — I wasn't expecting such a full panel; I appreciate the time.' Warm, unruffled, honest about the surprise without complaint.

Same content, shifted spotlight: the technical depth for the engineers, the business framing when the executive engages, the team-fit thread for the manager. Read the room per question — who asked owns the emphasis.
The surprise panel is often deliberate (how do they handle the unexpected?) or accidental (scheduling) — either way, the unruffled candidate who adapts the spotlight wins both versions.
scenarios.prompt: Four faces, one expected. Thirty seconds. Go.
choices: This is unexpected — I prepared for a 1:1

'Great to meet all of you — appreciate everyone making the time.' [Same preparation, recalibrated spotlight: depth for the engineers, business framing for the executive, fit for the manager — read each question's asker.]
Should we reschedule with proper notice?
[Freeze and wait for instructions]
scenarios.hint: Surprise panel. What are they watching in the first 30 seconds — your content, or your composure?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: warm welcome, honest-and-unruffled, then the spotlight recalibration per asker — adaptability demonstrated live. A is wrong: announcing the unpreparedness centers your discomfort, not their time. C is wrong: requesting a reschedule over a surprise panel reads as rigid. D is wrong: freezing surrenders the 30 seconds that matter most.

scenarios.title: The post-interview silence
scenarios.situation: They said 'we'll decide by Friday.' It's now the following Wednesday — silence. Your move?
evidence: Timelines slip constantly (headcount, calendars, competing candidates) — silence past the date is normal, not a verdict. One polite nudge is the professional move.

'Hi [name] — checking in on the [role] process. You'd mentioned Friday; no rush at all, just wanted to confirm I'm still very interested and available for any follow-ups. Thanks, [name].' Warm, zero pressure, interest reaffirmed.
One nudge now; if silence continues, one more in a week; then stop and move on. Two nudges max — dignity intact, pipeline full regardless.
scenarios.prompt: Friday came and went. Wednesday now. What do you send?
choices: Nothing — they'll contact you if interested

'Hi [name] — checking in on the [role] process; you'd mentioned Friday. Still very interested and happy to do any follow-ups. Thanks!' [One nudge; one more in a week if needed; then move on with dignity.]
Did I get the job?
Call the hiring manager directly
scenarios.hint: Silence past the promised date. What's the professional move — and where's the line?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: one warm, zero-pressure nudge reaffirming interest, with the two-nudge cadence understood — professional persistence. A is wrong: total silence surrenders the process to drift (timelines slip; nudges are expected). C is wrong: 'did I get the job' is the pressure the nudge must avoid. D is wrong: escalating to a direct call over a slipped timeline is the boundary crossed.

scenarios.title: The competing offer clock
scenarios.situation: You have Offer A (good, not dream) with a 48-hour deadline — and you're in final rounds at the dream company, deciding next week. Handle the clock.
evidence: Tell the dream company (once, warmly): 'I want to be transparent — I have an offer with a Friday deadline, but you're my first choice. Is there any way to know timing on your side?' Honesty plus preference stated — the ethical acceleration.
Ask Offer A for the extension professionally ('I'm very excited; I need until Wednesday to decide carefully') — extensions are routinely granted; the ask is normal.
Never fabricate a competing offer, never use an offer as a threat, never renege after accepting. The industry is small; the reputation is permanent.
scenarios.prompt: 48-hour clock, dream company deciding next week. Play it.
choices: Accept Offer A and renege if the dream comes through

[To dream company:] 'Transparently: I have an offer expiring Friday, and you're my first choice — any sense of timing on your end?' [To Offer A:] 'Very excited — could I have until Wednesday to decide carefully?' [Honest, parallel, no fabrication, no threats.]
Invent a higher competing offer for leverage
Let Offer A expire silently
scenarios.hint: Two clocks, one dream. What moves the process WITHOUT moving your ethics?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: transparent timeline-sharing with the preferred company (preference stated = ethical signal), professional extension ask of Offer A — both clocks managed honestly. A is wrong: accept-and-renege burns the bridge permanently. C is wrong: fabricated leverage is the ethics failure that can surface. D is wrong: letting it expire silently wastes the option.

scenarios.title: The reference ambush
scenarios.situation: 'We need three references by tomorrow.' You haven't warned anyone. What's the damage control?
evidence: Call (don't email) your three best work-witnesses TODAY: apologize for the short notice, brief them fast (the role, the themes, the story), confirm they're willing — then deliver the list on time with a note that they're briefed.
This scramble is why references get lined up BEFORE the process: the warned-and-briefed reference is an advocate; the ambushed one is a risk. Build the bench this week regardless of outcome.
Never list someone without asking — the unasked reference who gets the surprise call is the relationship damaged AND the lukewarm answer.
scenarios.prompt: Three references by tomorrow, nobody warned. Go.
choices: List three former colleagues without asking — fastest

[Call all three today:] 'I'm sorry for the short notice — I'm in final rounds for [role] and they need references tomorrow. Would you be willing? The themes are [X, Y]; the story I'd love told is [Z].' [Only the willing get listed; deliver on time, note they're briefed.]
Ask for a week's extension
List friends as professional references
scenarios.hint: Reference ambush, 24 hours. What's the non-negotiable — speed, or consent?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: call today, apologize for the rush, brief fast, confirm willingness — only the willing listed, delivered on time. A is wrong: listing without asking is the relationship damage AND the lukewarm-answer risk. C is wrong: extension asks over references signal unpreparedness (and may be denied). D is wrong: friends as professional references is the credibility failure.

scenarios.title: The thank-you that lands
scenarios.situation: Panel of three, interviews done. Tonight: the thank-you notes. What makes them land instead of blur?
evidence: Three notes, each with a genuine specific callback: the manager's wave-process point linked to your experience, the engineer's signed-binary question with the follow-up thought, the cross-functional's collaboration story echoed. Specificity = proof you listened.
Gratitude (one line), their-point-plus-your-fit (the callback), enthusiasm (one line, real). Sent tonight or tomorrow morning — within 24 hours.
'Thank you for your time, great speaking with you, I'm very interested' x3 — the generic template the panel forgets by morning.
scenarios.prompt: Three interviewers, tonight. Write the approach.
choices: One group email: 'Thanks everyone, great speaking with you!'

Three individual notes within 24 hours, each with a specific callback — [manager's point + your matching experience], [engineer's question + your follow-up thought], [collaboration story echoed] — gratitude, callback, genuine enthusiasm in each
Wait a week so you don't seem desperate
Send a gift basket
scenarios.hint: Three notes or one blast? What makes a thank-you REMEMBERED by Friday's decision meeting?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: individual notes, specific callbacks proving listening, the structure (gratitude/callback/enthusiasm), within 24 hours — the memorable follow-up. A is wrong: the group blast is the blur. C is wrong: waiting a week misses the decision window entirely. D is wrong: gifts are the boundary crossed (and often policy-violating).

domains.name: Compensation & Negotiation
domains.description: The money conversation, handled like a professional: research, range, total package, and negotiating without burning the offer.

scenarios.title: “What are your salary expectations?”
scenarios.situation: First-round recruiter screen, ten minutes in: 'So — what are your salary expectations?' You haven't discussed scope yet. Answer.
evidence: Naming a number now anchors everything that follows — before you know the scope, level, or their budget. The early number is almost always wrong (usually low).

Deflect professionally and reverse: 'I'd like to understand the full scope first — what's the budgeted range for the position?' If pressed: give the RESEARCHED range (not a single number), framed as market data.
Whoever names the number first anchors. Let it be them — or let it be your researched range, never a guess under pressure.
scenarios.prompt: Ten minutes in, scope unknown. Your answer?
choices: 'I'd like to understand the full scope of the role first so I can give you a thoughtful answer — what's the budgeted range for the position?' [If pressed: the researched range, framed as market data — never a guess.]
I'll take whatever you're offering
My last role paid $X so I'd need $X+20%
scenarios.hint: First money question, ten minutes in. What does naming a number NOW cost you?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: the professional deflection (scope first), the reversal (their budgeted range), and the researched-range fallback — no anchor dropped under pressure. A is wrong: the bare number with no scope is the anchor you'll regret. C is wrong: 'whatever you're offering' is the negotiation surrender. D is wrong: prior-pay-plus is both the anchor and (where restricted) the inappropriate basis.

scenarios.title: The lowball offer
scenarios.situation: Written offer arrives 15% below your researched target. You want the role. The team is great. Negotiate — without burning it.
evidence: Grateful and enthusiastic first — 'I'm excited about this offer.' Then the specific, market-justified ask, bundled in one round.

'Based on my research for this role and market, I was targeting [number]. Is there flexibility to get closer to that? I'm enthusiastic about the team and want to make this work.' One round, specific, justified — then decide.
Never: the ultimatum, the competing-offer bluff, the need-based plea. If they can't move: evaluate the package honestly against your floor — then decide with dignity either way.
scenarios.prompt: 15% below target, great team. Your negotiation?
choices: Accept immediately — don't risk it

'Thank you — I'm genuinely excited about this offer and the team. Based on my market research for this role, I was targeting [number]; is there flexibility to close the gap? I want to make this work.' [One bundled round, market-justified; then an honest package-vs-floor decision.]
This offer is insulting; I need $X or I walk
Invent a competing offer at your target
scenarios.hint: Below target, great team. What wins the gap — pressure, or the bundled market ask?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: gratitude first, the specific market-justified ask, bundled in one round, then the honest floor decision — collaborative, not adversarial. A is wrong: instant acceptance leaves the researched gap unasked (the ask is expected). C is wrong: the ultimatum burns the relationship the offer started. D is wrong: the bluff is the ethics failure.

scenarios.title: The exploding offer
scenarios.situation: 'We need your decision by tomorrow.' The exploding offer — pressure as a tactic. Respond.
evidence: Exploding offers are pressure tactics (sometimes legitimate — headcount timing; often not). The deadline is their urgency, not yours — and decisions made under manufactured pressure are regretted at leisure.

Grateful, boundaried: 'Thank you — I'm taking this seriously, which is why I need until [reasonable date] to decide carefully. If the timeline can't move, I understand.' Reasonable timelines are routinely granted; the ask tests whether the pressure was real.
A company that won't grant three days for a career decision is telling you about its culture. Listen.
scenarios.prompt: Decide by tomorrow. Your response?
choices: Decide tonight under pressure

'Thank you — because I'm taking this seriously, I need until [Wednesday] to decide carefully. Can the timeline move? If it truly can't, I understand — and I'll give you my answer by your deadline.' [The reasonable ask; their answer is data about the culture.]
Ignore the deadline and decide next week
Accept, then keep interviewing
scenarios.hint: 'By tomorrow.' Is the deadline information — or a tactic? And what does your response signal?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: grateful, boundaried, the reasonable extension asked (which is routinely granted), with the commitment to honor a truly firm deadline — and their response read as culture data. A is wrong: pressured decisions are the regret pipeline. C is wrong: ignoring a stated deadline is the professionalism failure. D is wrong: accept-and-continue is the integrity failure.

scenarios.title: The total-package comparison
scenarios.situation: Two offers: A = $95k base, thin benefits, flat role. B = $88k base, 6% 401(k) match, premium-free health, 4 weeks PTO, clear promotion path in 18 months. Decide like a professional.
evidence: B's lines: 6% match ≈ $5.3k, premium-free health ≈ $8–12k value, extra PTO weeks priced, the 18-month promotion path (the compounding line). B's real compensation meets or beats A's — before the growth.
The promotion path is the highest-value line: 18 months to the next band out-earns the $7k base gap within two years, then compounds. Flat roles don't.
Spreadsheet, not gut: every line priced, growth weighted, then the honest answer. 'A pays more' is the headline; 'B compensates more' is the math.
scenarios.prompt: $95k flat vs $88k rich. Decide.
choices: Take A — $95k is more than $88k

Run the package math: price B's match (~$5k), health value (~$8–12k), PTO, and weight the 18-month promotion path — B's real compensation meets/beats A before growth, and the growth compounds past it. Decide by the spreadsheet, likely B unless A's intangibles dominate
Take B because the people seemed nicer
Ask A to match B's benefits
scenarios.hint: Headline base vs full package. What does the professional decide by — the bigger number, or the math?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: prices every line (match, health, PTO), weights the growth path as the compounding line, decides by the spreadsheet — the total-package lens. A is wrong: headline-base thinking is the exact failure the domain teaches against. C is wrong: 'seemed nicer' is gut, not math (culture matters, but it's not the compensation analysis). D is wrong: benefit-matching asks are rarely productive and miss the point — evaluate what's offered.

scenarios.title: The non-compete in the offer
scenarios.situation: Written offer includes a 12-month non-compete: any 'endpoint security' employer, 100-mile radius. You're in Orlando — the industry's backyard. Handle it.
evidence: In Florida, non-competes have teeth — and this one's scope ('any endpoint security employer,' 100 miles from Orlando) could fence you out of your own industry. This is the line that matters most in the offer.

Raise it professionally BEFORE signing: 'I want to flag the non-compete's scope — 12 months across endpoint security within 100 miles would prevent me working in my field here. Can we narrow it to [specific competitors / shorter term]?' Negotiate the clause like the compensation — it IS compensation (of your future).
Concerning clauses get professional review before signing. Never sign a career-fencing clause hoping it won't be enforced.
scenarios.prompt: 12-month, 100-mile, 'any endpoint security employer.' Sign?
choices: Sign it — non-competes are never enforced

'Before I sign, I want to discuss the non-compete: 12 months / 100 miles / any endpoint security employer would prevent me from working in my field in Orlando. Can we narrow the scope [or term]? I'm excited about the role — I want the agreement to work for both of us.' [Negotiate the clause; get concerning language professionally reviewed.]
Refuse the offer over it immediately
Sign and ignore it
scenarios.hint: The clause fences your whole industry in your own city. What's the professional move — sign, refuse, or negotiate the line?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: flags the scope specifically, proposes narrowing (scope or term), treats the clause as negotiable compensation-of-the-future, with professional review as backstop — before signing. A is wrong: 'never enforced' is the Florida gamble you lose. C is wrong: immediate refusal skips the negotiation that routinely narrows these. D is wrong: sign-and-ignore is the hope-based legal strategy.

scenarios.title: The graceful decline
scenarios.situation: The package can't reach your floor. You've decided: decline. Write the decline that keeps the door open.
evidence: Gratitude (real), the decision (clear, no haggling), the reason (brief, package-fit — not blame), the door (open): 'I hope we can reconnect down the road.'

'Thank you for the offer and the time everyone invested — I genuinely enjoyed the process. After careful thought, the package isn't the right fit for me right now. I have real respect for the team and the mission, and I'd welcome staying in touch.'
Industries are small; hiring managers move; the declined offer today is the dream role in two years. The graceful decline is the cheapest career investment there is.
scenarios.prompt: Below floor. Decline it — gracefully.
choices: Ghost them — they'll get the message

'Thank you for the offer and everyone's time — I genuinely enjoyed meeting the team. After careful consideration, the package isn't the right fit for me at this time. I have real respect for the mission and the team, and I'd welcome staying in touch for the future.' [Clear, kind, door open.]
Your offer was too low; maybe next time offer more
Accept, then decline a week later
scenarios.hint: Below floor, decision made. What does the decline INVEST in?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: gratitude, clear decision, brief package-fit reason, the open door — the relationship preserved for the future (managers move; today's decline is tomorrow's role). A is wrong: ghosting is the reputation fire. C is wrong: 'offer more next time' is the parting shot that closes the door. D is wrong: accept-then-decline is the integrity failure.

domains.name: Day-One Readiness
domains.description: The offer's signed — now earn it: the first week, the first ticket, the first impression, and becoming the teammate they hired.

scenarios.title: The week-one temptation
scenarios.situation: Day 3: you spot it — a policy misconfiguration, obvious to you, affecting 200 endpoints. The fix is a one-line change. Your finger hovers. What do you do?
evidence: The fix is obvious, the impact is real, the change is small. Every instinct says: fix it now, be the hero.

Don't. Week one is learn-before-touch: flag it to your buddy/lead ('I spotted X — is this known? what's the change process?'), let the team own the fix, learn the process. The hero fix in week one bypasses the change control you haven't learned — and the blast radius you can't see.
The flagged-not-fixed week-one find earns MORE trust than the fix: it shows judgment (restraint), collaboration (flagged properly), and the eye (you spotted it). The team fixes it; you learn how.
scenarios.prompt: One-line fix, 200 endpoints, day 3. Your finger hovers. What wins — the hero fix, or the discipline?
choices: Fix it immediately — 200 endpoints need you, and it's one line
Flag it to your buddy/lead: 'I spotted a misconfiguration affecting ~200 endpoints — is this known? What's the change process here?' Let the team own the fix; learn how changes ship
Ignore it — not your place in week one
Post it in the team channel so everyone sees you found it
scenarios.hint: Week one is learn-before-touch. What earns more trust — the hero fix, or the flagged find?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: flag it through the proper channel, ask about the change process, let the team own the fix — the restraint that earns trust and teaches you the process. A is wrong: the week-one hero fix bypasses change control you haven't learned, with blast radius you can't see. C is wrong: ignoring it entirely wastes the find — flag, don't fix. D is wrong: the Slack blast is the visibility play without the judgment.

scenarios.title: The first on-call ticket
scenarios.situation: Week 2, your first real ticket: a wave of blocks after a vendor push — 40 endpoints, users locked out, the queue buzzing. It's yours. Work it.
evidence: Triage loop, narrated: acknowledge the wave, read the audit (who/what/rule/when/prevalence), hypothesize (version churn — signed vendor, changed hash, post-push), verify the signer, implement the scoped certificate rule, validate both ways.
Status early and often: 'Wave acknowledged — 40 endpoints, vendor push, looks like version churn. Verifying signer now, ETA 20 minutes.' The queue watches; the narration calms.
Full discipline: the note for the next person, the pattern logged (this vendor churns — pre-approve next time?), the follow-up if any endpoint didn't validate. Ticket one, closed like a senior.
scenarios.prompt: 40 endpoints, users locked out, week 2, yours. Work it.
choices: Fix it quietly and close the ticket

'Wave acknowledged — 40 endpoints post-vendor-push, reading the audit now.' [Triage narrated: version-churn hypothesis, signer verified, scoped certificate rule, double validation.] Status every 15 minutes; full close: the note, the pattern logged, follow-ups scheduled. [The method, visible.]
Escalate immediately — too big for week 2
Approve all the hashes to stop the bleeding
scenarios.hint: First real ticket, 40 endpoints, queue watching. What are they evaluating — the fix, or the method?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: the triage loop performed and narrated, status early and often, the full-discipline close — the method made visible under pressure. A is wrong: the quiet fix hides the method the team needs to see. C is wrong: escalating a diagnosable wave in week 2 is the ownership failure. D is wrong: hash-approval at wave scale is the wrong rule type AND the panic move.

scenarios.title: The feedback you didn't want
scenarios.situation: Week 3, you ask for feedback. Your lead: 'Your triage is solid, but your ticket notes are too thin — the next person can't replay your work.' Receive it.
evidence: 'Thank you — that's specific and useful. Can you show me a note that's the standard? I want to match it.' No defense, no explanation, just the receipt and the request for the bar.
Adopt the standard immediately: the next ticket's note written to the replayable bar, and tell the lead ('I rewrote today's notes to the standard — mind checking?'). The feedback loop closed visibly.
The new hire who receives feedback this well gets MORE of it — and the lead now invests in your growth. Defensiveness would have ended the coaching; receptivity multiplies it.
scenarios.prompt: 'Your notes are too thin.' You asked for this feedback. Receive it.
choices: My notes are fine; the work was correct
'Thank you — that's concrete. Can you point me at a note that's the standard, so I match it? I'll rewrite today's to that bar and have you check it.' [No defense; the fix visible on the next ticket.]
Other people's notes are thin too
I'll try to write more
scenarios.hint: You asked for feedback and got a real critique. What multiplies the coaching — and what ends it?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: thanks, asks for the standard (the bar made concrete), commits to the visible fix on the next ticket — receptivity that multiplies coaching. A is wrong: 'notes are fine' is the defensiveness that ends the coaching. C is wrong: 'others too' is the deflection. D is wrong: 'I'll try' is the vague commitment without the standard.

scenarios.title: The undocumented lore
scenarios.situation: Month 1: you discover the team has an unwritten rule — 'we never push policy changes on Fridays' — that exists nowhere in the docs. What do you do with it?
evidence: First: follow it (the lore exists for a reason — ask WHY: 'what happened on a Friday once?'). Then: propose documenting it — 'mind if I add this to the runbook with the reason? Future-me will thank us.'
The lore-to-doc pipeline is the new hire's superpower: you see the gaps the veterans are blind to. Documenting the unwritten (with the team's blessing) is the unglamorous contribution that compounds.
Propose, don't unilaterally publish: 'mind if I...' The lore belongs to the team; the documentation is your gift to it.
scenarios.prompt: Unwritten rule, nowhere in the docs. What do you do?
choices: Ignore it — if it's not documented, it's not real

'Noted — and now I'm curious about the Friday story. Mind if I add this to the runbook with the reason behind it? The next new hire will thank us.' [Follow the lore, learn the why, propose the documentation — the gap you can see because you're new.]
Push a policy change on Friday to test it
Tell the manager the team doesn't document properly
scenarios.hint: The lore isn't in the docs. Is that a complaint — or your first contribution?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: follows the lore, learns the why, proposes documenting it with the team's blessing — the new-hire documentation superpower. A is wrong: 'not documented, not real' is how Friday outages are born. C is wrong: testing the lore by violating it is the week-one hero move's cousin. D is wrong: the complaint to the manager skips the contribution entirely.

scenarios.title: The 90-day review approaches
scenarios.situation: Day 85: the 90-day review is next week. Your manager will evaluate you. What's your move before the meeting?
evidence: Write the self-review FIRST: what shipped (the tickets, the tuning win, the doc contributions — with the evidence), what you learned (the gaps closed), what's next (the 90–180 plan). Bring it to the meeting.

The self-review frames the conversation around your actual record (not recency bias), demonstrates the ownership mindset, and makes the manager's job easy — managers advocate for employees who evaluate themselves honestly.
End with the ask: 'What's the one thing I should focus on next?' The growth question — asked at 90 days — sets the next 90 in motion.
scenarios.prompt: Review next week. Your pre-meeting move?
choices: Wait for the manager's evaluation

[Write the self-review:] shipped (tickets closed, the tuning win, docs — evidence attached), learned (gaps closed, lore absorbed), next (the 90–180 plan). [Bring it; frame the conversation; close with 'what's the one thing I should focus on next?']
Prepare defenses for any criticism
Ask colleagues what the manager thinks of you
scenarios.hint: 90-day review next week. Who should write the first draft of your evaluation — them, or you?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: the self-review with shipped/learned/next (evidence attached), brought to frame the conversation, closed with the growth question — ownership that earns the honest evaluation. A is wrong: waiting surrenders the framing to recency bias. C is wrong: preparing defenses is the adversarial posture. D is wrong: polling colleagues about the manager is the hallway politics.

scenarios.title: The teammate test
scenarios.situation: Month 2: a peer is drowning — their queue is overflowing, they're skipping lunch, and nobody's noticed. You're caught up. What does 'teammate' do?
evidence: 'Hey, I see your queue's heavy — I'm caught up; want me to take the next three triage tickets?' Offered specifically (not 'let me know if you need help'), to the peer directly, no fanfare.
'Let me know if you need help' puts the burden on the drowning person to ask. The specific offer ('the next three triage tickets') is grabbable — and it normalizes the team covering each other.
This is the culture you were hired into, embodied: the teaching instinct, the customer-first reflex, the no-heroics teamwork. Teammate is a verb — conjugate it.
scenarios.prompt: Peer's drowning, you're caught up. Teammate is a verb — conjugate it.
choices: Let me know if you need any help!
'I see your queue's stacked and I'm caught up — want me to grab your next three triage tickets? No heroics, just coverage.' [Specific, direct, no fanfare — and mention it to no one.]
Tell the manager they're struggling
Stay out of it — not your queue
scenarios.hint: Drowning peer, you're free. What's the difference between 'let me know if you need help' and real help?
scenarios.why: Correct is B: the specific, grabbable offer made directly, no fanfare, no credit-seeking — help that doesn't burden the drowning person with asking. A is wrong: 'let me know' is the offer that never gets taken (the burden stays on them). C is wrong: reporting the struggle to the manager skips the peer-level help entirely. D is wrong: 'not my queue' is the anti-teammate.

lessons.title: Know the company cold: ThreatLocker in sixty seconds
concepts: Founded 2017 in Orlando, Florida — Danny Jenkins (CEO), Sami Jenkins (COO), John Carolan (QA)
Deny-by-default philosophy: approve known-good, deny everything else — prevention before detection
The stack: Allowlisting, Ringfencing, Storage Control, Elevation Control, Network Control, Web Control
Cyber Hero MDR: 24/7/365 US-based team, ~60-second average response
Go-to-market: MSP channel; 70,000+ organizations; $190M Series F (July 2026)
Culture signals: in-office five days in Orlando, free six-week bootcamp, peer-voted “most helpful” awards

example.code:
cat ~/prep/threatlocker-facts.txt
# 2017 · Orlando FL · deny-by-default
# Allowlisting / Ringfencing / Storage / Elevation / Network / Web
# Cyber Hero MDR · 70,000+ orgs · $190M Series F (Jul 2026)
example.walkthrough: Sixty seconds of specifics beats five minutes of adjectives. Keep a fact sheet with the founding year, the philosophy, the product names, and one recent milestone — then rehearse saying it out loud until the numbers come without thinking. Interviewers score preparation, not enthusiasm.

pitfalls: Claiming any affiliation with ThreatLocker — this is independent interview prep about their public concepts
Reciting slogans (“world-class synergy”) instead of verifiable facts
Inventing product details you have not verified — say what you know, flag what you do not
lessons.try_it: Record yourself giving the sixty-second company brief. Play it back and count the concrete facts — aim for six: year, city, philosophy, three products, one milestone.

lessons.title: Answer like an operator: STAR stories and the triage loop
concepts: STAR: Situation, Task, Action, Result — one story per question, two minutes max
The triage loop: scope → observe → hypothesize → smallest safe change → validate → explain
Evidence first: cite the audit or log line before the conclusion
Never disable the control to clear the symptom — fix narrowly
Translate for the audience: executives get outcomes, engineers get mechanisms

example.code:
echo "IMPACT: payroll updater blocked on 12 endpoints"
echo "EVIDENCE: audit denies unsigned child MSI; signer valid"
echo "ACTION: scoped certificate rule for updater + child"
echo "VALIDATE: install works; unrelated unsigned MSI still denied"
example.walkthrough: Write the brief before you speak it. Four lines — impact, evidence, action, validation — force you to lead with facts and close with proof, which is exactly the shape interviewers score. If you cannot write it in four lines, you do not understand it yet.

pitfalls: Answering with opinions before establishing facts
Skipping the validation step in your story — “it worked” is not validation
Badmouthing a previous employer, vendor, or customer to sound decisive
lessons.try_it: Take your hardest homelab problem (can you build a VM? what broke?) and write it as four echo lines. Then explain it out loud in under two minutes.

lessons.title: From Static Diagrams to Living Systems
concepts: A textbook diagram shows you one part in isolation — a living systems view shows you how all parts of Tl Interview move together in sequence
The four-step systems anatomy method: (1) See the whole in context, (2) Cut it open to reveal layers, (3) Walk through the process step-by-step, (4) Pull apart into labeled pieces
Apply this to any system in this course: start with the trigger action, trace through every component it touches, watch the data flow
Interview/exam power: when asked 'how does X work?', narrate the journey — 'it starts here, then...'. This demonstrates senior-level systems thinking

example.code:
TRIGGER event occurs
  → First system receives it (see the handoff)
  → Processing happens in sequence (watch each step)
  → State changes propagate (follow the ripple)
  → Final outcome delivered

Each arrow is a living handoff, not a static box.
example.walkthrough: This is the 'jet engine cutaway' for your field: instead of memorizing isolated facts, you see the entire flow as a moving sequence. Practice narrating this journey out loud.

pitfalls: Memorizing terms without understanding the processes they participate in
Drawing architecture diagrams as boxes without showing the data flow between them
Answering 'how does X work?' with a definition instead of walking through the sequence
lessons.try_it: Pick any process in this course. Write out the full journey from trigger to outcome, naming every system touched.

lessons.title: Anatomy of ThreatLocker Interview Prep
concepts: ThreatLocker Interview Prep is a multi-step process within ThreatLocker Interview Prep: trace the full sequence from initiation to completion
See it as a journey: identify the trigger, follow each handoff, watch state change at every step
Every step depends on the previous — a failure at any point breaks the chain. Map these dependencies
Connect ThreatLocker Interview Prep to the broader ThreatLocker Interview Prep ecosystem — nothing operates in isolation

example.code:
Step 1: Initiation
  ThreatLocker Interview Prep begins — what triggers it?

Step 2: Processing
  Data flows through — what transforms it?

Step 3: Handoff
  Result passes to next system — what is the interface?

Step 4: Completion
  Final state reached — how do you verify?
example.walkthrough: Apply the four-step anatomy method to ThreatLocker Interview Prep. Draw it as a flowing sequence, not a static diagram.

pitfalls: Treating ThreatLocker Interview Prep as an isolated component instead of part of a living flow
Skipping the dependency mapping — not asking 'what does this step need from the previous?'
Memorizing the steps without understanding WHY each one exists
lessons.try_it: Whiteboard the full ThreatLocker Interview Prep flow from memory. Label every handoff and dependency.

lessons.title: How this bootcamp is built (and how to move through it)
concepts: This bootcamp has four moving parts: Lessons build company knowledge and interview technique, Scenarios rehearse the questions interviewers actually ask, Labs build hands-on reps for the technical rounds, and the Mock Assessment simulates the full interview loop.

Domains group the material: company story, product depth, philosophy, culture, behavioral and technical questions, customer scenarios, demo skills, and logistics. Work them in order first, then loop back to your weakest domains.
Scenarios are the core: each puts you in the interview chair with evidence, a prompt, and four options. Answer like the candidate — then study the 'why,' especially on misses.
The Mock Assessment domain assembles scenarios from every domain at runtime. Use it for full timed runs after the domains — it measures readiness; it does not teach.

example.code:
SESSION (60 min)
  1. Read 2 lessons in one domain        (20 min)
  2. Work 3 scenarios, untimed             (20 min)
  3. Re-work every miss using the 'why'    (15 min)
  4. Log one line: what fooled you         ( 5 min)
example.walkthrough: Run every session in this shape. The reading builds the knowledge base, the scenarios build the answering reflex, and the re-work converts each miss into a permanent lesson. The one-line log compounds into your personal trap catalog.

pitfalls: Skipping the 'why' review — the mistake then repeats in the real interview.
Doing scenarios before the lessons — you burn rehearsal items without the framework to learn from them.
Using the Mock Assessment to learn instead of to measure — it measures readiness; it does not teach.
lessons.try_it: Run one 60-minute session today in exactly this shape and write your one-line log entry.

lessons.title: The interview-prep loop: learn, rehearse, mock, review
concepts: Interview skill is built in a loop: LEARN the material, REHEARSE it in scenarios, MOCK it under time and out loud, REVIEW the misses — then repeat on the weak spots.
Say answers OUT LOUD from day one: interviews are spoken performances. A perfect written answer that stumbles aloud is not ready.
Three 45-minute sessions across three days beat one 3-hour cram. Delivery smoothness consolidates between sessions.
Bucket every miss: knowledge gap (didn't know the fact), structure gap (knew it, rambled), or pressure gap (knew it, froze). Fix the bucket, not just the question.
Any domain under 80% after two passes gets re-studied from the lessons — not re-drilled. Re-drilling a misunderstood concept rehearses the misunderstanding.

example.code:
LOOP
  learn    -> read domain lessons, fact sheet in your words
  rehearse -> 5-8 scenarios, answers OUT LOUD
  mock     -> timed full runs, spoken
  review   -> bucket every miss, re-study weak domains
  repeat   -> loop only on domains still under 80%
example.walkthrough: Each loop should shrink the weak-domain set. If a domain stays weak after two loops, slow down: re-read, write your own examples, and explain the concept aloud to an empty room until it flows.

pitfalls: Silent rehearsal — the interview is spoken; practice spoken.
Memorizing scenario answers — mix domains to force real answering.
Treating 80% silent as ready — confirm out loud and under time.
lessons.try_it: Pick your weakest domain after today's session and run one full loop on it tomorrow.

lessons.title: What ThreatLocker interviews test
concepts: Interviewers test four things: MOTIVATION (why this company, why this role — specific, not generic), KNOWLEDGE (company facts, product stack, philosophy — homework visible), JUDGMENT (scenario rounds: the triage loop, narrow fixes, evidence-first), and SERVICE (Cyber Hero culture: empathy plus competence under pressure).

The scenario rounds are the filter: 'payroll is down, the updater is blocked, the customer is angry — walk me through it.' They score the ORDER of your thinking: scope, observe, hypothesize, smallest safe change, validate, explain.
Homelab depth is the differentiator: candidates who built things (a VM, a policy lab, a triage write-up) outscore candidates who read things. Evidence of doing beats claims of knowing.
Culture fit is scored in every answer: do you translate for the audience? Do you stay helpful under pressure? Do you own mistakes? The 'how' of your answers is the culture interview.

example.code:
CANDIDATE RUBRIC
  + specific motivation (facts, not flattery)
  + company/product knowledge (homework visible)
  + scenario judgment (triage loop, narrow fixes)
  + service under pressure (empathy + competence)
  + homelab evidence (built, not just read)
  - slogans, rambling, blaming, freezing
example.walkthrough: Read this rubric before every scenario. The winning option always shows homework, judgment, and service at once — and narrating the rubric aloud earns partial credit when you're unsure.

pitfalls: Generic motivation ('I love cybersecurity') — specific or silent.
Trivia without judgment — facts are the entry ticket; judgment is the test.
Hiding behind jargon with non-technical interviewers — translate, always.
lessons.try_it: Re-answer one completed scenario aloud as if to the panel, using the rubric.

lessons.title: Interview-week readiness checklist
concepts: The week before: fact sheet memorized (year, city, founders, philosophy, products, milestone), sixty-second company brief fluent, three STAR stories rehearsed, homelab talking points ready.

The day before: stop rehearsing two hours before sleep, review your miss log once, lay out logistics (route, parking, interviewer names, copies of resume). Cramming delivery the night before degrades it.
Day of: arrive early, breathe, lead with listening. Answer in structure (point, evidence, close) — structured answers sound confident even when you're nervous.

After: write down every question while fresh, send thank-you notes within 24 hours (one specific detail per interviewer), and debrief your answers honestly. The debrief is your prep for the next round.

example.code:
WEEK CHECKLIST
  [ ] fact sheet: 2017, Orlando, founders, philosophy
  [ ] 60-sec company brief: fluent aloud
  [ ] 3 STAR stories: rehearsed, 2 min each
  [ ] homelab: 3 talking points with specifics
  [ ] logistics: route, names, resume copies
  [ ] thank-you: within 24h, one detail each
example.walkthrough: Work this checklist in the final week. Interview readiness is a checklist, not a feeling — check the boxes and trust the preparation.

pitfalls: Cramming the night before — delivery degrades under fatigue.
Skipping the thank-you notes — they're scored; write them.
No debrief — the next round's prep is this round's notes.
lessons.try_it: Start your fact sheet tonight: year, city, founders, philosophy, six products, one milestone — from memory, then verify.

lessons.title: Capstone part 1: the sixty-second brief + fact sheet
concepts: Deliverable one: your sixty-second ThreatLocker company brief, rehearsed to fluency, plus the one-page fact sheet behind it. This is the answer to 'what do you know about us?' — the question every interview opens with.

The brief must contain: founding year and city (2017, Orlando), the founders (Danny Jenkins, Sami Jenkins, John Carolan), the philosophy (deny-by-default Zero Trust), the product stack (Allowlisting, Ringfencing, Storage, Elevation, Network, Web Control, Cyber Hero MDR), the channel (MSPs, 70,000+ organizations), and one recent milestone ($190M Series F, July 2026).
Fluency means: no notes, no umming, numbers without thinking, sixty seconds. Record yourself, count the facts (aim: eight), and re-record until it's clean.

The fact sheet behind it: one page, the same facts plus two more layers (the free six-week bootcamp, Zero Trust World conference, the ~60-second Cyber Hero response). Depth behind the brief for follow-up questions.

example.code:
DELIVERABLE 1 — brief + fact sheet
  60-sec brief: year, city, founders, philosophy,
    products, channel, milestone (8 facts, fluent)
  fact sheet: one page, brief facts + bootcamp +
    ZTW conference + Cyber Hero response stat
example.walkthrough: Write the brief as the artifact an interviewer grades: every fact verifiable, every number memorized, every sentence earning its sixty seconds. Then record it until it's fluent.

pitfalls: Slogans instead of facts — 'world-class' scores zero; '2017, Orlando' scores.
Memorizing without understanding — follow-ups will expose it.
Overrunning sixty seconds — brevity is the discipline.
lessons.try_it: Record your sixty-second brief tonight. Count the facts. Re-record until eight land cleanly.

lessons.title: Capstone part 2: three STAR stories + homelab proof
concepts: Deliverable two: three STAR stories (Situation, Task, Action, Result), two minutes each, rehearsed aloud — plus your homelab evidence write-up. Stories are what interviewers remember; everything else is screening.

Story 1 (technical judgment): a hard triage you ran — the block, the evidence, the narrow fix, the double validation. Story 2 (service under pressure): an angry user or a deadline — empathy first, then competence. Story 3 (learning/growth): something you got wrong and what it taught you — ownership is the culture signal.

The homelab write-up: what you built (VM lab, policy configs, triage exercises), what broke, what you learned — with specifics (tool names, config details). 'I have a homelab' is a claim; the write-up is evidence.
Each story ends with the lesson: 'what this taught me about operating default-deny.' Interviewers hire trajectories, not just histories.

example.code:
DELIVERABLE 2 — stories + homelab
  story 1: technical judgment (triage, narrow fix)
  story 2: service under pressure (empathy + competence)
  story 3: growth (got it wrong, learned)
  homelab: what built, what broke, specifics
example.walkthrough: Write each story in STAR, then rehearse aloud to two minutes. The homelab write-up should read like a lab report — specifics, not adjectives.

pitfalls: Stories without results — STAR needs the R; quantify it.
Homelab claims without specifics — 'I built a lab' needs the what and the broken.
Three technical stories — vary them: judgment, service, growth.
lessons.try_it: Draft story 1 tonight: your hardest triage, in STAR, two minutes aloud.

lessons.title: Capstone part 3: the mock panel
concepts: Deliverable three: run a full mock panel — 45 minutes, three 'interviewers' (a friend, a mirror, or a recording), covering: the company brief, two scenario rounds, one behavioral question, and your questions for them.

Score yourself with the candidate rubric after: motivation specific? Knowledge visible? Judgment ordered? Service under pressure? Homelab cited? Note every ramble, every freeze, every jargon-slip with a non-technical 'interviewer.'

Your questions for them matter: prepare three — one about the role's hardest problem, one about the team's definition of success, one about the culture in practice. 'No questions' is the fastest way to fail the final round.
Debrief in writing within an hour: what landed, what wobbled, what you'll fix before the real thing. The mock panel's debrief is the final prep document.

example.code:
DELIVERABLE 3 — mock panel
  45 min: brief + 2 scenarios + 1 behavioral + your questions
  score: candidate rubric, honest marks
  your 3 questions: role's hardest problem, success definition, culture
  debrief: written within the hour
example.walkthrough: Run the panel as the real thing: dressed, timed, no notes for the brief. The discomfort is the point — the real interview will feel easier by comparison.

pitfalls: Skipping your questions — prepare three, always.
Debriefing 'it went fine' — specifics or it didn't happen.
One mock panel — run it twice; the second is always better.
lessons.try_it: Schedule your first mock panel this week: who plays the interviewers, when, where?

lessons.title: The sixty-second company brief
concepts: The brief is the highest-ROI sixty seconds of the interview: 'Founded 2017 in Orlando by Danny Jenkins, Sami Jenkins, and John Carolan — a Zero Trust endpoint platform built on deny-by-default. The stack: Allowlisting, Ringfencing, Storage, Elevation, Network, and Web Control, plus the Cyber Hero MDR team. Sold through MSPs to 70,000+ organizations — fresh off a $190M Series F.'

Eight facts, sixty seconds, zero notes: year, city, founders, philosophy, products, service team, channel, milestone. Interviewers score preparation in the first minute — this is where it's won or lost.
Deliver it conversationally, not recited: the brief should sound like understanding, not memorization. Practice until the numbers come without thinking, then practice making it sound unpracticed.
End with the hook: '...and what drew me to it is [your specific reason].' The brief proves homework; the hook proves motivation. Both get scored.

example.code:
THE BRIEF (60 seconds)
  2017 · Orlando FL · Jenkins, Jenkins, Carolan
  deny-by-default Zero Trust endpoint platform
  Allowlisting / Ringfencing / Storage / Elevation /
    Network / Web + Cyber Hero MDR
  MSP channel · 70,000+ orgs · $190M Series F (Jul 2026)
  hook: what drew YOU (specific)
example.walkthrough: Rehearse the brief daily until it's fluent, then keep it warm with a weekly run. The brief decays without practice — and the interview opens with it.

pitfalls: Reciting like a robot — fluency plus conversational tone.
Forgetting the hook — homework without motivation is half the answer.
Inflating facts — every number must be verifiable; never invent.
lessons.try_it: Record the brief today. Count eight facts. Note where you stumble — that's tomorrow's drill.

lessons.title: Answering scenarios: the triage loop out loud
concepts: Scenario rounds test the ORDER of your thinking: SCOPE (who/what/where) → OBSERVE (what does the evidence say?) → HYPOTHESIZE (false positive? threat? policy gap?) → ACT (narrowest safe change) → VALIDATE (good path works, bad path denied) → EXPLAIN (plain language for the audience).

Narrate the loop as you go: 'First I'd scope it — which endpoints, which binary. Then I'd check the audit for...' Interviewers can't score silent thinking; narrated thinking earns partial credit even when the conclusion wobbles.

Evidence before verdict, always: 'The audit shows the updater is signed by the known vendor with a changed hash — so this looks like a version-change false positive.' Lead with what you SEE, then what you CONCLUDE.

Close with the double validation and the communication: 'I'd validate the install works and an unrelated unsigned binary is still denied — and I'd tell the user what happened in plain language.' The close is what separates operators from guessers.

example.code:
SCENARIO ANSWER SHAPE
  scope:    who/what/where (10 sec)
  observe:  evidence first, aloud (20 sec)
  hypothesize: name the verdict (10 sec)
  act:      narrowest safe change (15 sec)
  validate: good path + bad path (10 sec)
  explain:  plain language close (10 sec)
example.walkthrough: Practice every scenario answer in this shape, out loud, timed. The shape IS the skill — interviewers recognize it instantly, and it keeps you from rambling under pressure.

pitfalls: Silent thinking — narrate, or it doesn't count.
Verdict before evidence — the most common scenario-round failure.
Skipping validation in the answer — 'it worked' is not validation.
lessons.try_it: Take any scenario and answer it aloud in the six-step shape, timed at 75 seconds.

lessons.title: Translating: engineers, executives, customers
concepts: Three audiences, three translations of the same truth: ENGINEERS get mechanisms ('the app-to-app leash denied the PowerShell spawn'); EXECUTIVES get outcomes ('a hijacked Word document couldn't become ransomware'); CUSTOMERS get empathy plus plain language ('your payroll app was blocked by a security update — here's the fix and the timeline').
The interview tests translation directly: 'explain Ringfencing to our CFO.' The winning answer is one vivid image ('Word on a leash') plus the business outcome — never the kernel mechanics.
Read the room: the panel's composition tells you the audience. Two engineers and a hiring manager? Mechanisms for the engineers, outcomes for the manager — in the same answer, layered.
Practice the pivot: take one technical fact and deliver it three ways, back to back. The pivot is a rehearsable skill — and interviewers remember the candidate who translated.

example.code:
ONE FACT, THREE WAYS
  engineers:  'app-to-app leash denied the spawn'
  executives: 'hijacked Word couldn't become ransomware'
  customers:  'you're protected; here's the fix + timeline'
example.walkthrough: Build the pivot reflex: for every technical concept you learn, write the three versions. The executive version is usually the hardest — and the most scored.

pitfalls: Jargon at executives — the fastest way to lose the room.
Condescension at customers — plain language, never dumbed down.
One register for all — the panel has mixed audiences; layer the answer.
lessons.try_it: Take Ringfencing and deliver the three versions aloud, 30 seconds each.

lessons.title: Questions to ask them
concepts: Your questions are scored: they reveal what you value, how you think, and whether you did homework. 'No questions' reads as 'no curiosity' — always have three ready.
Question 1 (the role): 'What's the hardest problem someone in this role will face in the first 90 days?' — shows you think in problems, not perks.
Question 2 (success): 'How does the team define success for this role at six months?' — shows you plan to be measured, and want the rubric.
Question 3 (culture): 'Can you tell me about a time the team disagreed on a security-vs-usability call, and how it got resolved?' — shows you understand the real tension of the work.

Never ask: anything the website answers (homework failure), compensation in round one (timing failure), or 'how did I do?' (composure failure). Save compensation for when they raise it — or the final round.

example.code:
YOUR THREE
  1. hardest problem in the first 90 days?
  2. success at six months — the rubric?
  3. a security-vs-usability disagreement, resolved how?
  never: website-answerable, comp in round one, 'how did I do?'
example.walkthrough: Prepare your three, plus one spare. Ask them conversationally — the questions are a conversation, not an interrogation. And listen to the answers: they're telling you what the job is really like.

pitfalls: No questions — the fastest final-round failure.
Website-answerable questions — announces you didn't do homework.
Compensation first — timing is judgment; let them raise it.
lessons.try_it: Write your three questions now, tailored with one specific fact each (a product name, a conference, the bootcamp).

lessons.title: Founding and mission
concepts: Founded 2017 in Orlando, Florida, by Danny Jenkins (CEO), Sami Jenkins (COO), and John Carolan — a Zero Trust endpoint protection company built on the deny-by-default philosophy from day one.

The mission as the market reads it: bring enterprise-grade Zero Trust to the organizations that can't staff a SOC — delivered heavily through the MSP channel to 70,000+ organizations. Prevention-first security for the underserved middle of the market.

Why the founding story matters in interviews: 'why this company' answers need the origin. A 2017-founded, Orlando-grown, philosophy-first company is a specific story — learn it cold, tell it in two sentences.
What not to claim: any affiliation, any insider knowledge, any product details beyond public concepts. Independent prep means public facts only — say what you know, flag what you don't.

example.code:
FOUNDING (two sentences)
  2017, Orlando FL: Danny Jenkins, Sami Jenkins, John Carolan
  founded a deny-by-default Zero Trust endpoint company
  to protect the organizations that can't staff a SOC.
example.walkthrough: Practice the two-sentence founding story until it's conversational. It's the opening of every 'what do you know about us' answer — and the foundation the rest of the facts stack on.

pitfalls: Inventing founding details — public facts only, always.
Skipping the mission — the 'why they exist' is the interview's real question.
Claiming affiliation — independent prep, stated plainly.
lessons.try_it: Tell the founding story aloud in two sentences, then add one sentence on why the mission matters to you.

lessons.title: Growth and momentum
concepts: The channel: MSP-first go-to-market, reaching 70,000+ organizations — the scale story is 'protection for the many,' not 'fortress for the few.' Know the number; it signals homework.
The milestone: $190M Series F in July 2026 — the growth-stage signal. In interviews, growth stage translates to 'building, not maintaining' — which is both a fact and a motivation hook.

The community: a free six-week Zero Trust Cybersecurity Bootcamp and the annual Zero Trust World conference in Orlando. Community investment signals culture — mention it when asked about values, not just when asked about facts.
Momentum in answers: cite the milestone once (in the brief), then use it as a lens ('at this stage, I'd expect...'). One mention proves homework; repeated mentions sound like a pitch.

example.code:
MOMENTUM FACTS
  channel: MSP-first · 70,000+ organizations
  funding: $190M Series F (July 2026)
  community: free 6-week bootcamp · Zero Trust World (Orlando)
  use: cite once, then lens it
example.walkthrough: Fold one momentum fact into your 'why here' answer and one into a question for them ('with the Series F growth, how is the team scaling...?'). Facts earn double when they work twice.

pitfalls: Citing funding as flattery — it's a fact, then a lens, not praise.
Forgetting the community programs — they're the culture evidence.
Stale numbers — verify before the interview; momentum dates quickly.
lessons.try_it: Write one interview question that uses the Series F fact naturally — not as flattery, as curiosity.

lessons.title: Culture signals
concepts: The in-office signal: five days in-office in Orlando. In interviews, don't debate it — show you understand what it signals (collaboration density, mentorship, culture transmission) and that you're aligned.
The service signal: Cyber Hero — the 24/7/365 US-based MDR team with ~60-second average response. Culture expressed as a service standard: prevention plus white-glove response.

The peer signal: peer-voted 'most helpful' awards and the free community bootcamp. A culture that rewards helpfulness and teaches freely — mirror it in your answers (generous, plain-spoken, evidence-first).
Culture in answers: show, don't claim. 'I'm a culture fit' is empty; answering a scenario with empathy-first triage DEMONSTRATES the service culture. Every answer is a culture answer.

example.code:
CULTURE READS
  in-office 5 days: collaboration density (don't debate, align)
  Cyber Hero: service as a standard (~60-sec response)
  peer-voted helpfulness: generosity is rewarded
  show it: empathy-first answers > 'culture fit' claims
example.walkthrough: Audit your scenario answers for culture signals: does each one show empathy, plain speaking, and ownership? If not, the culture answer is missing.

pitfalls: Debating the office policy — understand and align, or don't apply.
Claiming 'culture fit' — demonstrate it in every answer instead.
Missing the service thread — Cyber Hero is the culture's sharpest expression.
lessons.try_it: Take one scenario answer and rewrite its opening line to lead with the customer impact — the Cyber Hero reflex.

lessons.title: What interviewers listen for
concepts: Homework: the year, the city, the founders, the philosophy, the products, the channel, the milestone — stated without notes. Missing basics is an instant filter; nailing them buys attention for the rest.
Specificity: 'the MSP channel protecting 70,000+ organizations' beats 'you help lots of companies.' Numbers and names are the difference between researched and skimmed.

Conviction: WHY deny-by-default — not just what it is. The philosophy question ('why not just better detection?') tests whether you've THOUGHT, not just read. Have the ninety-second prevention case ready.
Honesty: 'I don't know, but here's how I'd find out' beats a bluff every time. Interviewers at a security company can smell invented facts — and they score the candor.

example.code:
LISTENING CHECKLIST
  [ ] basics without notes (year, city, founders)
  [ ] numbers and names (70k+, Series F, products)
  [ ] conviction (the 90-sec prevention case)
  [ ] honesty ('don't know' > bluff)
example.walkthrough: Run this checklist against your own answers in the mock panel. The panel is listening for all four simultaneously — preparation means having all four ready at once.

pitfalls: Bluffing unknown facts — the fastest way to fail a security interview.
Basics with notes — the brief must be noteless.
Philosophy as slogan — conviction needs the 90-second case, not the tagline.
lessons.try_it: Score your last mock-panel company answer against the four-item checklist. Where's the gap?

lessons.title: The stack: six controls, one philosophy
concepts: Allowlisting: deny-by-default execution — only approved applications run. The foundation; everything else assumes it.
Ringfencing: containment of the allowed — what approved apps may do, across app-to-app, file, registry, and network dimensions.
Storage Control: deny-by-default for removable media — serial-scoped, user-bound, time-boxed device approval with encryption options.
Elevation Control: just-in-time, per-app, time-boxed admin rights — standing admin replaced, every session logged.
Network Control: host firewall under deny-by-default — egress allowlisted by destination, inbound denied by default.
Web Control: deny-by-default for browsing — category policy, download file-type rules, the delivery vector governed.
Cyber Hero MDR: the 24/7/365 US-based human layer — ~60-second average response. Technology plus people: prevention with a white-glove backstop.

example.code:
STACK MAP
  execute:   Allowlisting (may it run?)
  behave:    Ringfencing (what may it do?)
  media:     Storage Control (may data leave?)
  privilege: Elevation Control (may it elevate?)
  network:   Network Control (may it reach?)
  web:       Web Control (may it fetch?)
  humans:    Cyber Hero MDR (24/7/365, ~60-sec)
example.walkthrough: Memorize the stack map: seven lines, each answering one question. In interviews, the map lets you place any scenario ('where would this be caught?') in seconds — that fluency is the product-knowledge signal.

pitfalls: Listing products without the questions they answer — the map is the understanding.
Forgetting Cyber Hero — the human layer is part of the stack.
Inventing products or features — public concepts only, always.
lessons.try_it: Recite the stack map from memory: seven lines, one question each. Time yourself.

lessons.title: How the controls compose
concepts: The controls are layered, not redundant: Web Control governs the fetch, Allowlisting governs the execution, Ringfencing governs the behavior, Network/Storage govern the exfiltration paths, Elevation governs the privilege. Each catches what the earlier ones missed.

The composition story: a phishing document arrives (Web Control: allowed, trusted sender) → macro tries PowerShell (Ringfencing: denied) → the deny triggers investigation (Cyber Hero / analyst) → the delivery gets hunted. The incident is a LAYERED story — tell it that way.

Defense in depth means correlated signals: a ringfence deny PLUS an egress deny, same host, same hour, is an intrusion pattern — not two policy events. Interviewers test whether you see the composition or just the components.

The gaps are honest: no control covers malicious USE of fully-approved apps within their leashes, or the human clicking through. Name the limits when asked — candor about composition limits is senior.

example.code:
LAYERED STORY
  fetch:     Web Control allows (trusted sender)
  execute:   Allowlisting allows (signed Word)
  behave:    Ringfencing DENIES (Word -> PowerShell)
  investigate: the deny is a detection
  hunt:      the delivery, laterally
example.walkthrough: Practice narrating the layered story for three attack shapes: macro document, malicious download, USB drop. The narration — which layer, what it saw — is the product-depth performance.

pitfalls: Single-layer answers — 'the allowlist stops it' misses the composition.
Treating layers as redundant — each answers a different question.
Hiding the limits — honest gaps read as seniority.
lessons.try_it: Narrate the layered story for a malicious USB drop: which layers engage, in what order?

lessons.title: Allowlisting depth: the interview version
concepts: The ninety-second case: detection classifies AFTER execution begins — fileless, living-off-the-land, and zero-day techniques execute before any verdict exists. Allowlisting asks the question BEFORE execution: is this explicitly trusted? Unknown code never runs; no signature needed.

The operational honesty: the cost is real — every legitimate new app needs an approval path. Learning Mode, certificate rules, the Approval Center, the Testing Environment: the machinery that pays the cost. Interviewers listen for the tradeoff, not just the triumph.

Rule strength in one breath: certificate (survives updates) over hash (breaks every version) over path (never in user-writable locations). The version-change false positive is the classic interview probe — answer with the certificate rule.

The EDR relationship: allowlisting doesn't replace detection — it shrinks what detection must chase. Prevention first, detection as the backstop. Respect the panel's detection engineers; don't declare their field obsolete.

example.code:
90-SECOND CASE
  detection: classifies AFTER execution starts
  allowlisting: asks BEFORE: explicitly trusted?
  cost: real — paid via Learning Mode, cert rules,
         Approval Center, Testing Environment
  EDR: still vital — smaller, higher-signal workload
example.walkthrough: Rehearse the ninety-second case aloud until it's smooth. It's the answer to 'why allowlisting,' 'why not just EDR,' and 'isn't this too strict' — one case, three questions.

pitfalls: 'EDR is obsolete' — never trash the panel's field.
Skipping the operational cost — the tradeoff is the credibility.
Hash-rule answers for churning apps — the certificate rule is the probe's answer.
lessons.try_it: Deliver the ninety-second case aloud. Then deliver it again, 30 seconds shorter.

lessons.title: Ringfencing depth: the interview version
concepts: The one-liner: 'Word is allowed to run, but it may not launch PowerShell, read the credential store, or reach the internet — so a hijacked Word cannot become ransomware.' One image, four dimensions implied, business outcome stated.

The four leashes when pressed: application-to-application (may it launch others?), file (what may it touch?), registry (what keys?), network (where may it go?). Name them crisply — then return to the one-liner.

The threat model: living-off-the-land. Attackers don't bring malware; they bring instructions for your trusted tools. Ringfencing assumes the allowed app is already compromised — that's the Zero Trust sentence.
The executive translation is the test: CFOs remember 'Word on a leash,' not 'API-hooking minifilter.' Translate every time, unprompted, when the audience is non-technical.

example.code:
RINGFENCING (three depths)
  one-liner:  'Word on a leash'
  four leashes: app-to-app, file, registry, network
  threat model: living-off-the-land; assume the app
                is already compromised
example.walkthrough: Practice all three depths back to back: one-liner (10 sec), leashes (30 sec), threat model (30 sec). The interview picks the depth; you have them all ready.

pitfalls: Leading with kernel mechanics — the one-liner first, always.
Forgetting the assume-breach framing — it's the Zero Trust sentence.
One depth only — prepare all three; the panel varies.
lessons.try_it: Deliver the three depths aloud: 10 seconds, 30 seconds, 30 seconds. Then the CFO version.

lessons.title: Never trust, always verify
concepts: Zero Trust is not a product — it's the design principle: no implicit trust based on network location, identity history, or past approval. Every access, every execution, every connection is verified against policy, every time.

The three operational translations: DENY BY DEFAULT (unknown is denied until proven trusted), ASSUME BREACH (design as if the attacker is already inside — leashes, not just walls), LEAST PRIVILEGE (every grant is the minimum sufficient, bounded in scope and time).

Applied to the endpoint: Allowlisting is 'never trust' for execution; Ringfencing is 'assume breach' for approved apps; Elevation Control is 'least privilege' for admin rights; Network/Storage/Web extend the same thinking to every channel.

In interviews, anchor every product answer to the principle: 'Ringfencing exists because we assume the approved app is already compromised.' Principle-first answers sound like understanding; feature-first answers sound like memorization.
