example.code:
PRINCIPLE -> PRODUCT
  never trust (execution)  -> Allowlisting
  assume breach (behavior) -> Ringfencing
  least privilege (admin)  -> Elevation Control
  never trust (channels)   -> Network / Storage / Web
example.walkthrough: Practice the anchor: for each product, state the principle first, then the mechanism. 'Assume breach is why Word can't spawn PowerShell' — that sentence is the interview signal.

pitfalls: Treating Zero Trust as a product category — it's the principle; the products implement it.
Feature-first answers — anchor to the principle, then the mechanism.
Forgetting 'assume breach' — it's the sentence that explains Ringfencing.
lessons.try_it: For each of the six controls, write the principle-first sentence: '[principle] is why [control] [does X].'

lessons.title: The ninety-second prevention case
concepts: The case: detection classifies AFTER execution begins. Fileless techniques, living-off-the-land binaries, and zero-days execute before any verdict exists — the window every modern attack lives in. Prevention asks the question BEFORE execution: is this explicitly trusted?

The finite-vs-infinite frame: enumerating badness can never be complete (the infinite list); approving known-good is finite and knowable (the business's real footprint). Default-deny inverts the problem into the solvable shape.

The honest cost: operational weight — approvals, baselining, tuning. Name it unprompted: 'the tradeoff is real, and here's the machinery that pays it.' The candidate who names the cost is believed about the benefit.

The EDR respect: prevention shrinks what detection must chase; it doesn't replace it. 'EDR focuses on a smaller, higher-signal workload' — honor the panel's detection engineers while making the prevention case.

example.code:
90-SECOND CASE
  detection: AFTER execution (the window attacks live in)
  prevention: BEFORE — 'explicitly trusted?'
  frame: finite known-good beats infinite known-bad
  cost: real — Learning Mode, cert rules, approvals
  EDR: respected — smaller, higher-signal workload
example.walkthrough: Rehearse the case until it's conversational: 90 seconds, no notes, the cost named unprompted, the EDR respect genuine. It's the most-asked philosophical question in the loop.

pitfalls: Skipping the cost — unprompted honesty is the credibility.
'Detection is obsolete' — never trash the panel's field.
Slogan version — the case needs the window, the frame, and the cost.
lessons.try_it: Deliver the case aloud twice: once at 90 seconds, once at 45. Note what survives the cut.

lessons.title: Assume breach: designing for the inside
concepts: Assume breach means the walls already failed: the attacker has a foothold, a credential, a process. The design question shifts from 'keep them out' to 'limit what they can do in here.'

Endpoint translations: Ringfencing (the approved app is already compromised — leash it), no standing admin (the phished account must not inherit domain keys), egress allowlisting (the foothold must not phone home freely), storage control (the foothold must not walk out with data).

The interview sentence: 'We design as if Word is already compromised — that's why it can't spawn PowerShell.' One sentence that explains an entire product. Have three such sentences (Word, admin, egress).

The mindset test: when a scenario describes a trusted component misbehaving, the assume-breach candidate investigates the component — the trust-based candidate defends it. Interviewers watch which reflex you show.

example.code:
ASSUME-BREACH SENTENCES
  'We design as if Word is already compromised.'
  'We design as if the account is already phished.'
  'We design as if the agent is already beaconing.'
example.walkthrough: Memorize the three sentences. They're the assume-breach reflex in speakable form — and the panel listens for exactly this framing.

pitfalls: 'Our walls are strong' — the pre-Zero-Trust sentence.
Defending the trusted component — investigate it instead.
One sentence only — prepare all three; scenarios vary.
lessons.try_it: Write your own fourth assume-breach sentence for Storage Control, then say all four aloud.

lessons.title: Defending the philosophy under pushback
concepts: Pushback 1 — 'Too strict, breaks usability': answer with the machinery (Learning Mode, Approval Center, certificate rules) and the staged rollout. Strictness is a deployment question, not a philosophy flaw — and usability is engineered, not wished.

Pushback 2 — 'What about zero-days in approved apps?': answer with assume breach (Ringfencing) and honesty (no control covers everything; the human layer and practices complete it). The philosophy anticipates the question.
Pushback 3 — 'We already have EDR': the respect pivot — EDR is vital, and prevention makes it better (smaller, higher-signal workload). Never position as replacement; position as the foundation.

The meta-skill: steelman the pushback before answering ('you're right that...') — then the principled response. Candidates who steelman sound like thinkers; candidates who deflect sound like marketers.

example.code:
PUSHBACK PLAYBOOK
  'too strict'      -> machinery + staged rollout (deployment, not flaw)
  'zero-day in app' -> assume breach + honest limits
  'we have EDR'     -> respect pivot (foundation, not replacement)
  always: steelman first, then answer
example.walkthrough: Rehearse each pushback aloud: steelman (10 sec), principle (20 sec), machinery/limits (20 sec). The shape keeps you from rambling or deflecting.

pitfalls: Deflecting pushback — steelman it first, visibly.
Conceding the philosophy — the pushbacks attack deployment, not principle; keep them separated.
Rambling — the 50-second shape is the discipline.
lessons.try_it: Have a friend push back three times; answer each in the 50-second shape. Note where you ramble.

lessons.title: The service standard
concepts: Cyber Hero is the 24/7/365 US-based MDR team with ~60-second average response: prevention technology plus human analysts who answer fast, triage well, and communicate plainly. The standard is the product as much as the software.

The standard's two halves: COMPETENCE (the triage is right, the fix is narrow, the validation is double) and EMPATHY (the customer feels heard, the timeline is clear, the language is plain). Either half alone is half the standard.

In interviews, every scenario answer is a Cyber Hero audition: does your answer lead with the human impact? Do you give a timeline before the technical detail? Do you close with what the customer should expect? The panel scores the service in the substance.
The anti-pattern: the brilliant technician who lectures the customer. Competence without empathy is a support ticket that escalates — and interviewers have all met that technician.

example.code:
THE STANDARD
  competence: right triage, narrow fix, double validation
  empathy:    heard, timeline, plain language
  every answer: impact first, then mechanism
  anti-pattern: the brilliant lecturer
example.walkthrough: Audit your scenario answers: does each lead with impact, give a timeline, and close with expectations? If the empathy half is missing, the Cyber Hero answer is missing.

pitfalls: Leading with mechanism — impact first, always.
No timeline — 'we're working on it' is not a timeline.
Lecturing the customer — plain language, never condescension.
lessons.try_it: Rewrite one scenario answer's opening to lead with the customer impact and a timeline.

lessons.title: De-escalation: the angry customer
concepts: The de-escalation sequence: ACKNOWLEDGE the impact first ('I hear you — payroll blocked is urgent'), then GATHER facts (app, version, onset), then TIMELINE ('here's what happens in the next 30 minutes'), then FIX narrowly, then FOLLOW UP (confirm resolved, explain the why).

Acknowledgment is not agreement: 'I hear you' doesn't concede the policy was wrong — it concedes the IMPACT is real. Customers de-escalate when the impact is acknowledged; they escalate when it's debated.
Never: blame the customer, blame the vendor, debate the policy's wisdom, or promise what you can't deliver. Each converts a solvable ticket into a relationship incident.

The follow-up is the loyalty builder: the customer who got the timeline, the fix, AND the plain-language why ('the update changed the app's fingerprint') becomes the advocate. Third-call-frustrated to loyal is the Cyber Hero story.

example.code:
DE-ESCALATION
  1. acknowledge impact ('I hear you — urgent')
  2. gather facts (app, version, onset)
  3. timeline (next 30 min, explicitly)
  4. fix narrowly (scoped rule, validated)
  5. follow up (confirm + explain the why)
example.walkthrough: Rehearse the sequence aloud with a frustrated 'customer' (friend, mirror). The acknowledgment-first reflex is the muscle — everything after it is technique.

pitfalls: Debating the impact — acknowledge, don't litigate.
Skipping the timeline — uncertainty escalates; timelines calm.
No follow-up — the fix without the why is a future repeat call.
lessons.try_it: Role-play the payroll-blocked call: 2 minutes, acknowledgment first, timeline by minute one.

lessons.title: Ownership: the mistake and the miss
concepts: Ownership is the culture's sharpest test: when YOU caused the block (bad rule, missed inventory), the Cyber Hero response is immediate acknowledgment, fast remediation, and the process fix — in that order, without defensiveness.

The ownership script: 'That was my rule change — I narrowed it too far. I'm rolling it back now (2 min), then I'll re-issue it correctly with a canary. Here's what I'm changing in my process so it doesn't repeat.' Mistake, fix, prevention — 30 seconds.
Never: hide it, blame the tooling, minimize ('it was minor'), or fix it silently. Silent fixes teach the team that mistakes are shameful — and shameful mistakes get hidden, then repeated.
Interviewers probe ownership with 'tell me about a mistake': they're scoring the script, not the mistake. A good mistake story — owned, fixed, learned — outperforms a perfect record.

example.code:
OWNERSHIP SCRIPT (30 sec)
  'My change caused it — rolling back now (2 min).
   Re-issuing correctly with a canary.
   Process fix: [specific change] so it doesn't repeat.'
example.walkthrough: Prepare your mistake story in this script shape and rehearse it. The story's power is the process fix at the end — that's what interviewers remember.

pitfalls: Hiding or minimizing — the cover-up outranks the mistake.
Blaming tooling — ownership means the process, not the excuse.
No process fix — 'I learned' without the change is sentiment.
lessons.try_it: Write your mistake story in the 30-second script shape. What's the process fix?

lessons.title: Helpfulness as a competitive edge
concepts: Peer-voted 'most helpful' awards: the culture REWARDS helpfulness explicitly. In interviews, helpfulness shows as: answering the question behind the question, offering the path to yes, translating without being asked.

The helpful reflex in scenarios: after the verdict, add the enablement — 'and here's how you'd avoid this next time,' 'the docs page for this is...,' 'want me to show your team the approval flow?' The fix solves today; the enablement prevents tomorrow.

Helpfulness scales: the free bootcamp, the conference, the community teaching — the company exports helpfulness. Candidates who teach (in answers, in the homelab write-up, in questions) signal the same instinct.
The test: 'explain it like I'm new.' The helpful candidate lights up; the insecure candidate condescends. Watch which one you are in the mock panel — and rehearse the generous version.

example.code:
HELPFULNESS SIGNALS
  answer the question behind the question
  verdict + enablement ('avoid it next time: ...')
  translate without being asked
  teach generously (the bootcamp instinct)
example.walkthrough: Build one 'enablement' close for each of your STAR stories: what did the OTHER person learn? Helpfulness is remembered in the epilogue.

pitfalls: Verdict without enablement — the fix without the teaching.
Condescension disguised as teaching — generosity, not superiority.
Hoarding knowledge — the culture rewards the opposite.
lessons.try_it: Add an enablement close to your hardest triage story: what did the requester learn?

lessons.title: STAR: the story shape
concepts: STAR: Situation (the context, 20 sec), Task (your responsibility, 10 sec), Action (what YOU did, 60 sec — the heart), Result (the outcome, quantified, 20 sec). Two minutes total. The Action is the story; the Result is the proof.
The Action must be YOUR actions: 'I scoped the rule, I validated twice, I wrote the postmortem' — not 'we.' Interviewers hire the person in front of them; 'we' hides them.
Quantify the Result: 'block rate fell 40%,' 'approval time went from 3 days to 6 hours,' 'zero repeats in 90 days.' Numbers are the difference between a story and an anecdote.
End with the lesson: 'what it taught me about...' — the trajectory signal. Interviewers hire direction, not just history.

example.code:
STAR (2 min)
  S: context (20s)
  T: your responsibility (10s)
  A: YOUR actions (60s) — the heart
  R: quantified outcome (20s)
  + lesson: 'what it taught me...'
example.walkthrough: Write all three capstone stories in STAR on paper first — the writing exposes the 'we' problem and the missing numbers. Then rehearse aloud to the two-minute mark.

pitfalls: 'We' stories — the interviewer hires YOU; show your actions.
Unquantified results — numbers turn anecdotes into evidence.
No lesson — the trajectory is what they're buying.
lessons.try_it: Take one work story and STAR it on paper: circle every 'we' and rewrite as 'I.'

lessons.title: The mistake question
concepts: 'Tell me about a time you made a mistake.' They're scoring the ownership script, not the mistake's size: immediate acknowledgment, fast remediation, and the process fix — without defensiveness.

Pick a real mistake with a real cost (blocked users, an outage, a bad call) — then show the full arc: what happened, what you did in the first ten minutes, what you changed so it can't repeat. The arc is the answer.
Never: blame others, blame tooling, minimize ('it was minor'), or pick a humblebrag ('I work too hard'). Each is a scored evasion — interviewers have heard them all.
The process fix is the memorable part: 'now every change rides a canary, because of that Friday.' The mistake becomes the origin story of a good habit — that's the ownership culture in one anecdote.

example.code:
MISTAKE ARC
  what happened (real, with cost)
  first 10 min (acknowledge + remediate)
  process fix (the habit born from it)
  never: blame, minimize, humblebrag
example.walkthrough: Rehearse your mistake story to 90 seconds. The test: does a stranger hear ownership or excuse? Record it and listen for defensiveness — then cut it.

pitfalls: Humblebrag mistakes — 'I care too much' is an evasion.
Blaming the tooling — ownership means your process.
No process fix — the lesson without the change is sentiment.
lessons.try_it: Write your mistake arc on paper: cost, first-10-minutes, process fix. Time it at 90 seconds.

lessons.title: Conflict and disagreement
concepts: 'Tell me about a disagreement with a colleague.' They score: did you listen, did you argue the work (not the person), and did the relationship survive? Disagree-and-commit is the senior signal.

The story shape: the disagreement (technical, specific), your position and theirs (steelman THEIRS — 'they were right that...'), how it resolved (data, trial, escalation — not volume), and the relationship after.

Steelman the other side IN the answer: 'She was right that the rollout speed mattered; I was worried about the inventory gaps. We ran the pilot, the data showed...' Generosity about opponents reads as confidence.
Never: 'we never disagree' (dishonest), trash the colleague (character failure), or 'I won' (the point is the resolution, not the victory).

example.code:
DISAGREEMENT ARC
  the issue (technical, specific)
  their side, steelmanned ('they were right that...')
  resolution (data/trial/escalation)
  relationship after (intact, better?)
example.walkthrough: Prepare one disagreement story with a genuine steelman of the other side. The steelman is what the panel remembers — it signals the colleague you'd be.

pitfalls: 'We never disagree' — dishonest or disengaged.
Trashing the colleague — character scored, failed.
'I won' framing — resolution over victory, always.
lessons.try_it: Write your disagreement story: lead with their best argument, not yours.

lessons.title: Pressure and priorities
concepts: 'Tell me about working under pressure.' They score: triage (what did you do FIRST?), communication (who knew what, when?), and steadiness (did the process hold or did panic drive?).

The story needs the triage visible: 'three things on fire — I sequenced by blast radius: the fleet-wide block first, then the VIP ticket, then the routine queue — and I told each stakeholder their timeline within ten minutes.' Sequencing plus communication.
Show the process holding: 'the change control still applied — faster, not skipped.' Pressure that breaks process is the failure mode; pressure that compresses process is the skill.
End with what the pressure taught about preparation: 'that's why I pre-write rollback plans now.' The lesson converts the war story into judgment.

example.code:
PRESSURE ARC
  the pile-up (three things, one you)
  triage (sequenced by blast radius)
  communication (timelines in 10 min)
  process held (faster, not skipped)
  lesson (the preparation it taught)
example.walkthrough: Rehearse the pressure story with the triage explicit: name the sequencing criterion aloud. 'Blast radius' said out loud is the judgment signal.

pitfalls: 'I just worked harder' — effort without triage is panic.
No communication mentioned — stakeholders in the dark is the failure.
Process abandoned — 'we skipped change control' is the confession.
lessons.try_it: Write your pressure story: what's the sequencing criterion, and who got told what, when?

lessons.title: Narrating triage: think out loud
concepts: Technical rounds are narrated thinking: the interviewer can't score silent analysis. Verbalize the loop — 'I'm scoping first: which endpoints, which binary... now the audit: signed by the known vendor, hash changed...' — so every step is visible.

The narration has a pace: steady, not rushed. Pause to read (say 'let me look at the evidence'), then narrate the read. 'The evidence shows X, so my hypothesis is Y' — the sentence that turns observation into reasoning, aloud.

When stuck, narrate the stuckness: 'I'm torn between version-churn and push-regression — the timeline will decide: blocks started at 08:04, the push was at 08:00, so...' Showing the decision procedure earns credit even before the conclusion.
Close every technical answer with validation and communication: 'I'd validate the fix both ways and tell the user...' The close proves you operate, not just analyze.

example.code:
NARRATION PACES
  'Let me look at the evidence...' (pause, read)
  'The evidence shows X, so my hypothesis is Y.'
  'I'm torn between A and B — the [fact] decides.'
  close: validation + communication, always
example.walkthrough: Practice narrating one scenario fully aloud, recorded. Listen back: is every inference spoken? The unspoken steps are unscored steps.

pitfalls: Silent analysis — unscored by definition.
Rushing the read — 'let me look' is professional, not slow.
No close — analysis without the operational ending.
lessons.try_it: Record yourself narrating a triage end to end. Mark every silent inference — then speak them.

lessons.title: Rule-strength judgment on the spot
concepts: The interview probe: 'this app is blocked — how do you approve it?' The answer they want: the strength ladder applied — 'Is it signed? Certificate rule, scoped. Unsigned but stable? Hash rule, narrow. Only a path? Then where — user-writable is a no.'
Say the ladder aloud: 'Certificate over hash over path — and I'd never do path in a user-writable location.' The ladder said plainly is the judgment signal; hemming is the uncertainty signal.

The follow-up is always scope: '...scoped to what?' Have the four axes ready: who, what, where, when. 'Finance group, this vendor's updater plus child, FIN workstations, permanent with quarterly review.'

The trap answers: global hash approval ('approve it everywhere'), path rules for convenience, and 'ask the user what they need' as the whole answer. Each is a scored miss — the panel has heard them all.

example.code:
ON-THE-SPOT LADDER
  signed?    -> certificate rule, scoped
  unsigned?  -> hash rule, narrow + time-box
  path only? -> where? user-writable = NO
  always:    who/what/where/when (the scope)
example.walkthrough: Drill the ladder as a reflex: friend names an app state ('unsigned, updates monthly'), you answer the rule in one breath. Ten reps, no hesitation.

pitfalls: Global approvals — scope is the discipline.
Path-in-writable — the instant fail.
Hesitation on the ladder — drill it to reflex.
lessons.try_it: Ten rapid reps: app states in, rule-plus-scope out, one breath each.

lessons.title: Containment reasoning: the 'what now' questions
concepts: 'Word spawned PowerShell and it was blocked — what now?' The answer: the block is a detection, not a resolution — isolate the host, identify the delivery (the document), hunt laterally for the delivery, verify via sibling leashes, fix the upstream path.

The reasoning order: CONTAIN (the behavior is already contained — verify the siblings), INVESTIGATE (delivery, scope, persistence), ERADICATE (remove the content, verify clean), LEARN (upstream fix). Say the order explicitly.

Distinguish the questions: 'may it run?' (allowlist) vs 'what may it do?' (ringfence). When the interviewer describes approved-app misbehavior, name which question it is BEFORE answering — that naming is the senior signal.
The wrong answers: 'remove Word from the allowlist' (breaks the business), 'close the ticket, control worked' (ignores the intrusion), 'reinstall Windows' (destroys evidence, skips the hunt).

example.code:
WHAT-NOW ORDER
  contain:   verify siblings (already leashed?)
  investigate: delivery, lateral scope, persistence
  eradicate:  remove content, verify clean
  learn:      upstream fix (filtering, macro policy)
example.walkthrough: Rehearse the 'what now' for three shapes: macro doc, malicious download, USB drop. Same order every time — the order is the reasoning.

pitfalls: 'Control worked, closing' — the intrusion behind the block.
Allowlist answers to ringfence questions — name the question first.
Reinstall-first — evidence destroyed, hunt skipped.
lessons.try_it: Answer 'Word spawned PowerShell, blocked — what now?' aloud in the four-step order.

lessons.title: Depth probes: homelab and hands-on
concepts: 'Tell me about your homelab' is the depth probe: they want specifics — what you built, what broke, what you configured, what you learned. Vague homelabs ('I have some VMs') fail; specific ones ('three-VM lab: DC, workstation, attacker; I practiced allowlist triage with...') pass.
Prepare three homelab stories: the BUILD (what and why), the BREAK (what failed and the debugging), the LESSON (what it taught about the real world). Each 60 seconds, technical specifics included.

'What would you do with no budget?' tests creativity under constraint: free tiers, open-source tooling, trial environments, community resources. The answer shows resourcefulness — a valued operator trait.
Honesty about depth: 'I haven't done X, but here's how I'd approach it' beats bluffing. Interviewers probe until you hit the edge — the edge handled honestly is the pass; the bluff is the fail.

example.code:
HOMELAB STORIES (60s each)
  build:  what, why (specifics)
  break:  what failed, the debugging
  lesson: what it taught (real-world link)
  edge:   'haven't done X — here's my approach'
example.walkthrough: Write the three homelab stories with real specifics (names, configs, errors). If your homelab is thin, build one thing this week — even a single VM with a triage exercise — and story it.

pitfalls: Vague homelab — specifics or it didn't happen.
Bluffing past the edge — the probe continues until honesty.
No homelab at all — build one thing this week.
lessons.try_it: Write your build-break-lesson stories tonight. Time each at 60 seconds aloud.

lessons.title: The customer call shape
concepts: Every customer scenario follows the shape: ACKNOWLEDGE (the impact is real), DIAGNOSE (evidence-first, narrated simply), TIMELINE (what happens next, explicitly), FIX (narrow, validated), CLOSE (confirm resolved, explain the why, leave a path).

The acknowledgment is the highest-leverage sentence: 'Payroll blocked the morning of payroll — I hear you, that's urgent, and I'm on it right now.' One sentence that de-escalates more than ten minutes of technical explanation.

Diagnose in plain language AS you go: 'I can see the block in our audit — your updater changed with its new version, and our system needs to learn the new one. That's a two-minute fix on my side.' The customer watches competence happen.

The close prevents the repeat call: confirm it's working, explain the why in one sentence, and give the direct path ('if it ever happens again, here's exactly what to send me'). Third calls become last calls.

example.code:
CALL SHAPE
  acknowledge: impact is real, you're on it (1 sentence)
  diagnose:   evidence, narrated plainly (as you go)
  timeline:   what happens next, explicitly
  fix:        narrow, validated
  close:      confirm + why + direct path
example.walkthrough: Rehearse the call shape with a timer: acknowledgment in the first 15 seconds, timeline by minute one. The shape is the service skill — interviewers score its presence, not just the fix.

pitfalls: Technical monologue — narrate plainly AS you diagnose.
No timeline — uncertainty escalates; timelines calm.
Close without the why — the repeat call is born here.
lessons.try_it: Role-play a blocked-payroll call in the five-step shape, 3 minutes, acknowledgment first.

lessons.title: The confused user
concepts: Confused users aren't wrong users: 'my computer says no' is a valid bug report from their side of the glass. Your job: translate their confusion into diagnostic data with kind, specific questions.

The question technique: one question at a time, plain words, no jargon — 'What were you trying to open when it said no? Can you read me what the message says, word for word?' Each answer is a diagnostic step; rushing the questions loses the data.

Never make them feel foolish: 'That's a really common one — here's what's happening...' The user's dignity is part of the fix. Condescension is the service failure that no technical brilliance repairs.
Teach in the close: one sentence on what happened and one on what to do next time. The confused user who understands becomes the confident user — and the advocate.

example.code:
KIND DIAGNOSTICS
  one question at a time, plain words
  'read me the message, word for word'
  'that's a common one — here's what's happening'
  close: one sentence of teaching
example.walkthrough: Practice the kind-diagnostic questions aloud: they're harder than they look — every jargon word you catch yourself using is a point lost. Record and count them.

pitfalls: Jargon questions — 'what's the hash?' to a confused user.
Rushing — the data comes at their pace, not yours.
Impatience leaking — they hear it before you feel it.
lessons.try_it: Write five kind-diagnostic questions for 'my app won't open.' Zero jargon allowed.

lessons.title: The MSP technician
concepts: The MSP technician is a peer under pressure: they have THEIR client breathing down their neck, and you're their escalation path. Treat them as a colleague, not a customer — technical depth welcome, peer respect required.

Give them relayable status: everything you say should be quotable to their client. 'Contained at 14:22, root cause identified, fix validating now, update in 30 minutes' — they forward it verbatim, and you just made them look good.
Share the diagnostic reasoning, not just the verdict: MSP techs learn from your triage, and the next ticket from them arrives better-formed. Teaching the channel compounds.
Respect their context: they manage dozens of clients; your issue is one of fifty today. Brevity plus completeness — the peer standard.

example.code:
MSP PEER STANDARD
  colleague, not customer (depth welcome)
  relayable status (quotable to THEIR client)
  share the reasoning (they learn; tickets improve)
  brevity + completeness (their day has 50 fires)
example.walkthrough: Rehearse one MSP call: give the status update you'd want forwarded to an angry client. If it wouldn't calm the client, rewrite it.

pitfalls: Customer-voice to a peer — condescension to a technician.
Unrelayable status — 'we're looking into it' helps no one.
Verdict without reasoning — the teaching moment wasted.
lessons.try_it: Write the relayable status for: contained breach, 4 hosts, investigating. Three sentences.

lessons.title: The executive escalation
concepts: Executive escalations are business events wearing technical clothes: the VP doesn't care about the hash — they care about the payroll run, the deadline, the board meeting. Lead with the business impact and the timeline; the mechanism is appendix material.

The executive shape: IMPACT acknowledged ('I understand payroll is down'), TIMELINE given ('fix validating now, resolved in 20 minutes'), BUSINESS framing ('no data at risk; this was a policy update, not an attack'), and the FOLLOW-UP committed ('I'll send the postmortem summary by EOD').
Never: technical deep-dives unprompted, blame (theirs or yours), or 'it's complicated.' Executives buy confidence and clarity — the mechanism is available on request, not by default.
The follow-up is the relationship: the EOD summary (what happened, why, what prevents recurrence — one page) turns the escalation into trust. Executives remember the follow-through, not the fire.

example.code:
EXECUTIVE SHAPE
  impact:    acknowledged in business terms
  timeline:  explicit, short
  framing:   'policy update, not an attack' (risk stated)
  follow-up: one-page summary by EOD, committed
example.walkthrough: Draft the EOD summary for a payroll-block incident: what happened, why, recurrence prevention — one page, zero jargon.

pitfalls: Mechanism-first to executives — business terms first, always.
'It's complicated' — the confidence killer.
No follow-up committed — the escalation without the close.
lessons.try_it: Deliver the executive update for the payroll block: 60 seconds, business terms, timeline first.

lessons.title: Show, don't tell: the demo mindset
concepts: Interviews are demos: every answer is a showing, not a telling. 'I understand allowlisting' is telling; walking the hash-vs-certificate decision live is showing. Default to showing.
The demo unit is small: one concept, one example, one minute. 'Let me show you with the payroll updater...' — then the 60-second walk. Small demos land; big demos ramble.
Narrate while showing: 'I'm checking the signer first, because...' The narration turns the demo from a trick into thinking — and thinking is what's scored.
Invite the panel in: 'Want me to go deeper on the ringfence side?' Interactive demos beat monologues. The panel's questions during your demo are engagement — welcome them.

example.code:
DEMO UNIT
  one concept, one example, one minute
  narrate while showing ('I'm checking X, because...')
  invite in ('want me to go deeper on...?')
  small demos land; big demos ramble
example.walkthrough: Convert one 'telling' answer into a 'showing' demo this week: pick the payroll updater, walk it in 60 seconds, narrate every step. That's the demo muscle.

pitfalls: Telling without showing — 'I understand X' is unproven.
Big demos — one concept, one minute, or it rambles.
Monologue demos — invite the panel in.
lessons.try_it: Take your strongest 'telling' answer and rebuild it as a 60-second demo.

lessons.title: The whiteboard: thinking made visible
concepts: Whiteboard structure first, content second: draw the framework (layers, loops, trees) before filling it. Structure visible is thinking visible — the panel scores the structure.

Talk while drawing: silent whiteboarding hides the thinking the exercise exists to reveal. 'I'm starting with the layers because the question is architectural...' — narrate the choices, not just the content.
Keep it legible and labeled: boxes with names, arrows with verbs, the key insight circled at the end. The board should read like a diagram, not a ransom note.
End with the 'so what': circle the key insight and state it: '...which is why the certificate rule is the answer here.' The board without the conclusion is decoration.

example.code:
WHITEBOARD SHAPE
  structure first (layers/loops/trees)
  talk while drawing (choices narrated)
  legible + labeled (arrows with verbs)
  end: circle the insight, state the 'so what'
example.walkthrough: Practice one whiteboard exercise (the 25-person policy) timed at five minutes, narrated throughout. Record it if you can — the playback shows every silent stretch.

pitfalls: Silent drawing — the thinking is the test; show it.
Content without structure — rules before layers is the junior board.
No conclusion — circle the insight, state the so-what.
lessons.try_it: Whiteboard the triage loop from memory: six steps, labeled, narrated, 3 minutes.

lessons.title: Live triage as performance
concepts: Live triage is the technical interview's centerpiece: a real alert, your real thinking, narrated. Treat it as performance art with a method — the method is the triage loop, the art is the narration.

The performance beats: the pause ('let me look at the evidence'), the read ('the audit shows...'), the hypothesis ('so this looks like...'), the action ('the narrow fix is...'), the validation ('and I'd confirm both ways'). Five beats, every time.
Handle the stuck moment gracefully: 'I'm torn between X and Y — here's what would decide it...' The panel watches stuck-handling more than smoothness; graceful stuck beats fake smooth.
Ask for what you need: 'Can I see the prevalence column?' Questions during live triage show you know what evidence matters — they're scored as competence, not weakness.

example.code:
LIVE TRIAGE BEATS
  pause: 'let me look at the evidence'
  read: 'the audit shows...'
  hypothesis: 'so this looks like...'
  action: 'the narrow fix is...'
  validation: 'and I'd confirm both ways'
example.walkthrough: Rehearse the five beats on three different alerts until the rhythm is automatic. The rhythm carries you when the alert is unfamiliar — which is the point.

pitfalls: Fake smoothness — graceful stuck outscores it.
No questions asked — asking shows you know the evidence.
Skipping validation — the performance needs its ending.
lessons.try_it: Run a live triage on an invented alert, hitting all five beats aloud, timed.

lessons.title: Teaching as demo: the two-minute lesson
concepts: 'Teach me X in two minutes' is a demo of your teaching: the culture's core skill. Structure: hook (why it matters), core (the one idea), example (the concrete walk), close (their role in it).
The hook earns the attention: start with the story or the stake, not the definition. 'Last year a company lost 400 endpoints overnight to ransomware no signature caught...' — now they want the idea.
One idea only: the two-minute lesson that tries to teach three things teaches nothing. 'Deny-by-default means: unknown waits for approval.' One sentence, then the example that proves it.
Close with empowerment: '...and that's why your approval decisions matter.' The student leaves feeling capable, not lectured. Teaching that empowers is the Cyber Hero instinct in miniature.

example.code:
TWO-MINUTE LESSON
  hook: story/stake (20s)
  core: one idea, one sentence (20s)
  example: concrete walk (60s)
  close: empowerment (20s)
example.walkthrough: Prepare three two-minute lessons: deny-by-default, Ringfencing, least privilege. Rehearse each to the clock — the clock is the discipline.

pitfalls: Three ideas in two minutes — one idea, or it's noise.
Definition-first — hook first, always.
Lecture close — empower, don't dismiss.
lessons.try_it: Teach deny-by-default to a friend in two minutes. Ask them to repeat the one idea back.

lessons.title: Why homelab wins interviews
concepts: Homelab is the differentiator: every candidate read about allowlisting; the homelab candidate RAN a triage. 'Built, not just read' is the evidence interviewers remember — and the tiebreaker between equal resumes.

The homelab proves three things: INITIATIVE (you built it unprompted), CURIOSITY (you broke it to learn), and FLUENCY (you speak from doing, not reading). Each is scored; together they're the 'hire' signal.
It doesn't need to be big: three VMs (or one VM and a cloud trial), a documented triage exercise, a policy you wrote and tested. Specificity beats scale — one deep exercise outscores ten shallow VMs.
Document as you go: the build notes, the breakage log, the configs. The write-up IS the evidence — 'I have a homelab' without the write-up is a claim; with it, it's proof.

example.code:
WHY HOMELAB WINS
  initiative: built unprompted
  curiosity:  broke it to learn
  fluency:    speaks from doing
  scale:      specificity > size
  proof:      the write-up, not the claim
example.walkthrough: Start the write-up this week even if the lab is small: what exists, what's configured, what you've run. The document grows with the lab — and it's interview-ready from day one.

pitfalls: 'I have some VMs' — vague homelabs fail the probe.
Scale over specificity — one deep exercise beats ten idle VMs.
No write-up — the claim without the proof.
lessons.try_it: Write the one-paragraph homelab summary: what exists, what's configured, what's been run.

lessons.title: What to build: the interview-relevant lab
concepts: The triage VM: a Windows VM where you simulate blocks — install an app, change its hash (recompile/repack), watch the 'deny,' write the triage note, implement the fix. The full loop, hands-on, documented.

The policy exercise: write a three-layer allowlist policy for a fictional company (baseline, department, exceptions), then red-team it — attack your own rules, find the holes, fix them. The whiteboard exercise, rehearsed for real.
The log-reading reps: collect (or generate) deny-style logs and practice the 10-minute scan — patterns, prevalence reads, verdict trees. Speed at reading is the technical-round skill.
The teaching artifact: one two-minute lesson recorded (deny-by-default, Ringfencing, least privilege). The recording is both practice and proof — 'here's me teaching it' ends the depth question.

example.code:
LAB MENU
  triage VM:    simulate block -> triage -> fix -> validate
  policy paper: three layers, then red-team it
  log reps:     10-min scans, patterns, verdicts
  teach:        record one 2-min lesson (proof + practice)
example.walkthrough: Pick ONE from the menu and build it this week. One finished exercise with a write-up outscores a planned four-VM empire. Done beats ambitious.

pitfalls: The eternal build — one finished exercise beats the planned empire.
Undocumented tinkering — the write-up is the evidence.
Tutorial-following without breaking — break it; the breakage is the lesson.
lessons.try_it: Choose your one exercise from the menu and write its three-line plan: build, break, document.

lessons.title: Storying the homelab: build, break, lesson
concepts: The story shape: BUILD (what you set up and why — specifics: 'three VMs: DC, workstation, isolated attacker net'), BREAK (what failed — 'my first policy blocked the domain logon; the audit showed...'), LESSON (what it taught — 'inventory before enforcement, always').
Specifics are the credibility: tool names, config details, error messages, the fix. 'I configured X, it broke with Y, the logs showed Z, I fixed it by...' — the panel leans in at the specifics.

The break is the best part: every homelab breaks, and the debugging story is where the thinking shows. Don't hide the breakage — lead with it. 'Here's where it went wrong' is the most interesting sentence in the story.
Link to the role: '...which is why I'd canary every policy change here.' The homelab story that ends at the company's door is the interview answer, not just the anecdote.

example.code:
HOMELAB STORY (60s)
  build:  specifics (VMs, tools, configs)
  break:  what failed, the debugging
  lesson: what it taught (real-world link)
  close:  '...which is why I'd [practice] here'
example.walkthrough: Write three build-break-lesson stories with real specifics. Time each at 60 seconds aloud — the clock keeps them tight and the specifics keep them credible.

pitfalls: Vague builds — specifics or it didn't happen.
Hiding the breakage — the debugging IS the story.
No role link — the story should end at their door.
lessons.try_it: Write one build-break-lesson story tonight, 60 seconds, specifics throughout.

lessons.title: The no-budget lab
concepts: 'What would you build with no budget?' — the resourcefulness probe. Answer with the free tier: virtualization (free hypervisors), trial environments, open-source tooling, community resources (the free bootcamp!), documentation labs.
The no-budget lab that impresses: one VM, a documented triage exercise, a policy paper, a recorded lesson — total cost zero, total evidence high. Resourcefulness is the operator trait being tested.
Frame constraints as choices: 'With no budget I'd go deep on one VM rather than wide on four — the triage reps matter more than the topology.' Constraint-driven focus reads as maturity, not poverty.
The meta-answer: 'And I'd document everything publicly [where appropriate] — the write-ups are the portfolio.' Building in the open multiplies the evidence.

example.code:
NO-BUDGET LAB
  hypervisor: free tier | trials: vendor/community
  tooling: open-source | teaching: the free bootcamp
  depth > width: one VM, deep reps
  document: the write-ups are the portfolio
example.walkthrough: Sketch your no-budget lab on paper: the one VM, the three exercises, the write-up plan. Cost: zero. Interview value: high.

pitfalls: 'I need budget to learn' — the resourcefulness failure.
Width over depth — one deep VM beats four idle ones.
Undocumented free lab — the write-up is the portfolio.
lessons.try_it: Answer aloud: 'my no-budget lab' in 60 seconds — the VM, the exercises, the write-ups.

lessons.title: The research packet
concepts: Build the research packet before every round: the company (mission, recent news, the interviewer's role and background where public), the role (every responsibility in the posting, mapped to your stories), and the panel (who you'll meet, what they own). One page, reviewed the morning of.

The company research has a purpose: two genuine observations to deploy — 'I saw the Series F news; how does that change the roadmap for the team?' Research without a question is trivia; research WITH a question is engagement.

The role mapping is the core: every bullet of the posting gets a story or a skill beside it. Gaps get the learning plan, not the silence — 'light on X, here's how I'd close it in 30 days.' Prepared honesty beats discovered gaps.

Panel awareness: know who owns what (the manager owns the team, the engineer owns the depth probe, the cross-functional owns the collaboration story). Tailor the emphasis per interviewer — same you, right spotlight.

example.code:
RESEARCH PACKET (1 page)
  company: 2 genuine observations + questions
  role:    every bullet mapped to story/skill
  gaps:    learning plan, stated upfront
  panel:   who owns what; tailor the spotlight
example.walkthrough: Build a one-page research packet for a real role this week — company, role mapping, gaps-with-plans, panel. The discipline transfers to every future interview.

pitfalls: Trivia research — observations need questions attached.
Gap silence — prepared honesty beats discovered gaps.
Same pitch to everyone — tailor the spotlight per interviewer.
lessons.try_it: Map a real job posting: every bullet gets a story, skill, or learning plan.

lessons.title: Scheduling and confirmation discipline
concepts: Scheduling is the first impression: respond fast (within hours), offer specific windows ('Tue/Thu afternoons, or Friday morning'), and confirm everything in writing — date, time WITH timezone, format (video/onsite), who you'll meet, what to bring.

The confirmation reply is a template: 'Confirming [day, date] at [time, timezone] via [format]. I'll meet [names]. I'll bring [items]. Looking forward to it — [name].' Every ambiguity killed before it breeds.

Day-before: re-check the time (timezone!), the link or address, the parking/arrival details, the panel names. Day-of: arrive (or join) 10 minutes early, tech checked, water nearby, notes ready but not read from.
Rescheduling: as early as possible, with apology and new windows offered — never the bare cancellation. Life happens; the handling is the signal.

example.code:
SCHEDULING DISCIPLINE
  respond: within hours, specific windows
  confirm: date, time+TZ, format, panel, bring-list
  day-before: recheck everything (timezone!)
  day-of: 10 min early, tech checked
  reschedule: early, apologetic, new windows offered
example.walkthrough: Write your confirmation template now and save it — future-you under interview stress will thank present-you.

pitfalls: Timezone ambiguity — always state the zone explicitly.
Vague availability — 'whenever' is not a window.
Silent rescheduling — early, apologetic, with new windows.
lessons.try_it: Draft your confirmation reply template and save it for reuse.

lessons.title: Follow-up that actually follows up
concepts: The thank-you: within 24 hours, per interviewer (or per panel with individual touches), specific not generic — reference something THEY said ('your point about the wave process...'), reconnect it to your fit ('...is exactly how I ran...'), and close with enthusiasm.
The structure: gratitude (one line), the specific callback (theirs + yours), the enthusiasm (genuine, one line). Three paragraphs, five minutes to write, remembered for weeks.

Beyond the thanks: the follow-up cadence — if they gave a timeline, respect it; if it passes, one polite nudge ('checking in — still very interested'). Never more than two nudges without a response; silence is an answer you respect.

The value-add follow-up (rare, powerful): 'I kept thinking about your X question — here's the article/resource I mentioned.' Used once, it demonstrates the thinking continues after the interview. Used often, it's noise.

example.code:
THANK-YOU SHAPE
  gratitude: one line, genuine
  callback:  THEIR point + YOUR fit (specific)
  enthusiasm: one line, real
  cadence:   respect timelines; two nudges max
  value-add:  once, rare (the mentioned resource)
example.walkthrough: Draft a thank-you note for a real (or imagined) interviewer with a genuine callback. Specificity is the whole game — 'great conversation' is the failure mode.

pitfalls: Generic thanks — 'great speaking with you' says nothing.
Nudge spam — two unanswered nudges, then stop.
No follow-up at all — the interview ends at the door.
lessons.try_it: Write the three-paragraph thank-you: gratitude, specific callback, enthusiasm.

lessons.title: References and the final stretch
concepts: References: line them up BEFORE you need them — three people who've seen your work, warned and briefed ('they may call this week; the role is X; the stories I'd love you to tell are...'). Surprise reference calls produce surprise answers.

Brief each reference: the role, the key themes (reliability, triage skill, customer empathy — the role's language), and permission to be specific. A briefed reference is an advocate; an unbriefed one is a witness.

The offer stage: respond to offers with gratitude and a timeline ('thank you — I'd like to review carefully; can I respond by Friday?'). Never accept on the spot, never negotiate before the written offer, never use an offer as a weapon — all in the compensation domain.

Background and logistics: have the documents ready (ID, work authorization, the employment history with exact dates). The final stretch fails on paperwork more often than on merit — be the candidate with the folder ready.

example.code:
REFERENCE READINESS
  lineup: 3 work-witnesses, warned early
  brief:  role + themes + 'tell this story'
  offer:  gratitude + timeline (never on-the-spot)
  folder:  ID, authorization, exact-date history ready
example.walkthrough: Line up your three references this week and brief the top one — even before you need them. The folder-ready candidate wins the final stretch.

pitfalls: Surprise references — warn and brief, always.
On-the-spot acceptance — gratitude plus a timeline.
Paperwork scramble — the folder is ready before the ask.
lessons.try_it: List your three references and draft the briefing message for one.

lessons.title: Know your number before they ask
concepts: Research before the process: market ranges for the role, level, and market (Orlando IT infrastructure/support bands differ from national) — from postings, public salary data, and network conversations. Arrive with a researched range, not a feeling.

Your number has three parts: the TARGET (what the research says you're worth), the FLOOR (below which you walk — know it privately), and the PACKAGE view (base is one line of many). Decide all three before the first money question.

The early-question deflection: 'I'd like to understand the full scope of the role first — what's the budgeted range for the position?' Turning the question around first is standard and professional — whoever names a number first anchors.

Never lie about current/prior compensation: it's verifiable, it's the fastest trust-killer, and in many jurisdictions the question itself is restricted. 'I'd prefer to focus on the value for this role' is the honest deflection.

example.code:
YOUR NUMBER (decided upfront)
  target:  researched market value
  floor:   private walk-away (know it, don't state it)
  package: base + bonus + equity + benefits + growth
  anchor:  let them name the range first
example.walkthrough: Research the market band for your target role this week and write down target/floor/package-view. The candidate with the researched number negotiates; the candidate with the feeling hopes.

pitfalls: Naming a number first — let them anchor the range.
Lying about prior comp — verifiable, trust-killing.
Base-only thinking — the package is the compensation.
lessons.try_it: Write your target, floor, and package-view for the target role. Private document.

lessons.title: The total package lens
concepts: Base salary is one line: bonus (and its realistic payout), equity/options (vesting, value), benefits (health costs, retirement match, PTO), schedule (remote/hybrid, flexibility), and growth (the raise/promotion path) all price into the decision.

Price the benefits: a 6% 401(k) match is real money; premium-free health coverage can be worth five figures; three extra PTO weeks have a value. The lower-base/higher-benefits offer often wins the math.

Growth is compensation: the role with the promotion path in 18 months out-earns the flat higher base within two years. Ask about it explicitly — 'what does growth from this role look like?' — and price the answer.

Non-salary levers for the final close: start date, signing bonus, review timeline ('six-month compensation review tied to milestones'), professional development budget, title. When base won't move, the package still can.

example.code:
PACKAGE MATH
  base + bonus(realistic) + equity(vested value)
  benefits priced: match, health, PTO
  growth: the 18-month promotion path
  levers: signing, review date, dev budget, title
example.walkthrough: Build the package comparison sheet: columns for each offer, rows for every line (base, bonus, equity, match, health, PTO, growth). Decisions by math, not by base-salary headline.

pitfalls: Headline-base decisions — run the full package math.
Ignoring vesting — unvested equity is a promise, not pay.
Forgetting growth — the 18-month path is compensation.
lessons.try_it: Price one benefits line (health or 401k match) in dollars for a real offer or posting.

lessons.title: Negotiating without burning the offer
concepts: The posture: grateful, enthusiastic, collaborative — 'I'm excited about this offer and I want to make it work.' Negotiation is joint problem-solving, not adversarial haggling. The relationship starts here.

The ask shape: specific, justified, packaged — 'Based on [research/market data], I was targeting [number]. Is there flexibility to [specific ask]? I'm enthusiastic about the role and the team.' One round of asks, bundled, not dribbled.
Justify with market, not need: 'the market data shows...' beats 'I need...' every time. Need-based negotiating invites judgment; market-based invites agreement.

Know the walk-away and mean it: the floor you set privately is real. A graceful decline ('the package isn't the right fit right now; I hope we can reconnect') preserves the relationship — and sometimes the offer improves. Desperation discounts you; dignity compounds.

example.code:
NEGOTIATION SHAPE
  posture: grateful + enthusiastic + collaborative
  ask:     specific, justified (market), bundled
  rounds:   one bundled round, not dribbles
  floor:    private, real, honored gracefully
example.walkthrough: Script your negotiation ask (one bundled round, market-justified) for a hypothetical offer. Rehearse it aloud — the calm, grateful tone is the skill.

pitfalls: Adversarial haggling — the relationship starts at the offer.
Need-based justification — market data, not personal need.
Dribbled asks — bundle once, then decide.
lessons.try_it: Write your one-round bundled ask script: specific number, market justification, grateful close.

lessons.title: The written offer and the fine print
concepts: Nothing is real until it's written: the verbal offer is the celebration; the written offer is the agreement. Review every line — title, base, bonus terms, equity/vesting, start date, reporting line — against what was discussed. Discrepancies get clarified in writing before signing.

Read the fine print: non-compete/non-solicit clauses (scope, duration, geography — in Florida these have teeth), IP assignment, arbitration clauses, benefits waiting periods. Unknown clauses get questions; concerning ones get a professional review.

The acceptance: written, warm, clear — 'I'm delighted to accept...' with the key terms restated. Then: close the other processes gracefully (the decline that preserves relationships), notify your references, and prepare the start.
Between signing and starting: stay engaged (the pre-boarding), keep learning (the role's tech), and don't coast the notice period — the reputation you carry in is built in these weeks.

example.code:
WRITTEN-OFFER CHECKLIST
  terms: title, base, bonus, equity, date, reports-to
  fine print: non-compete, IP, arbitration, waiting periods
  acceptance: written, warm, terms restated
  after: close other processes gracefully; pre-board
example.walkthrough: Build your offer-review checklist now (terms + fine print) and keep it with the research packet. The signed offer deserves the same discipline as the interview.

pitfalls: Verbal-offer reliance — written terms or it didn't happen.
Skipping the fine print — non-competes have teeth.
Ghosting other processes — graceful closes preserve the network.

lessons.title: The first week: learn before you touch
concepts: Week one is reconnaissance, not action: learn the queue, the audit rhythms, the team's triage habits, the escalation paths, the unwritten rules. The new hire who changes things in week one breaks things in week one.

Map the operation: who owns what, where the docs live (and which are stale), how tickets flow, what 'done' looks like here. Ask the questions now — 'new hire questions' are free for about two weeks, then they cost credibility.
Earn trust in small units: take the well-scoped tickets, close them cleanly, document what you did. Trust is the currency that later buys you the big changes — spend week one earning it.
Find your onboarding buddy (or be the one who asks for one): the peer who'll answer the 'dumb' questions privately. Every team has the lore that isn't written down — the buddy is how you get it.

example.code:
WEEK ONE
  learn: queue, rhythms, habits, paths, lore
  map:   owners, docs (stale ones too), ticket flow
  earn:  small tickets, closed cleanly, documented
  buddy:  the unwritten rules, via a peer
example.walkthrough: Write your week-one learning checklist now (queue, audit, team habits, escalation paths, doc map). Arrive with the questions; leave week one with the map.

pitfalls: Week-one changes — learn before you touch.
Skipping the 'dumb' questions — they're free for two weeks.
No buddy — the lore isn't in the docs.

lessons.title: The first ticket
concepts: Your first ticket is a performance: pick (or accept) something well-scoped, work it visibly, communicate as you go, and close it with the full discipline — evidence, narrow fix, double validation, the note. The team is watching how you work, not just what you close.

Over-communicate on ticket one: 'Starting on X, here's my read, here's the plan, here's the fix, here's the validation.' The narration that felt heavy in the interview is exactly right in week one — it shows the method.

Ask before the point of no return: 'I'm about to [irreversible action] — does that match how the team does it?' The question costs nothing; the wrong irreversible action costs the trust you just earned.
Close it like a senior: the note written for the next person, the follow-up scheduled if needed, the pattern logged if it's a repeater. First impressions compound — make ticket one the template.

example.code:
FIRST TICKET
  scoped:  well-bounded, visible
  narrated: over-communicate the method
  checked:  ask before irreversible actions
  closed:   the note, the validation, the pattern log
example.walkthrough: Rehearse your first-ticket narration now: the status updates you'd post at each stage. The habit starts before the ticket exists.

pitfalls: Silent working — week one is the time to narrate.
Unilateral irreversible actions — ask first, always.
Thin close — ticket one sets your documentation standard.
lessons.try_it: Write the status-update script for a hypothetical first ticket: start, read, plan, fix, validate.

lessons.title: Becoming the teammate
concepts: Teammate is a verb: share what you learn (the wiki edit, the channel post, the 'hey, I found...'), credit generously ('Maria's note on the wave process saved me an hour'), and volunteer for the unglamorous work early — queue triage, doc updates, the Friday shift.

Feedback flows both ways from week two: ask for it explicitly ('what should I do more/less of?') and receive it without defense. The new hire who asks for feedback gets more of it — and improves faster than the one who waits.
Learn everyone's name and role in week one — including the adjacent teams (the SOC, the infra team, the support leads). The org chart is the map; the relationships are the territory.
Protect the culture you were hired into: the blameless postmortem, the teaching instinct, the customer-first reflex. You were hired for the fit — embody it from day one, and extend it.

example.code:
TEAMMATE (verb)
  share:   wiki edits, channel posts, findings
  credit:  generously, specifically, publicly
  volunteer: the unglamorous work, early
  feedback: ask explicitly, receive without defense
example.walkthrough: List three unglamorous contributions you'll volunteer for in month one. The teammate reputation is built in the small work.

pitfalls: Knowledge hoarding — share everything you learn.
Waiting for feedback — ask explicitly, early.
Culture coasting — embody the fit you were hired for.
lessons.try_it: Write your 'ask for feedback' message: specific, humble, actionable.

lessons.title: The 90-day plan, executed
concepts: The 90-day plan from the interview becomes the operating plan: 30 (learn the operation, earn trust, no big changes), 60 (contribute — own a domain, ship one improvement), 90 (lead something measurable). Review it with your manager in week one and calibrate.
The calibration conversation: 'Here's the 90-day plan I described in the interview — how does it map to what you need?' The manager's answer IS the real plan; yours was the draft. Adapt eagerly.
Track visibly: a simple doc (goals, progress, blockers) shared with your manager. Visibility isn't bragging — it's the trust infrastructure. Managers support what they can see.

At 90 days: the self-review before the review — what shipped, what you learned, what's next. Bring it to the conversation. The employee who evaluates themselves honestly earns the honest evaluation — and the growth that follows.

example.code:
90-DAY OPERATING PLAN
  30: learn + earn trust (calibrate w/ manager wk 1)
  60: contribute (own a domain, ship one win)
  90: lead something measurable
  track: visible doc (goals/progress/blockers)
  review: self-review first, then the conversation
example.walkthrough: Write the 90-day plan doc now (draft): the 30/60/90 with your real guesses. You'll calibrate it in week one — arriving with the draft is the signal.

pitfalls: The interview plan, forgotten — calibrate it, don't shelve it.
Invisible progress — track visibly, share the doc.
Waiting for the review — self-review first.

labs.title: Deny by default, hands on
labs.objective: Walk the allowlist decision end to end: verify a file's hash, record the verdict, and state what stays denied.
steps: Deny-by-default means nothing runs until it is proven known-good. This lab makes that muscle memory.
Open the Terminal tab for this bootcamp — every command below runs there.

Say out loud: 'Everything not on the allowlist stays denied.' That sentence is the whole philosophy.

labs.success_message: Lab complete — you verified before trusting, recorded the verdict, and restated the policy. That is the allowlist workflow in miniature.

labs.title: Read the log like an analyst
labs.objective: Extract signal from ~/logs/app.log: errors, warnings, and counts — the way a SOC analyst triages.

Type exactly: grep ERROR ~/logs/app.log — every error line, nothing else

Type exactly: grep WARN ~/logs/app.log — warnings are tomorrow's errors
Type exactly: tail -3 ~/logs/app.log — the most recent lines tell you how the story ends (so far)

checks.hint: Run `grep ERROR ~/logs/app.log`. You should see the cache connection error.
Run `wc -l ~/logs/app.log`. Six lines total -- two errors, one warning, three info.

labs.success_message: Lab complete — you filtered, counted, and read the tail. Two errors, one warning, latest line a timeout. That is a triage summary.

labs.title: Name resolution before escalation
labs.objective: Work a 'can't reach the share' ticket the operator way: DNS first, reachability second, escalate with evidence.
steps: Half of 'network is down' tickets are name resolution. Prove which half this is.

Type exactly: echo "DNS OK, ping OK — escalating to share permissions with evidence" — write the handoff note

checks.hint: Run `dig fileserver.corp.lan` and confirm an A record comes back.
Run `ping fileserver.corp.lan`. You want 0% packet loss.

labs.success_message: Lab complete — DNS resolves, host answers. You escalated the right ticket (permissions) instead of the wrong one (network). That judgment is what interviewers score.

labs.title: Process inventory and the odd one out
labs.objective: Build a process baseline and practice the 'what doesn't belong' read.
steps: You can't spot abnormal until you can state normal. Capture the baseline first.

Identify the process that doesn't belong on a standard user build. (Hint: a server process on a workstation.)
Type exactly: echo "SUSPICIOUS: node server.js PID 1337 — investigate before kill" — document, don't destroy
Rule: inventory first, hypotheses second, action last. Killing first destroys the evidence you need.

checks.hint: Run `ps`. Find the PID that stands out — 1337 is not a coincidence.
Run the echo command from step 4 with the word SUSPICIOUS in it.

labs.success_message: Lab complete — baseline captured, anomaly documented, no evidence destroyed. node server.js on PID 1337 gets investigated, not summarily killed.

labs.title: Correlate two logs, tell one story
labs.objective: Practice cross-log correlation: the access log shows WHAT the user saw, the app log shows WHY.
steps: One log is a symptom. Two logs are a diagnosis.
Type exactly: grep 504 ~/logs/access.log — when did the user see the failure?
Type exactly: grep ERROR ~/logs/app.log — what was the app doing around then?
Line the timestamps up: 09:15:02 (user-facing 504) against 09:14:47 and 09:20:02 (app errors)
Type exactly: echo "ROOT CAUSE: app timeout on /api/report, not network" — commit to a diagnosis in one line

checks.hint: Run `grep 504 ~/logs/access.log`.
Run `grep ERROR ~/logs/app.log` and find the timeout.

labs.success_message: Lab complete — user-facing 504 at 09:15, app timeouts bracketing it. Diagnosis: application, not network. Stated in one line, backed by two logs.

labs.title: The elevation decision
labs.objective: Practice the Elevation Control judgment call: investigate the request window, then approve or deny with written reasoning.
steps: Elevation requests are trust decisions. Trust comes from evidence, not from the requester's job title.

Weigh it: errors in the window + an unfamiliar requester = deny until verified. A clean window + a known admin = approve with logging.
Type exactly: echo "DECISION: DENY elevation — errors in request window, verify requester identity first" — write the decision down

checks.hint: Run `grep -n ERROR ~/logs/app.log` to see the failures in the request window.
