simulations.title: The blocked installer
simulations.brief: Monday 9:04 AM. A sales rep needs client-demo-3.1.msi installed before a 10:00 call. The endpoint blocked it: deny-by-default, unknown file. The rep is escalating. Work it like the real thing.

steps.symptom: User: 'The installer won't run. I need it for a client call in an hour. Just turn off the blocking.'
evidence:
BLOCKED: client-demo-3.1.msi — verdict: unknown (not on allowlist)
User: sales-rep-04 | Host: LT-1188 | Requested: disable protection
options: Disable the protection so the installer runs — the client call matters more
Verify the file's hash against the vendor's published value, then route an allowlist request through the proper channel
Tell the user to find the installer somewhere else online
Ignore the ticket until after the client call
steps.explain: Disabling protection for convenience is exactly what deny-by-default exists to prevent. The operator path: verify the hash (proves the file is what it claims to be), then use the legitimate allowlist workflow. Speed comes from process, not from bypasses.

steps.symptom: The hash matches the vendor's published value. The file is genuine — but it is still not on the allowlist.
evidence:
SHA-256 matches vendor published digest
File: client-demo-3.1.msi — genuine, unmodified
options: Run it now — verified genuine means safe to execute
Submit the allowlist request with the hash evidence and give the user a realistic ETA
Copy it to a USB and run it on an unmanaged machine
Add it to the allowlist yourself with no record
steps.explain: Genuine does not mean approved — the allowlist is a policy decision, not a technical one. The request goes through the channel with the evidence attached, and the user gets an honest ETA. Shadow IT (USB, unrecorded approvals) is how breaches start.

steps.symptom: The user asks: 'Why can't I just install things like on my home PC?'
evidence: Deny-by-default: only known-good executes. Home PCs run allow-by-default — the model that lets ransomware run.
options: Agree that the policy is too strict and promise to raise it
Explain the tradeoff in one sentence: the same control blocking this installer is what stops ransomware, then offer the allowlist path
Quote the policy manual at them
End the call
steps.explain: Cyber Hero service culture: respect the frustration, explain the why in plain language, and always leave the user with a path forward. 'This is the control that stops ransomware on your machine too' turns a blocker into a believer.

simulations.debrief: You held the deny-by-default line under time pressure, verified instead of bypassing, used the real workflow, and turned a frustrated user into an informed one. That is the whole job in one ticket.

simulations.title: The 4 PM share outage
simulations.brief: 4:02 PM. Three users in accounting can't reach \\fileserver\shared. One of them is loud. The last change window was 2 PM. Work it like the real thing.

steps.symptom: Three users, same share, same symptom: 'Windows cannot access \\fileserver\shared.' Started around 3:45 PM.
evidence:
3 users, 1 share, onset ~15:45
Last change window: 14:00 (firewall policy push)
options: Reboot the file server — fastest path
Check name resolution and reachability from an affected host first (dig, ping), then check what changed at 14:00
Reinstall the network drivers on all three machines
Tell users to work locally until tomorrow
steps.explain: Scope first: three users on one share points at the share or the path to it, not three machines. DNS and ping take sixty seconds and split the problem space — then the 14:00 firewall push becomes the prime suspect, not a coincidence.

steps.symptom: DNS resolves. Ping answers 0% loss. The share is reachable — but access is denied.
evidence:
dig fileserver.corp.lan → A record OK
ping → 0% loss
SMB: 'Access is denied' (not 'path not found')
options: The network is fine — close the ticket
Access denied with good connectivity means permissions or share config: check the 14:00 firewall policy push and the share ACLs
Replace the users' network cables
Flush DNS on the server
steps.explain: 'Access is denied' after good DNS and ping is a permissions story, not a network story. And the 14:00 firewall policy push lines up with the 15:45 onset — always check what changed. Evidence narrows; guessing widens.

steps.symptom: The 14:00 push tightened SMB rules and dropped the accounting group's access. You have the root cause.
evidence:
14:00 firewall policy push: SMB rule scoped to wrong group
Accounting lost access at ~15:45 (policy propagation delay)
options: Roll back the entire firewall push immediately
Scope the fix: correct the SMB rule to include the accounting group, verify with one user, then confirm with all three
Leave it — security is more important than access
Email everyone to reboot
steps.explain: Fix with a scalpel: correct the mis-scoped rule, verify on one host, then confirm the cluster. Rolling back the whole push would reopen whatever it was closing. And you communicate the cause — users forgive outages faster when they understand them.

simulations.debrief: You scoped before acting, split network from permissions with two cheap tests, checked what changed, and fixed with a scalpel. That is infrastructure troubleshooting at interview standard.

simulations.title: The elevation request
simulations.brief: A developer requests elevation for deploy-helper-v9.exe — an unsigned binary from a personal file share. 'I need it for today's release.' You own the decision. Work it like the real thing.

steps.symptom: Elevation request: deploy-helper-v9.exe, unsigned, sourced from a personal file share. Requester: dev team, release today.
evidence:
Binary: deploy-helper-v9.exe | Signed: NO | Source: personal file share
Justification: 'needed for today's release'
options: Approve — the release is today and the team is blocked
Deny until verified: unsigned + personal share is two red flags; ask for the signed build from the official pipeline
Approve but only for one hour
Ignore it — someone else will decide
steps.explain: Two red flags (unsigned, unofficial source) outweigh one deadline. Elevation is a trust decision: the fix is not 'no' forever, it is 'bring me the signed build from the pipeline and this is a five-minute approval.' Pressure does not change the evidence standard.

steps.symptom: The developer pushes back: 'The pipeline is broken, that's why I'm using this copy. Everyone does it.'
evidence:
Claim: 'everyone does it'
Pipeline status: unknown — unverified claim
options: Approve — if everyone does it, blocking one person is pointless
Hold the line: verify the pipeline claim yourself, and offer to expedite the official build instead
Approve and report the developer
Escalate to the developer's manager immediately
steps.explain: 'Everyone does it' is unverified and irrelevant to this binary. The operator move: check the pipeline claim directly (sixty seconds), and convert the conflict into help — 'let me get your official build expedited.' Firm on policy, generous with assistance.

steps.symptom: You check: the pipeline is fine. The 'broken pipeline' was a misconfigured local runner on the developer's machine.
evidence:
Official pipeline: HEALTHY
Developer issue: local runner misconfiguration
options: Approve the unsigned binary anyway — you already spent time on this
Deny the unsigned binary, document the decision with the evidence, and help fix the local runner
Say nothing and let the request expire
Approve and note 'exception' with no detail
steps.explain: The evidence closed the case: the premise was wrong, so the request stays denied — documented with the hash, the source, and the verification. And you still help: fixing the runner unblocks the release legitimately. Deny the binary, unblock the person.

simulations.debrief: You treated elevation as a trust decision, held the evidence standard under pressure, verified claims instead of accepting them, and helped while denying. That is Elevation Control judgment at senior-interview level.

simulations.title: The Cyber Hero call
simulations.brief: The phone queue shows a small-business owner, third call this week, 'my computers keep blocking my payroll software.' Frustration is high. You are the Cyber Hero on this call. Work it like the real thing.

steps.symptom: Caller, audibly frustrated: 'This is the third time I've called. Your software keeps blocking my payroll app and my people can't get paid.'
evidence:
3rd contact this week | Issue: payroll app blocked
Business impact: payroll delayed
options: Explain that the blocking is working as designed and they should be grateful
Acknowledge the impact first ('I hear you — payroll blocked is urgent'), then gather the facts: app name, version, when it started
Transfer to tier 2 immediately
Offer a discount
steps.explain: Cyber Hero rule one: lead with the human impact, not the technology. 'Payroll blocked is urgent — let's fix it right now' de-escalates in one sentence. Then facts: app name, version, onset. Empathy first is not softness — it is what gets you the details you need.

steps.symptom: The app is payroll-pro-2.8.exe. It updated Tuesday — the same day the blocking started. The hash changed with the update.
evidence:
payroll-pro-2.8.exe updated Tuesday
Hash changed → fell off the allowlist
Blocking started: Tuesday (matches)
options: Whitelist the whole payroll vendor folder permanently to stop future calls
Verify the new hash against the vendor, submit the allowlist update, and explain the Tuesday connection to the caller
Disable blocking on their machines until payroll is done
Tell them to downgrade to 2.7
steps.explain: The Tuesday connection is the diagnosis: updates change hashes, changed hashes leave the allowlist. Verify-then-allowlist is the fix; whitelisting whole folders or disabling protection trades one payroll delay for an open door. And telling the caller WHY (the update changed the fingerprint) prevents the fourth call.

steps.symptom: The allowlist is updated. Payroll runs. The caller asks: 'How do I stop this happening every update?'
options: Say updates will always break and there's nothing to do
Explain the update cycle (new version → new hash → re-verify), offer to set up the vendor's auto-update channel if available, and summarize what was fixed in one plain sentence
Give them your direct number for next time
End the call quickly — queue is long
steps.explain: Close the loop: teach the pattern (updates change fingerprints), offer the durable fix (managed update channel), and summarize plainly. The caller hangs up understanding their own system better — that is the Cyber Hero standard, and it is what turns a frustrated third call into a loyal customer.

simulations.debrief: Empathy first, evidence always, plain-language explanations, and a durable fix instead of a shortcut. You handled the human and the technical at the same time — that is the service culture interviewers are listening for.

consoleSims.title: Default-deny the workstation
consoleSims.brief: A new workstation joins the fleet. Policy: deny-by-default. Set the INPUT chain to DROP everything, then open exactly one hole: HTTPS (TCP 443) from the corporate network 10.0.0.0/8.

tasks.instruction: Add an ACCEPT rule: chain INPUT, TCP port 443, source 10.0.0.0/8.
tasks.hint: Use the Add rule form: CHAIN=INPUT, PROTOCOL=tcp, PORT=443, SOURCE=10.0.0.0/8, ACTION=ACCEPT.

tasks.instruction: Set the INPUT chain default policy to DROP.
tasks.hint: Open Default policies and set INPUT to DROP. Everything not explicitly allowed must fall through to deny.

consoleSims.debrief: One explicit allow, everything else denied. That is deny-by-default in its purest form — the same philosophy behind application allowlisting, expressed in firewall rules.

consoleSims.title: Allowlist the patch server
consoleSims.brief: Patch Tuesday: endpoints must reach the patch server at 10.20.30.40 on TCP 8443. There is also a stale rule allowing ALL TCP from anywhere — a hole from a forgotten troubleshooting session. Fix both.

tasks.instruction: Add an ACCEPT rule: chain INPUT, TCP port 8443, source 10.20.30.40.
tasks.hint: Add the precise rule first: INPUT, tcp, 8443, source 10.20.30.40, ACCEPT. Precision before cleanup.

tasks.instruction: Find and delete the stale rule that ACCEPTs all TCP from 0.0.0.0/0.
tasks.hint: Look at the Rules table for the overly broad ACCEPT rule (source 0.0.0.0/0) and delete it. Any delete of a rule counts — make sure it's the right one.

consoleSims.debrief: You added the precise allow and removed the forgotten hole. Stale permissive rules are how 'temporary' becomes 'breach' — auditing for them is a habit, not an event.

consoleSims.title: Segment the endpoint VLAN
consoleSims.brief: The flat network has to go. Create VLAN 20 for endpoints, assign access port Gi1/0/12 to it, and save the running config.

tasks.hint: At the CLI, type: create vlan 20
Type: save-config — unsaved changes die with the next reboot.

consoleSims.debrief: Segmented: endpoints on VLAN 20, config saved. Segmentation is deny-by-default for the network — a compromised host can only reach its own broadcast domain.

consoleSims.title: Quarantine the suspect host
consoleSims.brief: SOC flagged the host on Gi1/0/7: possible compromise. Quarantine it NOW: create VLAN 99 (quarantine), move Gi1/0/7 into it, and save. Speed matters — but so does not breaking the switch.

tasks.hint: Type: assign port Gi1/0/7 vlan 99 — the suspect host is now isolated at layer 2.
Type: save-config. A quarantine that vanishes on reboot is not a quarantine.

consoleSims.debrief: Quarantined at layer 2 in under a minute, config saved. You contained the blast radius before investigating — containment first, forensics second. That ordering is the interview answer.

terminalMissions.title: Verify before you allowlist
terminalMissions.brief: Helpdesk ticket #4182: a user downloaded agent-setup-4.2.exe and wants it allowlisted. Policy is deny-by-default: NOTHING gets approved without a verified hash. The vendor published SHA-256 03de3a29ed578edc18100f62291feff8b27fe053a41c498ab033c03dbfd2b327. Prove the file matches before anyone approves it.
objectives: Confirm it matches the published value exactly

checks.hint: In the Terminal tab, run `sha256sum agent-setup-4.2.exe`. The output digest must match the published value character for character.

terminalMissions.success_message: Hash matches — the installer is genuine. Allowlist it with confidence. Everything else stays denied: that is deny-by-default working as designed.

terminalMissions.title: Pull the denial lines
terminalMissions.brief: The SOC bridge starts in ten minutes and they want evidence, not adjectives: every ERROR line from the application log at ~/logs/app.log. Pull them now.

checks.hint: In the Terminal tab, run `grep ERROR ~/logs/app.log`. You want the lines containing ERROR, nothing else.

terminalMissions.success_message: Evidence first — exact denial lines in hand. That is what the SOC needs, not a paraphrase.

terminalMissions.title: Is it DNS or is it down?
terminalMissions.brief: Ticket: 'Can't reach the file share — is the network down?' Rookie move: escalate immediately. Operator move: check name resolution first, then reachability. The share is fileserver.corp.lan.

checks.hint: Run `dig fileserver.corp.lan`. Look for the ANSWER SECTION — a returned A record means DNS is fine.
Run `ping fileserver.corp.lan`. Zero percent packet loss means the host is reachable — the problem is elsewhere.

terminalMissions.success_message: DNS resolves and the host answers. Not a network outage — escalate with evidence, pointing at permissions or the share service itself.

terminalMissions.title: Inventory before you touch
terminalMissions.brief: A user reports 'the laptop is slow.' Policy: inventory running processes BEFORE changing anything, so you have a baseline. List every process.

checks.hint: Run `ps` (or `ps aux`). Read every line — one of these processes does not belong on a standard build.

terminalMissions.success_message: Baseline captured: bash, app.py, and an unexpected node server.js. You now have evidence to ask about — remediation starts from inventory, never from guesses.

terminalMissions.title: Offboard with a verified list
terminalMissions.brief: Offboarding ticket: a contractor's last day was Friday. Before disabling anything, verify exactly which accounts exist on this box. Dump the account database.

checks.hint: Run `cat /etc/passwd`. Every line is an account — read them all before you disable anything.

terminalMissions.success_message: Account list verified: root plus the candidate account. Offboarding starts from a verified list, never from memory.

terminalMissions.title: Check the window before you approve
terminalMissions.brief: Elevation Control queued requests from 09:14 this morning. Approving blind is how incidents happen: pull the ERROR lines WITH line numbers from ~/logs/app.log and read what was failing in that window.
objectives: Extract ERROR lines with line numbers from ~/logs/app.log

checks.hint: Run `grep -n ERROR ~/logs/app.log`. The -n flag adds line numbers — you need to cite exactly where each failure sits.

terminalMissions.success_message: Two errors at 09:14:47 and 09:20:02, both around the elevation window. Now your approve/deny decision is evidence-backed — that is what the interview panel wants to hear.

terminalMissions.title: Verify the blast radius
terminalMissions.brief: A Ringfence-style policy limits app.py to its own directory. Before you sign off on the policy, verify what the app actually does — read ~/app.py and confirm it stays in its lane.
objectives: Read ~/app.py and confirm its behavior is contained

checks.hint: Run `cat ~/app.py`. Read the whole file — you are looking for anything that reaches outside its own directory (network, shell, file writes).

terminalMissions.success_message: Contained: a greeting function and a loop, no network, no shell, no writes. The policy matches reality — Ringfencing is deny-by-default applied to behavior, and you verified it by reading code.

terminalMissions.title: Two logs, one story
terminalMissions.brief: The 504 on /api/report at 09:15 — app failure or network failure? Correlate: pull the 504 line from ~/logs/access.log AND the matching timeout from ~/logs/app.log. One story, two sources.
objectives: Find the 504 in the access log

checks.hint: Run `grep 504 ~/logs/access.log`. Find the exact timestamp of the failed request.
Run `grep timeout ~/logs/app.log`. Match it against the 504 timestamp — cause lives in the application log.

terminalMissions.success_message: Correlated: 504 at 09:15:02, app timeout at 09:20:02 on the same endpoint. The app hung — not the network. Two log lines, one story: that is triage.

sections.heading: Graph vocabulary
items: node — any entity tracked in the model (user, host, IP, domain, file hash, vulnerability)
edge — a labeled relationship between two nodes (logged into, resolved to, downloaded)
degree — number of edges on a node; high-degree nodes are attacker highways
centrality — how much traffic or how many paths flow through a node
directed edge — a relationship with a direction (A downloaded FROM B)
security graph — the living model of your whole environment as nodes and edges
attack graph — the subgraph of exploitable paths to your targets
knowledge graph — threat-intel indicators linked to campaigns and actors

sections.heading: Attack-graph playbook
items: inventory first — you cannot graph what you have not discovered
model flaws AND misconfigs as exploit edges
compute shortest paths to the crown jewels
find the choke point (highest betweenness on those paths)
break the path: patch, segment, or remove the edge
re-scan and re-run the graph to prove the path is gone
never trust yesterday's graph — redeployments redraw the map

sections.heading: Zero Trust + graphs
items: never trust, always verify — re-evaluate every access decision
assume breach — treat unexpected edges as hostile until proven otherwise
microsegmentation — allow-list approved edges, alert on new ones
ReBAC — policies are path queries on the identity graph
continuous verification — device/location/behavior edges change, trust follows
anomalous edge — a first-seen connection between strangers is the classic signal

sections.heading: ML detection vocabulary
items: Supervised learning — learns from labeled examples; strong on known threats, blind to novel ones
Unsupervised learning — finds structure without labels; clustering and dimensionality reduction
Anomaly detection — models 'normal' and flags deviations; the workhorse for novel threats
UEBA — user and entity behavior analytics: per-user baselines plus peer-group comparison
Feature engineering — encoding raw logs into model inputs (login velocity, rare processes, domain entropy)
Concept drift — model decay as attacker behavior and legitimate traffic shift over time

sections.heading: Detection metrics
items: Precision — of all flagged alerts, how many were real
Recall — of all real attacks, how many were flagged
Threshold tuning — sliding the decision cutoff trades precision against recall
Alert fatigue — when false positives train analysts to ignore the queue
DGA — domain generation algorithm; detected via character entropy of domain names

sections.heading: Agent and LLM security
items: Direct prompt injection — attacker input overrides app instructions (OWASP LLM01:2025, the #1 LLM risk)
Indirect prompt injection — hidden instructions inside retrieved data (email, web, docs)
Jailbreak — defeating the model's own safety policy; distinct from hijacking app behavior
Tool poisoning — malicious tool descriptions or metadata steer an agent to misuse its tools (MCP ecosystem risk)
Insecure output handling — executing or trusting model output without validation
Least-privilege tools — grant each tool only the scope its task requires

sections.heading: Adversarial ML and governance
items: Evasion — perturbing inputs at inference time to dodge a classifier
Poisoning — corrupting training data to corrupt the model
Extraction — querying a model to steal its behavior or parameters
MITRE ATLAS — knowledge base of adversarial ML tactics and techniques
Red-teaming and evals — adversarial testing of AI systems before deployment
Human-in-the-loop — required approval for high-impact or irreversible agent actions
SOAR — security orchestration, automation and response; automate enrichment, gate containment

glossary.def: Default-deny execution control: only explicitly approved applications, scripts, and installers may run.
Default-allow model: everything runs except recognized-bad items — the window zero-days live in.
Deny-by-default posture: unknown code, devices, or connections are refused unless explicitly approved.
Containment applied on top of allowlisting; restricts what a permitted app may do across app-to-app, file, registry, and network dimensions.
Agent mode that catalogs applications and dependencies and auto-builds policies before enforcement; temporarily disables file blocking.
Temporary mode that pauses file blocking for installs — must be tightly scoped and time-boxed.
Grants specific approved applications admin rights for standard users — just-in-time, per-app, time-boxed — without standing admin rights.
An elevated or trusted process spawning another tool (e.g., PowerShell) to inherit its privileges — countered by ringfencing the elevated process.
Device and path policy: USB approved by serial, user, file type, time, and encryption; unapproved devices do not connect.
Centrally managed host firewall; rules by port, source IP, and dynamic ACLs; egress allowlisting pins apps to approved destinations.
Zero Trust Network Access: per-session, per-application brokered connections (commonly over port 443) with no open inbound ports — deny-by-default for network access.
Portal queue where end-user software requests arrive for admin review and decision.
Real-time audit showing what was allowed or denied across endpoints — and why; the evidence layer for triage.
One-button cloud VDI sandbox launched from an approval request; logs AV flags, canary-file access, and registry/system changes.
24/7/365 US-based managed detection and response team; validates alerts, isolates hosts, acts on customer runbooks; ~60-second average response.
Design and operate as if the attacker already has a foothold — least privilege, containment, and monitoring everywhere.
Attacks that hijack trusted built-in tools (Word, PowerShell) instead of dropping malware — defeated by behavior containment, not signatures.
Scoped, ticketed, tested changes with validation and rollback — emergency speed never cancels the process.
A node in an attack graph representing a system or weakness, connected by edges that represent steps an attacker could take between them.
How central a node is to paths through the graph (for example, betweenness: how many shortest paths cross it).
The most valuable assets in the environment (customer data, finance systems, source code): what attack paths are measured against.
A labeled connection between two nodes, representing a relationship such as 'logged into' or 'resolved to'.
A graph of threat indicators (IPs, domains, hashes) linked to campaigns, actors, and each other through shared infrastructure.
The practice of mapping relationships in data to reveal hidden associations; rooted in Euler's 1736 graph theory, 1970s paper link charts, and post-2001 intelligence work.
A segment of the network so small that its allowed communications can be enumerated as a graph of approved edges.
An entity in the graph: a user, host, IP address, domain, file, or vulnerability.
Access control where policy is evaluated by traversing relationships on a graph (for example: user reports_to manager who owns the resource's project).
A machine-learning model that operates directly on graph structure to classify nodes or subgraphs, for example labeling attack vs normal behavior.
Monitoring user and entity behavior by modeling their normal relationship patterns and flagging structural anomalies.
ML trained on labeled examples; classifies new inputs into known categories.
ML approach that models normal behavior and flags statistically rare deviations.
Turning raw telemetry into numeric model inputs, e.g. login velocity or domain entropy.
Share of flagged alerts that were real; the false-positive economics of the queue.
Share of real attacks the detector flagged; the miss rate's complement.
Decay of model performance as the data distribution shifts over time.
Attacker-crafted instructions that override an LLM application's intended behavior; direct (user input) or indirect (retrieved data).
Crafted input that defeats an LLM's own safety policy or refusal behavior.
Malicious tool descriptions or metadata that manipulate an AI agent into misusing its tools.
Failing to validate LLM output before acting on it, e.g. executing generated commands.
Adversarial ML technique: perturbing inputs to cross a classifier's decision boundary.
Adversarial Threat Landscape for AI Systems; MITRE's knowledge base of AI attack tactics.
Security orchestration, automation and response; playbooks that enrich automatically and gate containment on humans.
Required human approval before high-impact or irreversible automated actions.
